abstract: An artificial neural network is developed to recognize spatio-temporal bipolar patterns associatively. The function of a formal neuron is generalized by replacing multiplication with convolution, weights with transfer functions, and thresholding with nonlinear transform following adaptation. The Hebbian learn(cid:173) ing rule and the delta learning rule are generalized accordingly, resulting in the learning of weights and delays. The neural network which was first developed for spatial patterns was thus generalized for spatio-temporal patterns. It was tested using a set of bipolar input patterns derived from speech signals, showing robust classification of 30 model phonemes.
originalAbstract: An artificial neural network is developed to recognize spatio-temporal bipolar patterns associatively. The function of a formal neuron is generalized by replacing multiplication with convolution, weights with transfer functions, and thresholding with nonlinear transform following adaptation. The Hebbian learn(cid:173) ing rule and the delta learning rule are generalized accordingly, resulting in the learning of weights and delays. The neural network which was first developed for spatial patterns was thus generalized for spatio-temporal patterns. It was tested using a set of bipolar input patterns derived from speech signals, showing robust classification of 30 model phonemes.

paragraphs: The paper extends an associative neural network from recognizing spatial patterns to recognizing patterns that also unfold over time. Its inputs are bipolar patterns, with two opposite signal values. The motivating application is phoneme classification, where the ordering and timing of speech-derived signals can be part of the pattern to recognize.

To accommodate time, the authors change the operations performed by a formal neuron. Convolution replaces multiplication, and transfer functions replace individual connection weights. A nonlinear transformation following adaptation takes the place of thresholding. These changes give a connection a temporal response, allowing the network to represent more than the instantaneous strength of an input.

The authors also generalize Hebbian and delta learning rules so that learning adjusts delays as well as weights. This connects the temporal representation directly to the learning process. Tests using bipolar patterns derived from speech signals show robust classification of 30 model phonemes. The stated result supports the usefulness of extending both neuron behavior and learning rules when the recognition task depends on patterns across time.
summary.tldr: A neural network learns connection strengths and delays to recognize temporal bipolar patterns, demonstrating robust classification of 30 model phonemes.

title: An Artificial Neural Network for Spatio-Temporal Bipolar Patterns: Application to Phoneme Classification

abstract: DCPS (the Distributed Connectionist Production System) is a neural network with complex dynamical properties. Visualizing the energy landscapes of some of its component modules leads to a better intuitive understanding of the model, and suggests ways in which its dynamics can be controlled in order to improve performance on difficult cases.
originalAbstract: DCPS (the Distributed Connectionist Production System) is a neural network with complex dynamical properties. Visualizing the energy landscapes of some of its component modules leads to a better intuitive understanding of the model, and suggests ways in which its dynamics can be controlled in order to improve performance on difficult cases.

paragraphs: The paper examines the dynamics of the Distributed Connectionist Production System, or DCPS. Its central concern is how this neural network behaves as its internal state changes. The abstract describes those dynamics as complex, motivating a way to understand the behavior of component modules more intuitively.

The authors use visualizations of the modules' energy landscapes. Such a view organizes possible network states according to an energy description, helping make the relationship between state and dynamics easier to reason about. The analysis focuses on some component modules, giving a way to inspect parts of the system rather than treating its behavior as an undifferentiated whole.

The visualizations also suggest ways to control the dynamics when the system encounters difficult cases. Their value is therefore both explanatory and practical: understanding how a module behaves can inform changes intended to improve performance. The stated contribution is an intuitive analysis that points toward control strategies; the abstract presents these strategies as suggestions arising from the landscape view.
summary.tldr: Visualizing energy landscapes of DCPS modules helps explain their dynamics and suggests ways to improve behavior on difficult cases.

title: Analyzing the Energy Landscapes of Distributed Winner-Take-All Networks

abstract: In order to detect the presence and location of immunoglobu(cid:173) lin (Ig) domains from amino acid sequences we built a system based on a neural network with one hidden layer trained with back propagation. The program was designed to efficiently identify proteins exhibiting such domains, characterized by a few localized conserved regions and a low overall homology. When the National Biomedical Research Foundation (NBRF) NEW protein sequence database was scanned to evaluate the program's performance, we obtained very low rates of false negatives coupled with a moderate rate of false positives.
originalAbstract: In order to detect the presence and location of immunoglobu(cid:173) lin (Ig) domains from amino acid sequences we built a system based on a neural network with one hidden layer trained with back propagation. The program was designed to efficiently identify proteins exhibiting such domains, characterized by a few localized conserved regions and a low overall homology. When the National Biomedical Research Foundation (NBRF) NEW protein sequence database was scanned to evaluate the program's performance, we obtained very low rates of false negatives coupled with a moderate rate of false positives.

paragraphs: This paper develops a neural network to detect immunoglobulin domains in proteins from their amino acid sequences. The task includes both deciding whether such a domain is present and finding its location. The network has one hidden layer and is trained through backpropagation, making sequence-based domain recognition a learned classification problem.

The difficulty is that the relevant proteins have low overall similarity. Their useful shared characteristics are concentrated in a few conserved regions rather than spread uniformly across the sequence. A detector therefore needs to recognize localized evidence of related structure even when the rest of the protein does not closely resemble other examples.

The authors evaluate the program by scanning the NBRF NEW protein sequence database. They report very few false negatives together with a moderate number of false positives. In practical terms, the detector rarely misses the domains it is meant to find, but some flagged sequences are incorrect matches. The reported result describes a sensitive screening approach with imperfect selectivity.
summary.tldr: A neural sequence detector finds immunoglobulin domains with very few misses but a moderate rate of false alarms.

title: A Neural Network to Detect Homologies in Proteins

paragraphs: This paper presents Dyna, a family of architectures that combines trial-and-error learning, world-model learning, and planning. The system alternates between interacting with the actual environment and operating on a learned forward model of it. That model represents how the world changes, allowing planning and direct experience to contribute within a single ongoing process.

Dyna draws on approximate dynamic programming. Conventional dynamic programming determines behavior from a complete task model; Dyna connects related methods to a model that is being learned. The supplied text emphasizes incremental planning through consideration of individual actions, making the approach suitable for execution-time computation with uncertain or incomplete models.

The paper reports results for Dyna-AHC and Dyna-Q. In a navigation task, a simple Dyna-AHC system simultaneously learns through trial and error, builds a world model, and plans optimal routes using the evolving model. Dyna-Q, based on Q-learning, is shown to adapt readily to changing environments. The contribution is an architecture in which learning about the world and using that knowledge to improve control proceed together.
summary.tldr: Dyna integrates reinforcement learning, learned world models, and incremental planning into a single process for adaptive control.

title: Integrated Modeling and Control Based on Reinforcement Learning and Dynamic Programming

abstract: A method for transforming performance evaluation signals distal both in space and time into proximal signals usable by supervised learning algo(cid:173) rithms, presented in [Jordan & Jacobs 90], is examined. A simple obser(cid:173) vation concerning differentiation through models trained with redundant inputs (as one of their networks is) explains a weakness in the original architecture and suggests a modification: an internal world model that encodes action-space exploration and, crucially, cancels input redundancy to the forward model is added. Learning time on an example task, cart(cid:173) pole balancing, is thereby reduced about 50 to 100 times.

A simple obser(cid:173) vation concerning differentiation through models trained with redundant inputs (as one of their networks is) explains a weakness in the original architecture and suggests a modification: an internal world model that encodes action-space exploration and, crucially, cancels input redundancy to the forward model is added. paragraphs: The paper examines a learning method that converts performance feedback arising far from an action, in both space and time, into signals usable by supervised learning. Such a conversion matters when a controller receives an evaluation of an eventual outcome but needs guidance about how to change the actions that produced it.

The authors identify a weakness in the original architecture by considering differentiation through a model trained with redundant inputs. They propose adding an internal world model that represents exploration in the action space and, crucially, cancels the redundancy presented to the forward model. The modification addresses how the model supplies learning guidance.

On the example task of balancing a cart-pole, the revised architecture reduces learning time by approximately 50 to 100 times. This is a result for the stated example task. Its conceptual importance is that the usefulness of predictive models for learning depends on how their inputs are organized and how differentiation through those models translates outcome evaluations into actionable training signals.
summary.tldr: Removing forward-model input redundancy through an added world model reduces cart-pole learning time by roughly 50 to 100 times.

title: Fast Learning with Predictive Forward Models

abstract: A model of the hippocampus is presented which forms rapid self -orga(cid:173) nized representations of input arriving via the perforant path, performs recall of previous associations in region CA3, and performs comparison of this recall with afferent input in region CA 1. This comparison drives feedback regulation of cholinergic modulation to set appropriate dynamics for learning of new representations in region CA3 and CA 1. The network responds to novel patterns with increased cholinergic mod(cid:173) ulation, allowing storage of new self-organized representations, but responds to familiar patterns with a decrease in acetylcholine, allowing recall based on previous representations. This requires selectivity of the cholinergic suppression of synaptic transmission in stratum radiatum of regions CA3 and CAl, which has been demonstrated experimentally.

This comparison drives feedback regulation of cholinergic modulation to set appropriate dynamics for learning of new representations in region CA3 and CA 1. The network responds to novel patterns with increased cholinergic mod(cid:173) ulation, allowing storage of new self-organized representations, but responds to familiar patterns with a decrease in acetylcholine, allowing recall based on previous representations. This requires selectivity of the cholinergic suppression of synaptic transmission in stratum radiatum of regions CA3 and CAl, which has been demonstrated experimentally.

paragraphs: This paper models how the hippocampus could coordinate learning new patterns with recalling familiar ones. The network rapidly organizes representations of incoming signals and retrieves previously learned associations. Its central mechanism uses a comparison between incoming information and recalled information to regulate which kind of processing the network emphasizes.

The model assigns distinct roles to hippocampal regions. Input arrives through the perforant path, region CA3 recalls associations, and region CA1 compares that recall with the incoming signal. The comparison controls feedback affecting acetylcholine, a chemical modulator of neural activity. Novel patterns increase cholinergic modulation and favor storage of new representations; familiar patterns decrease it and favor retrieval using existing representations.

This arrangement connects recognition of novelty directly to the dynamics needed for learning. The proposed mechanism requires cholinergic suppression of synaptic transmission to be selective within particular parts of CA3 and CA1. The abstract states that this selectivity has experimental support. Thus, the model combines self-organization and associative memory through a specific feedback mechanism tied to a stated biological property.
summary.tldr: A hippocampal model uses comparisons between incoming and recalled patterns to regulate acetylcholine and shift between learning and retrieval.

title: A model of the hippocampus combining self-organization and associative memory function

abstract: We give necessary and sufficient conditions for uniqueness of the support vector solution for the problems of pattern recognition and regression estimation, for a general class of cost functions. We show that if the solution is not unique, all support vectors are necessarily at bound, and we give some simple examples of non-unique solu(cid:173) tions. We note that uniqueness of the primal (dual) solution does not necessarily imply uniqueness of the dual (primal) solution. We show how to compute the threshold b when the solution is unique, but when all support vectors are at bound, in which case the usual method for determining b does not work.

We show that if the solution is not unique, all support vectors are necessarily at bound, and we give some simple examples of non-unique solu(cid:173) tions. We note that uniqueness of the primal (dual) solution does not necessarily imply uniqueness of the dual (primal) solution. We show how to compute the threshold b when the solution is unique, but when all support vectors are at bound, in which case the usual method for determining b does not work.

paragraphs: The paper investigates when a support vector machine has a unique solution. It covers both pattern recognition and regression estimation for a general class of cost functions. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions, providing a characterization of uniqueness rather than only a condition that guarantees it in some cases.

They show that non-uniqueness requires all support vectors to be at their bounds and give examples of non-unique solutions. The direction of this statement matters: having every support vector at a bound does not by itself establish non-uniqueness. They also explain that uniqueness in the primal optimization problem need not imply uniqueness in the dual, or vice versa.

A further contribution concerns the threshold parameter b. When all support vectors are at their bounds, the usual method for determining this threshold fails. The authors show how to compute it when the solution is nevertheless unique. This addresses a concrete consequence of the uniqueness analysis, distinguishing an exceptional computational case from the existence of multiple solutions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes SVM solution uniqueness and explains how to compute the threshold in a unique all-at-bound case.

title: Uniqueness of the SVM Solution
Using the Nyström Method to Speed Up Kernel Machines

abstract: The human figure exhibits complex and rich dynamic behavior that is both nonlinear and time-varying. Effective models of human dynamics can be learned from motion capture data using switching linear dynamic system (SLDS) models. We present results for human motion synthe(cid:173) sis, classification, and visual tracking using learned SLDS models. Since exact inference in SLDS is intractable, we present three approximate in(cid:173) ference algorithms and compare their performance. In particular, a new variational inference algorithm is obtained by casting the SLDS model as a Dynamic Bayesian Network. Classification experiments show the superiority of SLDS over conventional HMM's for our problem domain.
originalAbstract: The human figure exhibits complex and rich dynamic behavior that is both nonlinear and time-varying. Effective models of human dynamics can be learned from motion capture data using switching linear dynamic system (SLDS) models. We present results for human motion synthe(cid:173) sis, classification, and visual tracking using learned SLDS models. Since exact inference in SLDS is intractable, we present three approximate in(cid:173) ference algorithms and compare their performance. In particular, a new variational inference algorithm is obtained by casting the SLDS model as a Dynamic Bayesian Network. Classification experiments show the superiority of SLDS over conventional HMM's for our problem domain.

paragraphs: Human motion changes over time in ways that are both nonlinear and varied. This paper models that behavior with switching linear dynamic systems learned from motion-capture data. The approach represents motion through linear dynamics together with switches between them, providing a way to describe richer behavior than a single linear system could express.

The authors present results for generating motion, classifying it, and tracking it visually. A central computational obstacle is that exact inference in the switching model is intractable. They therefore introduce three approximate inference algorithms and compare their performance. One is a new variational algorithm derived by expressing the switching system as a dynamic Bayesian network.

In the reported classification experiments, switching linear models outperform conventional hidden Markov models for the human-motion domain studied. The finding supports the usefulness of the model in that setting. The work combines a representation of changing motion dynamics with practical inference methods, connecting the model's expressive structure to several motion-processing tasks.
summary.tldr: Switching linear models learned from motion capture support synthesis, tracking, and classification, outperforming conventional HMMs in the reported classification experiments.

title: Learning Switching Linear Models of Human Motion

abstract: Alexander Gray Computer Science Dept. Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh, PA 15213 agray@cs.cmu.edu This paper is about non-approximate acceleration of high dimensional nonparametric operations such as k nearest neighbor classiﬁers and the prediction phase of Support Vector Machine classiﬁers. We attempt to exploit the fact that even if we want exact answers to nonparametric queries, we usually do not need to explicitly ﬁnd the datapoints close to the query, but merely need to ask questions about the properties about that set of datapoints. This offers a small amount of computational lee- way, and we investigate how much that leeway can be exploited. For clarity, this paper concentrates on pure k-NN classiﬁcation and the pre- diction phase of SVMs. We introduce new ball tree algorithms that on real-world datasets give accelerations of 2-fold up to 100-fold compared against highly optimized traditional ball-tree-based k-NN. These results include datasets with up to 106 dimensions and 105 records, and show non-trivial speedups while giving exact answers.

paragraphs: This paper develops faster algorithms for high-dimensional nonparametric classification while preserving exact answers. It concentrates on k-nearest-neighbor classification and the prediction stage of support vector machines. The motivation is that computing the final answer may require less information than explicitly identifying every nearby data point.

The authors exploit a distinction between finding a set of relevant points and determining properties of that set. If the classification query only needs those properties, there may be room to reduce computation without approximating the result. They investigate that opportunity through new algorithms based on ball trees.

On real-world datasets, the reported accelerations range from twofold to one hundredfold compared with highly optimized traditional ball-tree-based nearest-neighbor methods. The results include high-dimensional datasets and retain exact answers. The contribution is therefore an empirical demonstration that changing what a search explicitly resolves can yield meaningful speedups. The reported range describes the tested datasets, rather than a guaranteed acceleration for every classification query.
summary.tldr: New ball-tree algorithms preserve exact classification answers while reporting twofold to one hundredfold speedups on tested real-world datasets.

title: New Algorithms for Efficient High Dimensional Non-parametric Classification

abstract: We address the problem of identifying specific instances of a class (cars) from a set of images all belonging to that class. Although we cannot build a model for any particular instance (as we may be provided with only one "training" example of it), we can use information extracted from observ- ing other members of the class. We pose this task as a learning problem, in which the learner is given image pairs, labeled as matching or not, and must discover which image features are most consistent for matching in- stances and discriminative for mismatches. We explore a patch based representation, where we model the distributions of similarity measure- ments defined on the patches. Finally, we describe an algorithm that selects the most salient patches based on a mutual information criterion. This algorithm performs identification well for our challenging dataset of car images, after matching only a few, well chosen patches.

paragraphs: The task is to identify particular cars among images that all depict cars. A specific instance may have only one training image, leaving too little evidence to build a dedicated model for that car. The paper instead learns what makes images match by observing other members of the same class.

Training examples are image pairs labeled as matching or nonmatching. The learner looks for features that remain consistent across matching instances while distinguishing mismatches. Images are represented through patches, and the method models distributions of similarity measurements on those patches. This makes the learning problem about the usefulness of local comparisons for identity.

An algorithm then selects informative patches using a mutual information criterion. The authors report good identification performance on their challenging car-image dataset after comparing only a few selected patches. The result supports the idea that experience with a class can guide instance matching when examples of a particular instance are scarce, and that carefully chosen local evidence can be sufficient for useful performance in this setting.
summary.tldr: Learning from matching and nonmatching car images identifies a few informative patches that support instance recognition with scarce examples.

title: Learning Hyper-Features for Visual Identification

abstract: Co-training is a method for combining labeled and unlabeled data when examples can be thought of as containing two distinct sets of features. It has had a number of practical successes, yet previous theoretical analyses have needed very strong assumptions on the data that are unlikely to be satisfied in practice. In this paper, we propose a much weaker “expansion” assumption on the underlying data distribution, that we prove is sufficient for iterative cotraining to succeed given appropriately strong PAC-learning algorithms on each feature set, and that to some extent is necessary as well. This expansion assumption in fact motivates the iterative nature of the original co-training algorithm, unlike stronger assumptions (such as independence given the label) that allow a simpler one-shot co-training to succeed. We also heuristically analyze the effect on performance of noise in the data. Predicted behavior is qualitatively matched in synthetic experiments on expander graphs.

paragraphs: Co-training combines labeled and unlabeled examples when each example has two distinct sets of features. Although the approach has worked in practice, previous theoretical explanations relied on strong assumptions about the data. This paper seeks a weaker foundation that better explains why the original method repeatedly exchanges information between the two feature sets.

The authors introduce an expansion assumption on the underlying data distribution. They prove that it is sufficient for iterative co-training to succeed when each feature set has an appropriately strong PAC-learning algorithm. They also establish that expansion is necessary to some extent, without claiming it is an unrestricted requirement for every successful use of co-training.

The assumption helps explain the value of iteration: stronger conditions, such as independence given the label, can support success with a single round. The paper also gives a heuristic analysis of noise and tests its predictions using synthetic experiments on expander graphs. The experiments qualitatively match the predicted behavior, supporting the analysis without turning the heuristic noise discussion into a general theorem.
summary.tldr: A weaker expansion assumption provides conditional guarantees for iterative co-training and helps explain why repeated interaction between feature sets matters.

title: Co-Training and Expansion: Towards Bridging Theory and Practice

abstract: Survival in the natural world demands the selection of relevant visual cues to rapidly and reliably guide attention towards prey an d predators in cluttered environments. We investigate whether our visu al system selects cues that guide search in an optimal manner. We formall y obtain the optimal cue selection strategy by maximizing the signal to noise ratio (S N R) between a search target and surrounding distractors. This optimal strategy successfully accounts for several phenom ena in visual search behavior, including the effect of target-distracto r discriminability, uncertainty in target's features, distractor heterogenei ty, and linear separability. Furthermore, the theory generates a new predict ion, which we verify through psychophysical experiments with human subj ects. Our results provide direct experimental evidence that humans sel ect visual cues so as to maximize S N R between the targets and surrounding clutter.

paragraphs: Visual search requires selecting cues that distinguish a target from surrounding clutter. This paper asks whether the human visual system makes that selection optimally. The authors define an optimal strategy by maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio between the target and distractors, turning a question about attention into a specific mathematical objective.

The resulting strategy accounts for several established aspects of search behavior. These include how easily targets can be distinguished from distractors, uncertainty about target features, variation among distractors, and linear separability. Addressing these effects through one objective gives the theory a common explanation for several influences on cue selection.

The theory also produces a new prediction, which the authors verify in psychophysical experiments with human participants. They interpret the findings as direct experimental evidence that people select visual cues to maximize target-versus-clutter signal-to-noise ratio. The result ties the proposed optimality criterion to measured behavior, supporting it as an explanation of cue choice in the studied visual search setting.
summary.tldr: A signal-to-noise-maximizing cue selection theory explains visual search effects and receives support from a verified human behavioral prediction.

title: Optimal cue selection strategy

abstract: Recent experimental results suggest that dendritic and back-propagating spikes can influence synaptic plasticity in different ways [1]. In this study we investigate how these signals could temporally interact at dendrites leading to changing plasticity properties at local synapse clusters. Similar to a previous study [2], we employ a differential Hebbian plasticity rule to emulate spike-timing dependent plasticity. We use dendritic (D-) and back-propagating (BP-) spikes as post-synaptic signals in the learning rule and investigate how their interaction will influence plasticity. We will analyze a situation where synapse plasticity characteristics change in the course of time, depending on the type of post-synaptic activity momentarily elicited. Starting with weak synapses, which only elicit local D-spikes, a slow, unspecific growth process is induced. As soon as the soma begins to spike this process is replaced by fast synaptic changes as the consequence of the much stronger and sharper BP-spike, which now dominates the plasticity rule. This way a winner-take-all-mechanism emerges in a two-stage process, enhancing the best-correlated inputs. These results suggest that synaptic plasticity is a temporal changing process by which the computational properties of dendrites or complete neurons can be substantially augmented.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how different postsynaptic signals could change the learning behavior of local groups of synapses over time. It focuses on dendritic spikes and spikes that propagate back from the cell body. The authors use both signals in a differential Hebbian learning rule that emulates spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

The studied process begins with weak synapses that produce only local dendritic spikes. At this stage, synaptic growth is slow and relatively unspecific. Once the cell body starts firing, stronger and sharper back-propagating spikes dominate the learning rule. The same modeled system then undergoes faster synaptic changes because the postsynaptic signal driving learning has changed.

This transition produces a two-stage winner-take-all mechanism that strengthens the best-correlated inputs. The result suggests that synaptic learning characteristics need not remain fixed: they can shift with the activity generated as learning proceeds. The authors propose that such changing plasticity could substantially expand the computational properties of dendrites or whole neurons, presenting this as an implication of the modeled mechanism.
summary.tldr: A model shows how a shift from dendritic to back-propagating spikes can turn slow synaptic growth into selective competition.

title: Temporally changing synaptic plasticity

abstract: We introduce a method to automatically improve character models for a handwritten script without the use of transcriptions and using a minimum of document speciﬁc training data. We show that we can use searches for the words in a dictionary to identify portions of the document whose transcriptions are unambiguous. Using templates extracted from those regions, we retrain our character prediction model to drastically improve our search retrieval performance for words in the document.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to improve character models for a handwritten script without requiring supplied transcriptions. It also aims to use very little training data specific to the document. The practical objective is better word retrieval: finding occurrences of words within the handwriting using a character model adapted to that document.

The method begins with searches for dictionary words. Those searches identify portions of the document whose transcriptions can be determined unambiguously. The system then extracts templates from those regions and uses them to retrain its character prediction model. Search therefore supplies document-specific training evidence that can improve subsequent search.

The authors report a drastic improvement in word-search retrieval after this retraining. The central contribution is the connection between searching and adaptation: confidently identified text regions become material for improving the model that interprets the handwriting. Although supplied transcriptions are unnecessary, the method still uses a dictionary and the unambiguous regions found through it. The stated outcome concerns retrieval performance for words in the document.
summary.tldr: Dictionary searches identify reliable handwriting examples that retrain character models and substantially improve word retrieval.

title: Searching for Character Models

abstract: Consider the problem of joint parameter estimation and prediction in a Markov random field: i.e., the model parameters are estimated on the basis of an initial set of data, and then the fitted model is used to perform prediction (e.g., smoothing, denoising, interpolation) on a new noisy observation. Working in the computation-limited setting, we analyze a joint method in which the same convex variational relaxation is used to construct an M-estimator for fitting parameters, and to perform approximate marginalization for the prediction step. The key result of this paper is that in the computation-limited setting, using an inconsistent parameter estimator (i.e., an estimator that returns the "wrong" model even in the infinite data limit) is provably beneficial, since the resulting errors can partially compensate for errors made by using an approximate prediction technique. En route to this result, we analyze the asymptotic properties of M-estimators based on convex variational relaxations, and establish a Lipschitz stability property that holds for a broad class of variational methods. We show that joint estimation/prediction based on the reweighted sum-product algorithm substantially outperforms a commonly used heuristic based on ordinary sum-product. 1 Keywords: Markov random fields; variational method; message-passing algorithms; sum-product; belief propagation; parameter estimation; learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies a two-stage use of Markov random fields: estimate parameters from training data, then use the fitted model to predict from a new noisy observation. When computation is limited, the prediction stage uses approximate marginalization. The authors ask how parameter estimation should be designed when that approximation is part of the eventual prediction procedure.

Their joint method uses the same convex variational relaxation for parameter fitting and prediction. The key result is that an inconsistent estimator, which approaches the wrong model even with unlimited data, can be provably beneficial in this setting. Its parameter errors can partially offset errors introduced by approximate prediction, improving the combined procedure.

A joint method based on reweighted sum-product substantially outperforms a common ordinary sum-product heuristic. The lesson is specific to computation-limited prediction: estimating model parameters and choosing an inference approximation can be more effective when treated as a coupled problem.
summary.tldr: Under limited computation, biased parameter estimation can improve prediction by partially compensating for approximate-inference errors.

title: Estimating the wrong Markov random field: Benefits in the computation-limited setting

abstract: We propose a method for reconstruction of human brain states directly from functional neuroimaging data. The method extends the traditional multivariate regression analysis of discretized fMRI data to the domain of stochastic functional measurements, facilitating evaluation of brain responses to naturalistic stimuli and boosting the power of functional imaging. The method searches for sets of voxel timecourses that optimize a multivariate functional linear model in terms of Rsquare-statistic. Population based incremental learning is used to search for spatially distributed voxel clusters, taking into account the variation in Haemodynamic lag across brain areas and among subjects by voxel-wise non-linear registration of stimuli to fMRI data. The method captures spatially distributed brain responses to naturalistic stimuli without attempting to localize function. Application of the method for prediction of naturalistic stimuli from new and unknown fMRI data shows that the approach is capable of identifying distributed clusters of brain locations that are highly predictive of a specific stimuli.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for reconstructing brain states from functional neuroimaging measurements, with an emphasis on responses to naturalistic stimuli. It extends multivariate regression from discretized fMRI observations to stochastic functional measurements. This allows the analysis to work with voxel timecourses as functional data within the regression model.

The method searches for spatially distributed sets of voxel timecourses that optimize a multivariate functional linear model according to an R-squared criterion. Population-based incremental learning carries out that search. Voxel-wise nonlinear registration aligns stimuli with the fMRI data while accounting for variation in haemodynamic delay across brain regions and across people.

The aim is to capture distributed patterns that predict the stimulus, without trying to assign a function to a single localized brain area. Applied to previously unknown fMRI data, the method identifies distributed clusters that are highly predictive of particular stimuli. The result supports combining functional regression, spatial search, and timing alignment to recover predictive information spread across multiple brain locations.
summary.tldr: Functional regression with voxel-wise timing alignment identifies distributed fMRI patterns that predict naturalistic stimuli in unseen data.

title: Predicting Brain States from fMRI Data: Incremental Functional Principal Component Regression

abstract: Neural activity is non-stationary and varies across time. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) have been used to track the state transition among quasi-stationary discrete neural states. Within this context, independent Poisson models have been used for the output distribution of HMMs; hence, the model is incapable of tracking the change in correlation without modulating the firing rate. To achieve this, we applied a multivariate Poisson distribution with correlation terms for the output distribution of HMMs. We formulated a Variational Bayes (VB) inference for the model. The VB could automatically determine the appropriate number of hidden states and correlation types while avoiding the overlearning problem. We developed an efficient algorithm for computing posteriors using the recursive relationship of a multivariate Poisson distribution. We demonstrated the performance of our method on synthetic data and a real spike train recorded from a songbird.

Within this context, independent Poisson models have been used for the output distribution of HMMs; hence, the model is incapable of tracking the change in correlation without modulating the firing rate. To achieve this, we applied a multivariate Poisson distribution with correlation terms for the output distribution of HMMs. We formulated a Variational Bayes (VB) inference for the model. The VB could automatically determine the appropriate number of hidden states and correlation types while avoiding the overlearning problem. We demonstrated the performance of our method on synthetic data and a real spike train recorded from a songbird.

paragraphs: Neural activity changes over time, and hidden Markov models describe this through transitions between discrete states that are approximately stable for a while. A common version models each neuron's spike counts independently using Poisson distributions. That choice cannot represent changes in correlations while keeping firing rates unchanged, potentially overlooking an important aspect of changing population activity.

The authors replace the independent output model with a multivariate Poisson distribution containing correlation terms. Hidden states can consequently describe patterns of dependence as well as firing activity. They formulate variational Bayesian inference that can automatically determine suitable numbers of hidden states and correlation types while avoiding overlearning.

The paper also develops an efficient posterior-computation algorithm using a recursive property of the multivariate Poisson distribution. Demonstrations involve synthetic data and a real songbird spike train. The central contribution is a state-transition model that can track changes in neural coordination without requiring those changes to appear as shifts in firing rate.
summary.tldr: A correlated Poisson hidden Markov model tracks changing neural dependencies alongside firing activity.

title: Extracting State Transition Dynamics from Multiple Spike Trains with Correlated Poisson HMM

abstract: Correlations between spike counts are often used to analyze neural coding. The noise is typically assumed to be Gaussian. Yet, this assumption is often inappropriate, especially for low spike counts. In this study, we present copulas as an alternative approach. With copulas it is possible to use arbitrary marginal distributions such as Poisson or negative binomial that are better suited for modeling noise distributions of spike counts. Furthermore, copulas place a wide range of dependence structures at the disposal and can be used to analyze higher order interactions. We develop a framework to analyze spike count data by means of copulas. Methods for parameter inference based on maximum likelihood estimates and for computation of Shannon entropy are provided. We apply the method to our data recorded from macaque prefrontal cortex. The data analysis leads to three significant findings: (1) copula-based distributions provide better fits than discretized multivariate normal distributions; (2) negative binomial margins fit the data better than Poisson margins; and (3) a dependence model that includes only pairwise interactions overestimates the information entropy by at least 19% compared to the model with higher order interactions.

paragraphs: Neural coding studies often examine correlations between spike counts while assuming Gaussian noise. That assumption can fit poorly when counts are low. This paper introduces a copula-based framework, allowing the distribution of each individual count to be chosen separately from the structure describing dependence between counts.

The framework accommodates marginal distributions such as Poisson and negative binomial distributions, along with a broad range of dependence structures. It can also represent interactions involving more than pairs of variables. The authors provide maximum-likelihood parameter-inference methods and a way to calculate Shannon entropy, connecting distribution fitting with measurements of uncertainty.

On recordings from macaque prefrontal cortex, copula-based distributions fit better than discretized multivariate normal distributions, and negative binomial margins fit better than Poisson margins. A model restricted to pairwise interactions overestimates entropy by at least 19% relative to the model with higher-order interactions. In these data, both the choice of individual count distributions and the inclusion of richer dependencies materially affect the analysis.
summary.tldr: Copula models better fit the studied neural spike counts and reveal substantial entropy differences when higher-order dependencies are included.

title: Modeling Short-term Noise Dependence of Spike Counts in Macaque Prefrontal Cortex

abstract: The inter-subject alignment of functional MRI (fMRI) data is important for improving the statistical power of fMRI group analyses. In contrast to existing anatomically-based methods, we propose a novel multi-subject algorithm that derives a functional correspondence by aligning spatial patterns of functional connectivity across a set of subjects. We test our method on fMRI data collected during a movie viewing experiment. By cross-validating the results of our algorithm, we show that the correspondence successfully generalizes to a secondary movie dataset not used to derive the alignment.
originalAbstract: The inter-subject alignment of functional MRI (fMRI) data is important for improving the statistical power of fMRI group analyses. In contrast to existing anatomically-based methods, we propose a novel multi-subject algorithm that derives a functional correspondence by aligning spatial patterns of functional connectivity across a set of subjects. We test our method on fMRI data collected during a movie viewing experiment. By cross-validating the results of our algorithm, we show that the correspondence successfully generalizes to a secondary movie dataset not used to derive the alignment.

paragraphs: Combining fMRI measurements across people requires a way to match corresponding cortical locations. This alignment matters for the statistical power of group analyses. The paper proposes finding correspondence through functional connectivity, using patterns of functional relationships across the cortex as the information that guides alignment.

The algorithm works across multiple subjects and aligns spatial patterns of connectivity. Its organizing principle differs from alignment based on anatomy: correspondence is derived from how cortical locations participate in functional patterns. This provides a way to match subjects according to the functional organization represented in their fMRI data.

The authors test the method using measurements collected while participants view a movie. They then cross-validate the learned correspondence on a second movie dataset that was not used to construct the alignment. The correspondence successfully generalizes to that separate dataset. This finding matters because it shows that the alignment captures functional relationships that remain useful beyond the particular movie measurements from which it was derived.
summary.tldr: Aligning subjects through functional connectivity produces cortical correspondences that generalize to a separate movie-viewing fMRI dataset.

title: fMRI-Based Inter-Subject Cortical Alignment Using Functional Connectivity

abstract: In system identification both the input and the output of a system are available to an observer and an algorithm is sought to identify parameters of a hypothesized model of that system. Here we present a novel formal methodology for identifying dendritic processing in a neural circuit consisting of a linear dendritic processing filter in cascade with a spiking neuron model. The input to the circuit is an analog signal that belongs to the space of bandlimited functions. The output is a time sequence associated with the spike train. We derive an algorithm for identification of the dendritic processing filter and reconstruct its kernel with arbitrary precision.
originalAbstract: In system identification both the input and the output of a system are available to an observer and an algorithm is sought to identify parameters of a hypothesized model of that system. Here we present a novel formal methodology for identifying dendritic processing in a neural circuit consisting of a linear dendritic processing filter in cascade with a spiking neuron model. The input to the circuit is an analog signal that belongs to the space of bandlimited functions. The output is a time sequence associated with the spike train. We derive an algorithm for identification of the dendritic processing filter and reconstruct its kernel with arbitrary precision.

paragraphs: System identification asks what can be learned about a system's internal parameters when its input and output are both observed. This paper applies that question to dendritic processing in a neural circuit. The goal is to recover the processing that occurs before the circuit generates spikes, using the relationship between an incoming signal and spike-associated timing.

The assumed circuit consists of a linear dendritic filter followed by a spiking neuron model. Its input is an analog signal restricted to the space of bandlimited functions, and its output is a time sequence associated with the spike train. These assumptions define the mathematical setting in which the hidden filter is identified.

The authors derive an identification algorithm and show that the filter's kernel can be reconstructed with arbitrary precision within this setting. The result gives a formal route from observed input and spike timing to the dendritic filter itself. Its scope rests on the specified linear-filter cascade and bandlimited input model.
summary.tldr: An identification algorithm reconstructs a linear dendritic filter with arbitrary precision in a specified spiking circuit with bandlimited inputs.

title: Identifying Dendritic Processing

abstract: Deep networks can potentially express a learning problem more efficiently than local learning machines. While deep networks outperform local learning machines on some problems, it is still unclear how their nice representation emerges from their complex structure. We present an analysis based on Gaussian kernels that measures how the representation of the learning problem evolves layer after layer as the deep network builds higher-level abstract representations of the input. We use this analysis to show empirically that deep networks build progressively better representations of the learning problem and that the best representations are obtained when the deep network discriminates only in the last layers.
originalAbstract: Deep networks can potentially express a learning problem more efficiently than local learning machines. While deep networks outperform local learning machines on some problems, it is still unclear how their nice representation emerges from their complex structure. We present an analysis based on Gaussian kernels that measures how the representation of the learning problem evolves layer after layer as the deep network builds higher-level abstract representations of the input. We use this analysis to show empirically that deep networks build progressively better representations of the learning problem and that the best representations are obtained when the deep network discriminates only in the last layers.

paragraphs: The paper asks how useful internal representations emerge as information passes through a deep network. Deep architectures can express some learning problems efficiently and outperform local learning methods on some tasks, but that observation alone does not explain what successive layers contribute to the representation.

The authors develop an analysis based on Gaussian kernels to assess the learning problem at each layer. This provides a way to examine how the representation changes as the network constructs more abstract descriptions of its input. The focus is the progression through the network, allowing intermediate representations to be assessed alongside later ones.

Using this analysis, the authors find empirically that representations improve progressively through the layers. They also report that the best representations occur when discrimination is concentrated in the final layers. These findings connect the placement of discriminative processing with representation quality in the studied networks, offering evidence about how useful depth develops rather than only comparing final predictive outcomes.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-kernel analysis finds progressively better deep-network representations, with the best observed when discrimination occurs only in the final layers.

title: Layer-wise analysis of deep networks with Gaussian kernels

abstract: An important task in exploring and analyzing real-world data sets is to detect unusual and interesting phenomena. In this paper, we study the group anomaly detection problem. Unlike traditional anomaly detection research that focuses on data points, our goal is to discover anomalous aggregated behaviors of groups of points. For this purpose, we propose the Flexible Genre Model (FGM). FGM is designed to characterize data groups at both the point level and the group level so as to detect various types of group anomalies. We evaluate the effectiveness of FGM on both synthetic and real data sets including images and turbulence data, and show that it is superior to existing approaches in detecting group anomalies.
originalAbstract: An important task in exploring and analyzing real-world data sets is to detect unusual and interesting phenomena. In this paper, we study the group anomaly detection problem. Unlike traditional anomaly detection research that focuses on data points, our goal is to discover anomalous aggregated behaviors of groups of points. For this purpose, we propose the Flexible Genre Model (FGM). FGM is designed to characterize data groups at both the point level and the group level so as to detect various types of group anomalies. We evaluate the effectiveness of FGM on both synthetic and real data sets including images and turbulence data, and show that it is superior to existing approaches in detecting group anomalies.

paragraphs: An unusual phenomenon may appear in the aggregate behavior of a group of observations. This paper studies group anomaly detection, shifting the object of analysis from individual data points to collections of points. The goal is to discover groups whose combined behavior is unusual and potentially informative when exploring real-world data.

The authors propose the Flexible Genre Model, or FGM, to describe groups at two levels. It characterizes individual points while also representing properties of the group containing them. This joint perspective is intended to support detection of different kinds of group anomalies. It makes group-level behavior an explicit part of the model rather than relying exclusively on point-level descriptions.

The evaluation uses synthetic and real datasets, including images and turbulence data. The authors report that FGM detects group anomalies more effectively than the existing approaches considered. These findings support the usefulness of modeling both levels together for the evaluated tasks. The contribution is therefore both a formulation of the group-focused problem and a model designed around its particular information needs.
summary.tldr: The Flexible Genre Model represents individual observations and their groups to detect unusual aggregate behavior.

title: Group Anomaly Detection using Flexible Genre Models

abstract: This paper introduces timeline trees, which are partial models of partially observable environments. Timeline trees are given some specific predictions to make and learn a decision tree over history. The main idea of timeline trees is to use temporally abstract features to identify and split on features of key events, spread arbitrarily far apart in the past (whereas previous decision-tree-based methods have been limited to a finite suffix of history). Experiments demonstrate that timeline trees can learn to make high quality predictions in complex, partially observable environments with high-dimensional observations (e.g. an arcade game).
originalAbstract: This paper introduces timeline trees, which are partial models of partially observable environments. Timeline trees are given some specific predictions to make and learn a decision tree over history. The main idea of timeline trees is to use temporally abstract features to identify and split on features of key events, spread arbitrarily far apart in the past (whereas previous decision-tree-based methods have been limited to a finite suffix of history). Experiments demonstrate that timeline trees can learn to make high quality predictions in complex, partially observable environments with high-dimensional observations (e.g. an arcade game).

paragraphs: In a partially observable environment, the current observation does not reveal everything needed for prediction. Relevant information may lie in earlier events, including events separated by long intervals. This paper introduces timeline trees, partial models designed to learn particular requested predictions from an environment's history.

A timeline tree learns a decision tree whose splits use temporally abstract features. These features identify properties of important past events without requiring those events to fall within a fixed recent window. This extends earlier decision-tree approaches that were restricted to a finite suffix of history. The change matters because a recent window can exclude an informative event even when its consequences remain relevant.

Experiments show that timeline trees can make high-quality predictions in complex partially observable settings with high-dimensional observations, including an arcade game. The contribution is a way to organize historical information around events useful for specified predictions. Its scope as a partial model keeps the emphasis on learning those predictions, while allowing the relevant events to be arbitrarily far apart in the past.
summary.tldr: Timeline trees predict from temporally abstract historical events, extending decision-tree models beyond a fixed window of recent observations.

title: Learning Partially Observable Models Using Temporally Abstract Decision Trees

abstract: Inspired by real-time ad exchanges for online display advertising, we consider the problem of inferring a buyer's value distribution for a good when the buyer is repeatedly interacting with a seller through a posted-price mechanism. We model the buyer as a strategic agent, whose goal is to maximize her long-term surplus, and we are interested in mechanisms that maximize the seller's long-term revenue. We present seller algorithms that are no-regret when the buyer discounts her future surplus --- i.e. the buyer prefers showing advertisements to users sooner rather than later. We also give a lower bound on regret that increases as the buyer's discounting weakens and shows, in particular, that any seller algorithm will suffer linear regret if there is no discounting.
originalAbstract: Inspired by real-time ad exchanges for online display advertising, we consider the problem of inferring a buyer's value distribution for a good when the buyer is repeatedly interacting with a seller through a posted-price mechanism. We model the buyer as a strategic agent, whose goal is to maximize her long-term surplus, and we are interested in mechanisms that maximize the seller's long-term revenue. We present seller algorithms that are no-regret when the buyer discounts her future surplus --- i.e. the buyer prefers showing advertisements to users sooner rather than later. We also give a lower bound on regret that increases as the buyer's discounting weakens and shows, in particular, that any seller algorithm will suffer linear regret if there is no discounting.

paragraphs: A seller offering prices repeatedly must learn about a buyer's value for a good. This becomes more complicated when the buyer acts strategically to maximize surplus over the whole interaction. Motivated by online advertising exchanges, the paper studies posted-price mechanisms in which the seller seeks long-term revenue while learning the buyer's value distribution.

The authors present seller algorithms with no-regret guarantees when the buyer discounts future surplus. Discounting means the buyer values an earlier benefit more than the same benefit received later. In the advertising interpretation, the buyer prefers showing advertisements sooner. This preference is a substantive condition enabling the seller's learning guarantee.

A lower bound shows that regret becomes harder to control as the buyer's discounting weakens. With no discounting, every seller algorithm suffers linear regret in the studied setting. Together, these results identify buyer patience as a central determinant of what the seller can learn and earn, rather than treating purchase decisions as passive observations.
summary.tldr: Seller algorithms achieve no regret against a strategic buyer who discounts future surplus, while no discounting makes linear regret unavoidable.

title: Learning Prices for Repeated Auctions with Strategic Buyers

abstract: The problem of drawing samples from a discrete distribution can be converted into a discrete optimization problem. In this work, we show how sampling from a continuous distribution can be converted into an optimization problem over continuous space. Central to the method is a stochastic process recently described in mathematical statistics that we call the Gumbel process. We present a new construction of the Gumbel process and A* sampling, a practical generic sampling algorithm that searches for the maximum of a Gumbel process using A* search. We analyze the correctness and convergence time of A* sampling and demonstrate empirically that it makes more efficient use of bound and likelihood evaluations than the most closely related adaptive rejection sampling-based algorithms.
originalAbstract: The problem of drawing samples from a discrete distribution can be converted into a discrete optimization problem. In this work, we show how sampling from a continuous distribution can be converted into an optimization problem over continuous space. Central to the method is a stochastic process recently described in mathematical statistics that we call the Gumbel process. We present a new construction of the Gumbel process and A* sampling, a practical generic sampling algorithm that searches for the maximum of a Gumbel process using A* search. We analyze the correctness and convergence time of A* sampling and demonstrate empirically that it makes more efficient use of bound and likelihood evaluations than the most closely related adaptive rejection sampling-based algorithms.

paragraphs: Drawing a random sample and finding an optimum usually appear to be different computational tasks. This paper establishes a connection between them for continuous distributions. It shows how a sampling problem can be transformed into an optimization problem over continuous space, extending an idea already available for discrete distributions.

The construction centers on a stochastic process that the authors call the Gumbel process. They give a new way to construct this process and introduce A* sampling, an algorithm that uses A* search to find its maximum. Randomness is therefore built into the object being optimized, allowing a search procedure to perform the sampling task.

The authors analyze both correctness and convergence time. They also compare the method empirically with closely related algorithms based on adaptive rejection sampling. In those comparisons, A* sampling uses bound and likelihood evaluations more efficiently. This finding concerns the computational evaluations needed to obtain samples, supporting the practical value of the optimization-based formulation alongside its theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: A* sampling turns continuous sampling into randomized optimization and empirically uses fewer bound and likelihood evaluations than closely related rejection-based methods.

title: A* Sampling

abstract: We propose an exploratory approach to statistical model criticism using maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) two sample tests. Typical approaches to model criticism require a practitioner to select a statistic by which to measure discrepancies between data and a statistical model. MMD two sample tests are instead constructed as an analytic maximisation over a large space of possible statistics and therefore automatically select the statistic which most shows any discrepancy. We demonstrate on synthetic data that the selected statistic, called the witness function, can be used to identify where a statistical model most misrepresents the data it was trained on. We then apply the procedure to real data where the models being assessed are restricted Boltzmann machines, deep belief networks and Gaussian process regression and demonstrate the ways in which these models fail to capture the properties of the data they are trained on.

MMD two sample tests are instead constructed as an analytic maximisation over a large space of possible statistics and therefore automatically select the statistic which most shows any discrepancy. We demonstrate on synthetic data that the selected statistic, called the witness function, can be used to identify where a statistical model most misrepresents the data it was trained on. We then apply the procedure to real data where the models being assessed are restricted Boltzmann machines, deep belief networks and Gaussian process regression and demonstrate the ways in which these models fail to capture the properties of the data they are trained on.

paragraphs: Statistical model criticism asks how a fitted model fails to represent its data. Conventional approaches often require a practitioner to choose a particular statistic for detecting a mismatch. This paper proposes an exploratory alternative based on maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, two-sample tests, which search analytically over a large collection of possible statistics.

The procedure selects the statistic that most clearly exposes a discrepancy within that collection. This selected statistic is called the witness function. Its role extends beyond indicating that a mismatch exists: it can help identify where the model misrepresents the observations. Synthetic-data demonstrations show how the witness function provides this more localized diagnostic information.

The authors also examine real-data models including restricted Boltzmann machines, deep belief networks, and Gaussian process regression. These applications reveal ways that the fitted models fail to capture properties of their training data. The contribution is an automated way to choose an informative diagnostic statistic and use it to explore the nature of a model's errors.
summary.tldr: MMD tests automatically select a witness function that helps reveal where a statistical model misrepresents its data.

title: Statistical Model Criticism using Kernel Two Sample Tests

abstract: Compressive Sensing (CS) is an effective approach for fast Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). It aims at reconstructing MR image from a small number of under-sampled data in k-space, and accelerating the data acquisition in MRI. To improve the current MRI system in reconstruction accuracy and computational speed, in this paper, we propose a novel deep architecture, dubbed ADMM-Net. ADMM-Net is defined over a data flow graph, which is derived from the iterative procedures in Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for optimizing a CS-based MRI model. In the training phase, all parameters of the net, e.g., image transforms, shrinkage functions, etc., are discriminatively trained end-to-end using L-BFGS algorithm. In the testing phase, it has computational overhead similar to ADMM but uses optimized parameters learned from the training data for CS-based reconstruction task. Experiments on MRI image reconstruction under different sampling ratios in k-space demonstrate that it significantly improves the baseline ADMM algorithm and achieves high reconstruction accuracies with fast computational speed.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing MRI aims to reconstruct an image from fewer measurements in k-space, reducing the data acquisition needed for a scan. This paper proposes ADMM-Net to improve reconstruction accuracy and computational speed. The architecture starts from the iterative steps of ADMM, an optimization algorithm used to solve a compressive sensing reconstruction model.

The authors turn those steps into a data-flow graph whose parameters can be learned jointly. Image transforms and shrinkage functions are among the components trained end to end using L-BFGS. The resulting network therefore retains a structure derived from an existing reconstruction procedure while adapting its parameters to the reconstruction task through training data.

At test time, ADMM-Net has computational overhead similar to ADMM, but uses its learned parameters. Experiments at different k-space sampling ratios show significant improvements over the baseline ADMM algorithm, alongside high reconstruction accuracy and fast computation. The findings support learning the components of an optimization-derived architecture as a useful approach to MRI reconstruction.
summary.tldr: ADMM-Net turns an MRI reconstruction algorithm into a trainable network that improves reconstruction while retaining similar computational overhead.

title: Deep ADMM-Net for Compressive Sensing MRI

abstract: Starting with the Thomspon sampling algorithm, recent years have seen a resurgence of interest in Bayesian algorithms for the Multi-armed Bandit (MAB) problem. These algorithms seek to exploit prior information on arm biases and while several have been shown to be regret optimal, their design has not emerged from a principled approach. In contrast, if one cared about Bayesian regret discounted over an infinite horizon at a fixed, pre-specified rate, the celebrated Gittins index theorem offers an optimal algorithm. Unfortunately, the Gittins analysis does not appear to carry over to minimizing Bayesian regret over all sufficiently large horizons and computing a Gittins index is onerous relative to essentially any incumbent index scheme for the Bayesian MAB problem. The present paper proposes a sequence of 'optimistic' approximations to the Gittins index. We show that the use of these approximations in concert with the use of an increasing discount factor appears to offer a compelling alternative to a variety of index schemes proposed for the Bayesian MAB problem in recent years. In addition, we show that the simplest of these approximations yields regret that matches the Lai-Robbins lower bound, including achieving matching constants.

paragraphs: Bayesian bandit algorithms use prior information to guide repeated choices among uncertain alternatives. Gittins indices offer a principled optimal solution when future rewards are discounted at a fixed rate over an infinite horizon. However, that analysis does not readily transfer to regret minimization across sufficiently large horizons, and computing the indices is relatively demanding.

This paper proposes a sequence of optimistic approximations to the Gittins index. It combines those approximations with an increasing discount factor, linking the classical discounted formulation to a different regret objective. The authors describe this combination as appearing to offer a compelling alternative to other Bayesian index schemes, which is a qualified assessment rather than a universal ranking.

The strongest stated guarantee concerns the simplest approximation: its regret matches the Lai–Robbins lower bound, including the constants. Matching constants is stronger than matching only the broad growth order of regret. The contribution therefore uses an established optimal-control idea to motivate practical index approximations while obtaining a precise regret result for one member of the proposed family.
summary.tldr: Optimistic Gittins-index approximations connect discounted Bayesian bandit reasoning to regret minimization, with the simplest matching the Lai–Robbins bound and constants.

title: Optimistic Gittins Indices

abstract: Tensor decomposition is positioned to be a pervasive tool in the era of big data. In this paper, we resolve many of the key algorithmic questions regarding robustness, memory efficiency, and differential privacy of tensor decomposition. We propose simple variants of the tensor power method which enjoy these strong properties. We propose the first streaming method with a linear memory requirement. Moreover, we present a noise calibrated tensor power method with efficient privacy guarantees. At the heart of all these guarantees lies a careful perturbation analysis derived in this paper which improves up on the existing results significantly.

paragraphs: This paper tackles three practical requirements for tensor decomposition: robustness, limited memory use, and differential privacy. Its starting point is the tensor power method, for which the authors propose simple variants. The aim is to give this decomposition approach stronger guarantees that address how it behaves when processing large amounts of data.

One contribution is a streaming method with a linear memory requirement, which the authors identify as the first of its kind. A second is a tensor power method with calibrated noise that provides efficient privacy guarantees. These contributions address different operational needs while remaining variants of the same underlying algorithmic approach.

The common mathematical foundation is a careful perturbation analysis that significantly improves on previous results. Perturbation analysis studies how changes or noise affect the decomposition, making it central to understanding robustness and the consequences of privacy-related noise. The paper's stated contribution is therefore a connected set of algorithmic guarantees: improved analysis supports methods designed for streaming computation, robustness, and differential privacy.
summary.tldr: Improved perturbation analysis supports tensor power methods with robustness, linear-memory streaming, and differential privacy guarantees.

title: Online and Differentially-Private Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Arising from many applications at the intersection of decision-making and machine learning, Marginal Maximum A Posteriori (Marginal MAP) problems unify the two main classes of inference, namely maximization (optimization) and marginal inference (counting), and are believed to have higher complexity than both of them. We propose XOR MMAP, a novel approach to solve the Marginal MAP problem, which represents the intractable counting subproblem with queries to NP oracles, subject to additional parity constraints. XOR MMAP provides a constant factor approximation to the Marginal MAP problem, by encoding it as a single optimization in a polynomial size of the original problem. We evaluate our approach in several machine learning and decision-making applications, and show that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art Marginal MAP solvers.

paragraphs: Marginal MAP combines choosing the best decision with summing over uncertain variables. These maximization and counting requirements make it more difficult than either inference task on its own. The paper proposes XOR MMAP for applications where decision-making and probabilistic inference must be solved together.

The approach represents the intractable counting component using queries to NP oracles with added parity constraints. It encodes the marginal-MAP task as a single optimization problem whose size is polynomial in the original problem, and provides a constant-factor approximation guarantee.

Experiments on several machine-learning and decision-making applications show improvements over multiple state-of-the-art marginal-MAP solvers. The abstract does not name the application instances or report runtimes. The theoretical reduction is not a claim that every resulting optimization is easy; its value is connecting a harder combined inference problem to an oracle-based formulation with an explicit approximation guarantee.
summary.tldr: XOR MMAP reduces difficult marginal-MAP inference to optimization with parity constraints.

title: Solving Marginal MAP Problems with NP Oracles and Parity Constraints

abstract: We analyze sources of error in prediction market forecasts in order to bound the difference between a security's price and the ground truth it estimates. We consider cost-function-based prediction markets in which an automated market maker adjusts security prices according to the history of trade. We decompose the forecasting error into three components: sampling error, arising because traders only possess noisy estimates of ground truth; market-maker bias, resulting from the use of a particular market maker (i.e., cost function) to facilitate trade; and convergence error, arising because, at any point in time, market prices may still be in flux. Our goal is to make explicit the tradeoffs between these error components, influenced by design decisions such as the functional form of the cost function and the amount of liquidity in the market. We consider a specific model in which traders have exponential utility and exponential-family beliefs representing noisy estimates of ground truth. In this setting, sampling error vanishes as the number of traders grows, but there is a tradeoff between the other two components. We provide both upper and lower bounds on market-maker bias and convergence error, and demonstrate via numerical simulations that these bounds are tight. Our results yield new insights into the question of how to set the market's liquidity parameter and into the forecasting benefits of enforcing coherent prices across securities.
