paragraphs: Prediction markets use trading prices as forecasts, but those prices can differ from the quantity they are meant to estimate for several reasons. This paper separates forecast error into three parts: noise in traders’ information, bias introduced by the automated market maker, and error because trading has not yet settled into a stable outcome.

The analysis concerns markets whose prices are updated through a cost function. It uses a specific model in which traders have exponential utility and beliefs from an exponential family. Within that setting, the information-related error disappears as the number of traders increases. The other two errors involve a tradeoff affected by market design, including the liquidity parameter.

The authors derive upper and lower bounds on market-maker bias and convergence error, and numerical simulations demonstrate that these bounds are tight. The decomposition makes liquidity choices more interpretable: designers can examine distinct sources of forecast error instead of treating accuracy as one undifferentiated outcome. It also clarifies the forecasting benefits of maintaining coherent prices across securities.
summary.tldr: A three-part decomposition explains how trader information, market-maker design, and unfinished convergence affect prediction-market accuracy.

title: A Decomposition of Forecast Error in Prediction Markets

abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is an effective approach to recover a reward function that explains the behavior of an expert by observing a set of demonstrations. This paper is about a novel model-free IRL approach that, differently from most of the existing IRL algorithms, does not require to specify a function space where to search for the expert's reward function. Leveraging on the fact that the policy gradient needs to be zero for any optimal policy, the algorithm generates a set of basis functions that span the subspace of reward functions that make the policy gradient vanish. Within this subspace, using a second-order criterion, we search for the reward function that penalizes the most a deviation from the expert's policy. After introducing our approach for finite domains, we extend it to continuous ones. The proposed approach is empirically compared to other IRL methods both in the (finite) Taxi domain and in the (continuous) Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) and Car on the Hill environments.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that explains an expert's demonstrated behavior. Many approaches require specifying in advance a space of candidate reward functions. This paper introduces a model-free method that instead constructs a suitable reward space using a condition associated with optimal policies.

The starting point is that an optimal policy must have a zero policy gradient. The algorithm generates basis functions spanning a subspace of rewards that make this gradient vanish. This narrows the search to rewards compatible with that first-order condition. Within the resulting subspace, a second-order criterion selects the reward that most strongly penalizes deviations from the expert's policy.

The distinction between these stages matters: making a gradient vanish supplies the candidate space, while the second-order criterion supplies a preference among its rewards. The authors develop the method for finite domains and extend it to continuous ones. They compare it empirically with other inverse reinforcement learning methods in Taxi, Linear Quadratic Gaussian, and Car on the Hill environments.
summary.tldr: A model-free inverse reinforcement learning method constructs candidate rewards from policy-gradient conditions and selects among them using a second-order criterion.

title: Compatible Reward Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper shows how metric learning can be used with Nadaraya-Watson (NW) kernel regression. Compared with standard approaches, such as bandwidth selection, we show how metric learning can significantly reduce the mean square error (MSE) in kernel regression, particularly for high-dimensional data. We propose a method for efficiently learning a good metric function based upon analyzing the performance of the NW estimator for Gaussian-distributed data. A key feature of our approach is that the NW estimator with a learned metric uses information from both the global and local structure of the training data. Theoretical and empirical results confirm that the learned metric can considerably reduce the bias and MSE for kernel regression even when the data are not confined to Gaussian.

paragraphs: Kernel regression depends on how the model judges similarity between inputs. This paper studies learning that notion of similarity for the Nadaraya-Watson estimator, rather than relying only on standard adjustments such as bandwidth selection. It argues that a learned metric can substantially reduce prediction error, particularly when the data have many dimensions.

The proposed procedure derives an efficient way to learn the metric by analyzing the estimator for Gaussian-distributed data. Its distinguishing feature is that the resulting estimator draws on both global and local structure in the training set. The similarity function can therefore reflect broader patterns while still responding to the structure relevant near a prediction.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical results showing that the learned metric can considerably reduce both bias and mean squared error. These benefits also appear beyond Gaussian data, so the distribution used to develop the method does not confine all of its reported benefits. The findings emphasize that choosing the geometry of similarity can be an important part of improving kernel regression.
summary.tldr: Learning a metric from global and local data structure can reduce kernel-regression bias and mean squared error, including beyond Gaussian data.

title: Generative Local Metric Learning for Kernel Regression

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of escaping from saddle points in smooth nonconvex optimization problems subject to a convex set $\mathcal{C}$. We propose a generic framework that yields convergence to a second-order stationary point of the problem, if the convex set $\mathcal{C}$ is simple for a quadratic objective function. Specifically, our results hold if one can find a $\rho$-approximate solution of a quadratic program subject to $\mathcal{C}$ in polynomial time, where $\rho<1$ is a positive constant that depends on the structure of the set $\mathcal{C}$. Under this condition, we show that the sequence of iterates generated by the proposed framework reaches an $(\epsilon,\gamma)$-second order stationary point (SOSP) in at most $\mathcal{O}(\max\{\epsilon^{-2},\rho^{-3}\gamma^{-3}\})$ iterations. We further characterize the overall complexity of reaching an SOSP when the convex set $\mathcal{C}$ can be written as a set of quadratic constraints and the objective function Hessian has a specific structure over the convex $\mathcal{C}$. Finally, we extend our results to the stochastic setting and characterize the number of stochastic gradient and Hessian evaluations to reach an $(\epsilon,\gamma)$-SOSP.

paragraphs: The paper studies smooth nonconvex optimization when solutions must remain inside a convex set. Its focus is escaping saddle points and reaching a second-order stationary point, where both gradient and curvature conditions are satisfied to specified tolerances. Constraints make this problem depend on the geometry of the permitted solution set.

The proposed framework has a conditional guarantee: a quadratic program over that set must admit a polynomial-time rho-approximate solution, for a positive constant rho below one. Under this condition, it reaches an (epsilon, gamma)-second-order stationary point within O(max{epsilon^-2, rho^-3 gamma^-3}) iterations. The bound explicitly connects accuracy requirements and the quadratic approximation quality to the iteration count.

The authors also characterize overall complexity for sets described by quadratic constraints when the objective's Hessian has a specified structure over the set. They extend the analysis to stochastic optimization and count the stochastic gradient and Hessian evaluations needed. The contribution is therefore a framework whose guarantees follow from tractable quadratic subproblems, with further results for structured constraints and stochastic information.
summary.tldr: A constrained optimization framework reaches approximate second-order stationary points when suitable quadratic subproblems can be approximated efficiently.

title: Escaping Saddle Points in Constrained Optimization

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have achieved significant success in generating real-valued data. However, the discrete nature of text hinders the application of GAN to text-generation tasks. Instead of using the standard GAN objective, we propose to improve text-generation GAN via a novel approach inspired by optimal transport. Specifically, we consider matching the latent feature distributions of real and synthetic sentences using a novel metric, termed the feature-mover's distance (FMD). This formulation leads to a highly discriminative critic and easy-to-optimize objective, overcoming the mode-collapsing and brittle-training problems in existing methods. Extensive experiments are conducted on a variety of tasks to evaluate the proposed model empirically, including unconditional text generation, style transfer from non-parallel text, and unsupervised cipher cracking. The proposed model yields superior performance, demonstrating wide applicability and effectiveness.

paragraphs: Adversarial generation has worked well for real-valued data, but text presents an obstacle because its outputs are discrete. This paper changes the training objective for text-generating adversarial networks. Its central proposal is to compare distributions of sentence features, giving training a measure of disagreement between real and generated language.

The authors introduce feature-mover's distance, a metric inspired by optimal transport, to match these latent feature distributions. The comparison happens in a representation of sentences rather than through the standard GAN objective. They describe the resulting critic as highly discriminative and the objective as easy to optimize, addressing unstable training and mode collapse, where generation loses variety.

Experiments cover unconditional text generation, style transfer using non-parallel text, and unsupervised cipher cracking. The proposed model achieves superior performance in the reported evaluations. The breadth of those tasks matters because they place different demands on language generation and transformation. Together, the results support the authors' claim that feature-distribution matching is an effective and broadly applicable training approach across the tasks studied.
summary.tldr: Feature-mover's distance improves adversarial text generation by matching real and generated sentence-feature distributions through an optimal-transport-inspired objective.

title: Adversarial Text Generation via Feature-Mover's Distance

abstract: Tensor decompositions are fundamental tools for multiway data analysis. Existing approaches, however, ignore the valuable temporal information along with data, or simply discretize them into time steps so that important temporal patterns are easily missed. Moreover, most methods are limited to multilinear decomposition forms, and hence are unable to capture intricate, nonlinear relationships in data. To address these issues, we formulate event-tensors, to preserve the complete temporal information for multiway data, and propose a novel Bayesian nonparametric decomposition model. Our model can (1) fully exploit the time stamps to capture the critical, causal/triggering effects between the interaction events, (2) flexibly estimate the complex relationships between the entities in tensor modes, and (3) uncover hidden structures from their temporal interactions. For scalable inference, we develop a doubly stochastic variational Expectation-Maximization algorithm to conduct an online decomposition. Evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our model not only improves upon the predictive performance of existing methods, but also discovers interesting clusters underlying the data.

paragraphs: Multiway interaction data often contain timestamps that reveal how events unfold. Conventional tensor decompositions may discard this information or group it into time steps, obscuring temporal patterns. This paper introduces event-tensors to preserve the complete timing information and a Bayesian nonparametric model to analyze them.

The model aims to capture both complex relationships among entities and temporal triggering effects among their interactions. Its flexible decomposition moves beyond multilinear forms, allowing nonlinear relationships to be represented. Using timestamps also supports uncovering hidden structure through the way entities interact over time, rather than relying only on aggregated interaction values.

For scalable learning, the authors develop an online decomposition procedure based on doubly stochastic variational expectation-maximization. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets report improved predictive performance over existing methods and the discovery of meaningful-looking clusters in the data. The findings support modeling interaction timing and nonlinear entity relationships together. The contribution is both a representation that retains event times and an inference approach designed to make the resulting richer decomposition scalable.
summary.tldr: Event-tensors preserve interaction timestamps, enabling a scalable nonlinear Bayesian decomposition that improves prediction and reveals clusters.

title: Stochastic Nonparametric Event-Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Complex numbers have long been favoured for digital signal processing, yet complex representations rarely appear in deep learning architectures. RNNs, widely used to process time series and sequence information, could greatly benefit from complex representations. We present a novel complex gated recurrent cell, which is a hybrid cell combining complex-valued and norm-preserving state transitions with a gating mechanism. The resulting RNN exhibits excellent stability and convergence properties and performs competitively on the synthetic memory and adding task, as well as on the real-world tasks of human motion prediction.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks process sequences by repeatedly updating an internal state. This makes the design of the state transition central to how information moves through a sequence. The paper explores complex-valued representations, which have a long history in digital signal processing but are less common in deep learning architectures.

The proposed recurrent cell combines complex-valued, norm-preserving state transitions with a gating mechanism. Norm preservation constrains how a transition changes the size of the state, while gating provides a way to regulate information flow. Bringing these elements together creates a hybrid recurrent design that incorporates both structured transitions and learned control over the evolving representation.

The authors report strong stability and convergence properties for the resulting network. They also find competitive performance on synthetic memory and adding tasks, along with human motion prediction. These evaluations connect the architectural proposal to both controlled sequence tasks and a real-world prediction setting. The stated finding supports complex gated recurrence as a useful design option, without claiming that it dominates every sequence model.
summary.tldr: A recurrent cell combines complex-valued, norm-preserving transitions with gates and achieves competitive sequence-task performance.

title: Complex Gated Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the minimum cost intervention design problem: Given the essential graph of a causal graph and a cost to intervene on a variable, identify the set of interventions with minimum total cost that can learn any causal graph with the given essential graph. We first show that this problem is NP-hard. We then prove that we can achieve a constant factor approximation to this problem with a greedy algorithm. We then constrain the sparsity of each intervention. We develop an algorithm that returns an intervention design that is nearly optimal in terms of size for sparse graphs with sparse interventions and we discuss how to use it when there are costs on the vertices.
originalAbstract: We consider the minimum cost intervention design problem: Given the essential graph of a causal graph and a cost to intervene on a variable, identify the set of interventions with minimum total cost that can learn any causal graph with the given essential graph. We first show that this problem is NP-hard. We then prove that we can achieve a constant factor approximation to this problem with a greedy algorithm. We then constrain the sparsity of each intervention. We develop an algorithm that returns an intervention design that is nearly optimal in terms of size for sparse graphs with sparse interventions and we discuss how to use it when there are costs on the vertices.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose interventions that reveal a causal graph while keeping total intervention cost low. The starting information is an essential graph, representing the remaining possibilities for the causal structure, together with a cost for intervening on each variable. The intervention design must be sufficient to identify any causal graph compatible with that starting information.

The authors first prove that finding the minimum-cost design is NP-hard. They then provide a greedy algorithm with a constant-factor approximation guarantee. This gives a principled way to control how far the selected design's cost can be from the optimum, even though solving the optimization problem exactly is computationally difficult.

A second part limits how many variables can be included in an individual intervention. For sparse graphs and sparse interventions, the authors develop a design that is nearly optimal in size and discuss how variable costs can be incorporated. The results distinguish two practical concerns: the total cost of experiments and the restrictions on each experiment.
summary.tldr: Approximation algorithms select cost-aware causal interventions, with additional guarantees for sparse graphs and interventions.

title: Experimental Design for Cost-Aware Learning of Causal Graphs

abstract: Online learning to rank is a sequential decision-making problem where in each round the learning agent chooses a list of items and receives feedback in the form of clicks from the user. Many sample-efficient algorithms have been proposed for this problem that assume a specific click model connecting rankings and user behavior. We propose a generalized click model that encompasses many existing models, including the position-based and cascade models. Our generalization motivates a novel online learning algorithm based on topological sort, which we call TopRank. TopRank is (a) more natural than existing algorithms, (b) has stronger regret guarantees than existing algorithms with comparable generality, (c) has a more insightful proof that leaves the door open to many generalizations, (d) outperforms existing algorithms empirically.

Many sample-efficient algorithms have been proposed for this problem that assume a specific click model connecting rankings and user behavior. We propose a generalized click model that encompasses many existing models, including the position-based and cascade models. Our generalization motivates a novel online learning algorithm based on topological sort, which we call TopRank. TopRank is (a) more natural than existing algorithms, (b) has stronger regret guarantees than existing algorithms with comparable generality, (c) has a more insightful proof that leaves the door open to many generalizations, (d) outperforms existing algorithms empirically.

paragraphs: Online ranking repeatedly presents a list of items and learns from the clicks it receives. Learning efficiently requires accounting for how the displayed order affects user behavior. Many existing algorithms assume a particular click model, which ties their reasoning and guarantees to a specific description of how users inspect and select items.

This paper proposes a generalized click model that includes both position-based and cascade models. That broader formulation motivates TopRank, an online ranking algorithm built around topological sorting. The approach uses an ordering procedure as the basis for learning rankings while working within assumptions broad enough to encompass several established click models.

The authors establish stronger regret guarantees than existing algorithms with comparable generality and report better empirical performance than existing methods. Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning relative to a better ranking strategy, so the theoretical result addresses performance over repeated interactions. The paper also presents its proof as a foundation for further generalizations, connecting the algorithm's practical results with a broader framework for online ranking.
summary.tldr: TopRank uses topological sorting under a generalized click model, achieving stronger regret guarantees and improved empirical ranking performance.

title: TopRank: A practical algorithm for online stochastic ranking

abstract: We consider a dynamic assortment selection problem where the goal is to offer a sequence of assortments that maximizes the expected cumulative revenue, or alternatively, minimize the expected regret. The feedback here is the item that the user picks from the assortment. The distinguishing feature in this work is that this feedback has a multinomial logistic distribution. The utility of each item is a dynamic function of contextual information of both the item and the user. We propose two Thompson sampling algorithms for this multinomial logit contextual bandit. Our first algorithm maintains a posterior distribution of the true parameter and establishes $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T})$ Bayesian regret over $T$ rounds with $d$ dimensional context vector. The worst-case computational complexity of this algorithm could be high when the prior distribution is not a conjugate. The second algorithm approximates the posterior by a Gaussian distribution, and uses a new optimistic sampling procedure to address the issues that arise in worst-case regret analysis. This algorithm achieves $\tilde{O}(d^{3/2}\sqrt{T})$ worst-case (frequentist) regret bound. The numerical experiments show that the practical performance of both methods is in line with the theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper studies choosing assortments of items over time to maximize cumulative revenue. The learner observes which offered item a user selects. Choices follow a multinomial logistic model, and each item's utility depends on changing contextual information about both the item and the user.

The authors propose two Thompson sampling algorithms. The first maintains a posterior over the unknown parameter and achieves Bayesian regret of roughly d times the square root of T, ignoring logarithmic factors. Its worst-case computational cost can be high when the prior is non-conjugate, motivating the second approach.

The second algorithm approximates the posterior with a Gaussian distribution and introduces an optimistic sampling procedure. Its worst-case frequentist regret is roughly d to the 3/2 times the square root of T, again up to logarithmic factors. These bounds use different notions of regret, so they describe distinct guarantees. Numerical experiments find practical behavior consistent with the theory, supporting both approaches to learning from contextual assortment choices.
summary.tldr: Two Thompson sampling methods provide Bayesian and frequentist regret guarantees for contextual assortment selection under multinomial-logit choices.

title: Thompson Sampling for Multinomial Logit Contextual Bandits

abstract: Existing deep learning based facial landmark detection methods have achieved excellent performance. These methods, however, do not explicitly embed the structural dependencies among landmark points. They hence cannot preserve the geometric relationships between landmark points or generalize well to challenging conditions or unseen data. This paper proposes a method for deep structured facial landmark detection based on combining a deep Convolutional Network with a Conditional Random Field. We demonstrate its superior performance to existing state-of-the-art techniques in facial landmark detection, especially a better generalization ability on challenging datasets that include large pose and occlusion.

paragraphs: Facial landmark detection involves locating a set of points whose positions are geometrically related. A prediction can therefore be judged both by the placement of individual points and by whether their arrangement is consistent. The paper argues that existing deep learning methods, despite strong performance, do not explicitly represent these dependencies and consequently struggle to preserve landmark geometry under difficult conditions.

The proposed method combines a deep convolutional network with a conditional random field. This brings image-based prediction together with a structured model of relationships among landmarks. The purpose is to make those relationships part of the prediction process, so that the model explicitly accounts for how landmark positions depend on one another.

The authors report superior performance over existing leading facial landmark methods, with particularly improved generalization on challenging datasets containing large pose changes and occlusion. These findings support the value of explicitly modeling facial structure when visual evidence becomes difficult to interpret. The stated result concerns performance on those evaluations, where preserving relationships among points accompanies better landmark detection.
summary.tldr: Combining a convolutional network with a conditional random field improves facial landmark detection by explicitly modeling relationships among landmark positions.

title: Deep Structured Prediction for Facial Landmark Detection

abstract: Visual commonsense reasoning (VCR) has been introduced to boost research of cognition-level visual understanding, i.e., a thorough understanding of correlated details of the scene plus an inference with related commonsense knowledge. Recent studies on neuroscience have suggested that brain function or cognition can be described as a global and dynamic integration of local neuronal connectivity, which is context-sensitive to specific cognition tasks. Inspired by this idea, towards VCR, we propose a connective cognition network (CCN) to dynamically reorganize the visual neuron connectivity that is contextualized by the meaning of questions and answers. Concretely, we first develop visual neuron connectivity to fully model correlations of visual content. Then, a contextualization process is introduced to fuse the sentence representation with that of visual neurons. Finally, based on the output of contextualized connectivity, we propose directional connectivity to infer answers or rationales. Experimental results on the VCR dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Particularly, in $Q \to AR$ mode, our method is around 4\% higher than the state-of-the-art method.

paragraphs: Visual commonsense reasoning asks a model to connect details within a scene and use relevant commonsense knowledge to infer an answer or explanation. The paper proposes a connective cognition network, inspired by the idea that cognition involves relationships that change with the task. Here, questions and answers provide the context for reorganizing visual connections.

The network first represents correlations among visual content through what the authors call visual neuron connectivity. It then combines sentence representations with the visual representations, making those connections responsive to the language under consideration. Finally, a directional connectivity component uses the contextualized connections to infer answers or rationales.

This design makes the relationships among scene details part of the reasoning process: the language influences how visual information is connected before a conclusion is produced. Experiments on the VCR dataset support the method’s effectiveness. In the Q-to-AR evaluation mode, the authors report a result around 4% higher than the leading comparison method. That finding concerns the tested benchmark and mode, while the proposed architecture supplies the broader methodological contribution.
summary.tldr: A connective cognition network adapts relationships among visual features to question-and-answer context, improving reported visual commonsense reasoning performance.

title: Connective Cognition Network for Directional Visual Commonsense Reasoning

abstract: Few-shot classification (FSC) is challenging due to the scarcity of labeled training data (e.g. only one labeled data point per class). Meta-learning has shown to achieve promising results by learning to initialize a classification model for FSC. In this paper we propose a novel semi-supervised meta-learning method called learning to self-train (LST) that leverages unlabeled data and specifically meta-learns how to cherry-pick and label such unsupervised data to further improve performance. To this end, we train the LST model through a large number of semi-supervised few-shot tasks. On each task, we train a few-shot model to predict pseudo labels for unlabeled data, and then iterate the self-training steps on labeled and pseudo-labeled data with each step followed by fine-tuning. We additionally learn a soft weighting network (SWN) to optimize the self-training weights of pseudo labels so that better ones can contribute more to gradient descent optimization. We evaluate our LST method on two ImageNet benchmarks for semi-supervised few-shot classification and achieve large improvements over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification asks a model to recognize classes from very few labeled examples, sometimes only one per class. Unlabeled examples offer additional information, but using the model’s own predictions as labels requires deciding which predictions deserve influence. This paper proposes learning that decision through experience across many few-shot tasks.

The learning-to-self-train method trains on a large collection of semi-supervised tasks. Within each task, a few-shot classifier assigns provisional labels to unlabeled examples. It then repeatedly trains using the original labels together with these pseudo labels, with fine-tuning after each self-training step. The broader training process learns how to select and label useful unlabeled data.

A soft weighting network additionally learns how strongly each pseudo label should contribute to optimization, allowing better pseudo labels to carry more weight. Evaluation on two ImageNet benchmarks shows large improvements over the previous state of the art. The result supports learning the self-training procedure itself: experience across tasks can guide how a classifier expands its limited labeled evidence with predictions on unlabeled examples.
summary.tldr: Learning to self-train uses meta-learning to select, label, and weight unlabeled examples for few-shot classification.

title: Learning to Self-Train for Semi-Supervised Few-Shot Classification

abstract: Minimum expected distance estimation (MEDE) algorithms have been widely used for probabilistic models with intractable likelihood functions and they have become increasingly popular due to their use in implicit generative modeling (e.g.\ Wasserstein generative adversarial networks, Wasserstein autoencoders). Emerging from computational optimal transport, the Sliced-Wasserstein (SW) distance has become a popular choice in MEDE thanks to its simplicity and computational benefits. While several studies have reported empirical success on generative modeling with SW, the theoretical properties of such estimators have not yet been established. In this study, we investigate the asymptotic properties of estimators that are obtained by minimizing SW. We first show that convergence in SW implies weak convergence of probability measures in general Wasserstein spaces. Then we show that estimators obtained by minimizing SW (and also an approximate version of SW) are asymptotically consistent. We finally prove a central limit theorem, which characterizes the asymptotic distribution of the estimators and establish a convergence rate of $\sqrt{n}$, where $n$ denotes the number of observed data points. We illustrate the validity of our theory on both synthetic data and neural networks.

paragraphs: Some probabilistic models can generate samples even when evaluating their likelihood is intractable. Minimum expected distance estimation fits such models by minimizing a discrepancy between distributions. The Sliced-Wasserstein distance is attractive for this purpose because of its computational simplicity, but empirical success alone does not establish how the resulting estimates behave as more observations arrive.

This paper provides asymptotic foundations for that approach. First, it proves that convergence in Sliced-Wasserstein distance implies weak convergence of probability measures in general Wasserstein spaces. This connects shrinking the training discrepancy to a standard mathematical notion of distributional convergence. The authors then establish asymptotic consistency for estimators minimizing either the distance itself or an approximate version.

A central limit theorem further describes the estimators’ limiting distribution, with a square-root-of-sample-size convergence rate. These results explain the large-data behavior of the estimators, rather than merely their computational appeal. Illustrations using synthetic data and neural networks support the theory. Together, the findings give a theoretical basis for using Sliced-Wasserstein objectives to fit generative models whose likelihoods are difficult to evaluate.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes consistency and asymptotic distributional guarantees for generative-model estimators trained with Sliced-Wasserstein distance.

title: Asymptotic Guarantees for Learning Generative Models with the Sliced-Wasserstein Distance

abstract: The statistical decision theoretic foundations of modern machine learning have largely focused on the minimization of the expectation of some loss function for a given task. However, seminal results in behavioral economics have shown that human decision-making is based on different risk measures than the expectation of any given loss function. In this paper, we pose the following simple question: in contrast to minimizing expected loss, could we minimize a better human-aligned risk measure? While this might not seem natural at first glance, we analyze the properties of such a revised risk measure, and surprisingly show that it might also better align with additional desiderata like fairness that have attracted considerable recent attention. We focus in particular on a class of human-aligned risk measures inspired by cumulative prospect theory. We empirically study these risk measures, and demonstrate their improved performance on desiderata such as fairness, in contrast to the traditional workhorse of expected loss minimization.

paragraphs: Machine learning commonly trains models by minimizing expected loss: an average of how costly their predictions are. This paper questions whether that objective adequately reflects human attitudes toward risk. Its motivation comes from behavioral economics, where human decision-making has been shown to follow risk measures that differ from expected loss.

The authors investigate a class of alternative risk measures inspired by cumulative prospect theory. They analyze properties of these objectives and ask whether optimizing them could better align learning with human preferences. The inquiry also considers fairness, examining the possibility that changing how losses are assessed could support goals beyond average predictive performance.

Empirical studies show improvements on desiderata such as fairness compared with conventional expected-loss minimization. The result gives evidence that the choice of risk measure can matter for these broader objectives. The paper’s claim remains qualified: the analyzed measures may offer better alignment, and the experiments demonstrate improvements in the studied settings rather than a universal guarantee of fairness.
summary.tldr: Risk measures inspired by cumulative prospect theory offer an alternative to expected loss and improve fairness-related outcomes in the reported experiments.

title: On Human-Aligned Risk Minimization

abstract: Deep neural networks have received dramatic success based on the optimization method of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, it is still not clear how to tune hyper-parameters, especially batch size and learning rate, to ensure good generalization. This paper reports both theoretical and empirical evidence of a training strategy that we should control the ratio of batch size to learning rate not too large to achieve a good generalization ability. Specifically, we prove a PAC-Bayes generalization bound for neural networks trained by SGD, which has a positive correlation with the ratio of batch size to learning rate. This correlation builds the theoretical foundation of the training strategy. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale experiment to verify the correlation and training strategy. We trained 1,600 models based on architectures ResNet-110, and VGG-19 with datasets CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 while strictly control unrelated variables. Accuracies on the test sets are collected for the evaluation. Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficients and the corresponding $p$ values on 164 groups of the collected data demonstrate that the correlation is statistically significant, which fully supports the training strategy.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how batch size and learning rate should be considered together when training neural networks with stochastic gradient descent. Its proposed strategy is to keep the ratio of batch size to learning rate from becoming too large. This frames the two hyperparameters as a coupled choice relevant to performance on unseen data.

The theoretical contribution is a PAC-Bayes generalization bound that is positively correlated with this ratio. A larger ratio is associated with a larger bound, providing a mathematical basis for the proposed training strategy. This is a statement about the bound, rather than a guarantee that every individual model's test performance changes monotonically with the ratio.

The empirical study trains 1,600 models using ResNet-110 and VGG-19 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 while controlling unrelated variables. Analysis across 164 groups uses Spearman rank correlations and associated p values, finding statistically significant relationships that support the strategy. Together, the evidence motivates tuning batch size relative to learning rate when seeking good generalization.
summary.tldr: A generalization bound and controlled experiments support keeping the batch-size-to-learning-rate ratio from becoming too large.

title: Control Batch Size and Learning Rate to Generalize Well: Theoretical and Empirical Evidence

abstract: In many real-world deployments of machine learning systems, data arrive piecemeal. These learning scenarios may be passive, where data arrive incrementally due to structural properties of the problem (e.g., daily financial data) or active, where samples are selected according to a measure of their quality (e.g., experimental design). In both of these cases, we are building a sequence of models that incorporate an increasing amount of data. We would like each of these models in the sequence to be performant and take advantage of all the data that are available to that point. Conventional intuition suggests that when solving a sequence of related optimization problems of this form, it should be possible to initialize using the solution of the previous iterate---to ``warm start'' the optimization rather than initialize from scratch---and see reductions in wall-clock time. However, in practice this warm-starting seems to yield poorer generalization performance than models that have fresh random initializations, even though the final training losses are similar. While it appears that some hyperparameter settings allow a practitioner to close this generalization gap, they seem to only do so in regimes that damage the wall-clock gains of the warm start. Nevertheless, it is highly desirable to be able to warm-start neural network training, as it would dramatically reduce the resource usage associated with the construction of performant deep learning systems. In this work, we take a closer look at this empirical phenomenon and try to understand when and how it occurs. We also provide a surprisingly simple trick that overcomes this pathology in several important situations, and present experiments that elucidate some of its properties.

paragraphs: When data arrive incrementally, practitioners repeatedly train models on an expanding dataset. Reusing the previous model’s parameters seems like a natural way to save time. This paper examines an empirical complication: such warm starts can generalize worse than training from a fresh random initialization, even when the resulting training losses are similar.

The distinction matters because fitting the available training data equally well does not ensure equally good performance on new data. The authors investigate when and how this gap appears. They also note that some hyperparameter choices seem to close it, but in regimes that weaken the wall-clock advantage that made warm starting attractive.

The paper offers a simple modification that overcomes the problem in several important situations and presents experiments examining its properties. Its contribution is both a closer study of a counterintuitive training behavior and a practical way to address it in the reported cases. The findings make clear that reusing a trained model involves a generalization question as well as a computational one.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates why warm starts can hurt generalization and presents a simple remedy effective in several situations.

title: On Warm-Starting Neural Network Training

abstract: In federated learning, heterogeneity in the clients' local datasets and computation speeds results in large variations in the number of local updates performed by each client in each communication round. Naive weighted aggregation of such models causes objective inconsistency, that is, the global model converges to a stationary point of a mismatched objective function which can be arbitrarily different from the true objective. This paper provides a general framework to analyze the convergence of federated heterogeneous optimization algorithms. It subsumes previously proposed methods such as FedAvg and FedProx and provides the first principled understanding of the solution bias and the convergence slowdown due to objective inconsistency. Using insights from this analysis, we propose FedNova, a normalized averaging method that eliminates objective inconsistency while preserving fast error convergence.

This paper provides a general framework to analyze the convergence of federated heterogeneous optimization algorithms. It subsumes previously proposed methods such as FedAvg and FedProx and provides the first principled understanding of the solution bias and the convergence slowdown due to objective inconsistency. paragraphs: Federated learning combines models trained locally by different clients. Because clients have different datasets and computation speeds, they may perform very different numbers of updates before their models are aggregated. This paper shows that naive weighted averaging can then create objective inconsistency: the global model approaches a stationary point of an objective that differs from the intended one.

The mismatch can be arbitrarily large, so making progress on the aggregated objective does not necessarily mean solving the intended learning problem. The authors develop a general convergence-analysis framework covering heterogeneous federated optimization methods, including FedAvg and FedProx. It explains both the bias in the resulting solution and the slowdown associated with objective inconsistency.

Using that analysis, the paper introduces FedNova, a normalized averaging method that eliminates the objective inconsistency while preserving fast error convergence. The contribution links a specific failure mechanism to an aggregation correction. It clarifies why unequal amounts of local computation affect what is optimized, and provides a method designed to align aggregation with the true objective.
summary.tldr: FedNova normalizes federated averaging to eliminate objective mismatch caused by unequal local updates while retaining fast error convergence.

title: Tackling the Objective Inconsistency Problem in Heterogeneous Federated Optimization

abstract: The work studies how node-to-node communications over an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random network influence distributed online convex optimization, which is vital in solving large-scale machine learning in antagonistic or changing environments. At per step, each node (computing unit) makes a local decision, experiences a loss evaluated with a convex function, and communicates the decision with other nodes over a network. The node-to-node communications are described by the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi rule, where independently each link takes place with a probability $p$ over a prescribed connected graph. The objective is to minimize the system-wide loss accumulated over a finite time horizon. We consider standard distributed gradient descents with full gradients, one-point bandits and two-points bandits for convex and strongly convex losses, respectively. We establish how the regret bounds scale with respect to time horizon $T$, network size $N$, decision dimension $d$, and an algebraic network connectivity. The regret bounds scaling with respect to $T$ match those obtained by state-of-the-art algorithms and fundamental limits in the corresponding centralized online optimization problems, e.g., $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) $ and $\mathcal{O}(\ln(T)) $ regrets are established for convex and strongly convex losses with full gradient feedback and two-points information, respectively. For classical Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi networks over all-to-all possible node communications, the regret scalings with respect to the probability $p$ are analytically established, based on which the tradeoff between the communication overhead and computation accuracy is clearly demonstrated. Numerical studies have validated the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies distributed online optimization when communication between computing nodes is random. At each step, every node chooses a local decision, incurs a convex loss, and communicates with other nodes. Each potential link in a prescribed connected graph independently appears with probability p.

The authors analyze distributed gradient methods with full-gradient feedback and with one-point or two-point bandit information, covering convex and strongly convex losses. Their regret bounds describe dependence on the time horizon, number of nodes, decision dimension, and algebraic network connectivity. This connects optimization performance to both the feedback available and the communication structure.

The time dependence matches the corresponding centralized rates discussed in the paper, including square-root and logarithmic regret in the specified settings. For networks permitting all-to-all communication, the authors also derive how the bounds depend on p. This makes the tradeoff between communication overhead and optimization accuracy explicit. Numerical studies support the theoretical findings, showing how random connectivity can be incorporated into performance analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies how random communication affects distributed online optimization and exposes a tradeoff between communication cost and accuracy.

title: Online Convex Optimization Over Erdos-Renyi Random Networks

abstract: As a popular approach to modeling the dynamics of training overparametrized neural networks (NNs), the neural tangent kernels (NTK) are known to fall behind real-world NNs in generalization ability. This performance gap is in part due to the \textit{label agnostic} nature of the NTK, which renders the resulting kernel not as \textit{locally elastic} as NNs~\citep{he2019local}. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach from the perspective of \emph{label-awareness} to reduce this gap for the NTK. Specifically, we propose two label-aware kernels that are each a superimposition of a label-agnostic part and a hierarchy of label-aware parts with increasing complexity of label dependence, using the Hoeffding decomposition. Through both theoretical and empirical evidence, we show that the models trained with the proposed kernels better simulate NNs in terms of generalization ability and local elasticity.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernels are used to model how heavily overparameterized neural networks train, but their generalization can lag behind that of practical networks. This paper attributes part of the gap to their lack of label awareness. In the authors' account, ignoring labels also makes these kernels less locally elastic than the networks they aim to represent.

The authors propose two kernels that explicitly incorporate label information. Each combines a label-independent component with a hierarchy of label-dependent components. The hierarchy uses the Hoeffding decomposition, organizing the additional components by increasingly complex dependence on labels. This gives a structured way to add label sensitivity to the kernel.

The paper supplies both theoretical and empirical evidence that models using these kernels better reproduce neural networks' generalization and local elasticity. The claim is an improvement in the correspondence between kernel models and networks, with label awareness addressing one identified source of the gap. The contribution therefore concerns both predictive behavior and the usefulness of kernels as models of neural-network learning.
summary.tldr: Two label-aware neural tangent kernels better reproduce neural networks' generalization and local elasticity through structured label-dependent components.

title: Label-Aware Neural Tangent Kernel: Toward Better Generalization and Local Elasticity

abstract: Multiclass extensions of the support vector machine (SVM) have been formulated in a variety of ways. A recent empirical comparison of nine such formulations [Doǧan et al. 2016] recommends the variant proposed by Weston and Watkins (WW), despite the fact that the WW-hinge loss is not calibrated with respect to the 0-1 loss. In this work we introduce a novel discrete loss function for multiclass classification, the ordered partition loss, and prove that the WW-hinge loss is calibrated with respect to this loss. We also argue that the ordered partition loss is minimally emblematic among discrete losses satisfying this property. Finally, we apply our theory to justify the empirical observation made by Doǧan et al that the WW-SVM can work well even under massive label noise, a challenging setting for multiclass SVMs.

paragraphs: Multiclass support vector machines can be formulated with different training losses. An empirical comparison favored the Weston-Watkins formulation even though its hinge loss is not calibrated to ordinary 0-1 classification loss. This creates a theoretical question: what discrete prediction objective does the Weston-Watkins loss appropriately represent?

The paper introduces an ordered partition loss and proves that the Weston-Watkins hinge loss is calibrated with respect to it. Calibration supplies a principled relationship between the surrogate used during optimization and the discrete loss used to evaluate decisions. The result identifies such a relationship for a different target than simple correct-versus-incorrect classification.

The authors also argue that ordered partition loss is minimally emblematic among discrete losses with this calibration property, giving it a distinguished role in their account. Finally, they use the theory to justify the observed ability of Weston-Watkins SVMs to perform well under massive label noise. The contribution explains an empirical success by identifying the loss structure behind it, without changing the stated lack of calibration to 0-1 loss.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that Weston-Watkins hinge loss is calibrated to a new ordered partition loss and uses this theory to explain observed robustness to heavy label noise.

title: Weston-Watkins Hinge Loss and Ordered Partitions

abstract: This paper studies the statistical complexity of kernel hyperparameter tuning in the setting of active regression under adversarial noise. We consider the problem of finding the best interpolant from a class of kernels with unknown hyperparameters, assuming only that the noise is square-integrable. We provide finite-sample guarantees for the problem, characterizing how increasing the complexity of the kernel class increases the complexity of learning kernel hyperparameters. For common kernel classes (e.g. squared-exponential kernels with unknown lengthscale), our results show that hyperparameter optimization increases sample complexity by just a logarithmic factor, in comparison to the setting where optimal parameters are known in advance. Our result is based on a subsampling guarantee for linear regression under multiple design matrices which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Choosing a kernel's hyperparameters introduces an extra learning problem beyond fitting with a known kernel. This paper quantifies that statistical cost for active regression under adversarial noise. The goal is to select the best interpolant from a kernel class whose hyperparameters are unknown.

The noise assumption is square-integrability, and the authors derive finite-sample guarantees under that assumption. Their analysis connects the complexity of the kernel family to the difficulty of learning its hyperparameters. This makes the range of kernels under consideration an explicit part of the sample requirements.

For common families, including squared-exponential kernels with an unknown lengthscale, tuning adds only a logarithmic factor to sample complexity compared with knowing the optimal parameters beforehand. The proof relies on a subsampling guarantee for linear regression with multiple design matrices, which may also be useful separately. The main finding is that searching over these kernel parameters can have a relatively modest statistical overhead, even in the stated adversarial-noise setting.
summary.tldr: For common kernel families, robust hyperparameter tuning adds only a logarithmic sample-complexity factor over knowing the optimal parameters.

title: The Statistical Cost of Robust Kernel Hyperparameter Turning

abstract: Multi-person pose estimation in crowded scenes is challenging because overlapping and occlusions make it difficult to detect person bounding boxes and infer pose cues from individual keypoints. To address those issues, this paper proposes a direct pose-level inference strategy that is free of bounding box detection and keypoint grouping. Instead of inferring individual keypoints, the Pose-level Inference Network (PINet) directly infers the complete pose cues for a person from his/her visible body parts. PINet first applies the Part-based Pose Generation (PPG) to infer multiple coarse poses for each person from his/her body parts. Those coarse poses are refined by the Pose Refinement module through incorporating pose priors, and finally are fused in the Pose Fusion module. PINet relies on discriminative body parts to differentiate overlapped persons, and applies visual body cues to infer the global pose cues. Experiments on several crowded scenes pose estimation benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of PINet. For instance, it achieves 59.8% AP on the OCHuman dataset, outperforming the recent works by a large margin.

paragraphs: Estimating human poses in crowds is difficult because people overlap and hide parts of one another. These conditions make both person bounding boxes and individual body keypoints unreliable. The paper introduces PINet, a network that infers complete pose cues directly from visible body parts without requiring bounding-box detection or keypoint grouping.

PINet first generates several coarse pose estimates for each person from their body parts. A refinement module improves these estimates using pose priors, and a fusion module combines them. The method uses distinctive visible parts to distinguish overlapping people while drawing on body appearance cues to infer a person’s overall pose.

This design connects partial visual evidence directly to whole-person hypotheses, addressing the difficulty of assembling poses from separately detected keypoints in crowded images. Experiments on several crowded-scene benchmarks demonstrate the method’s superiority in the reported comparisons. On OCHuman, PINet achieves 59.8% average precision and outperforms recent work by a large margin. The results support direct pose-level inference as an effective strategy for the evaluated overlap and occlusion settings.
summary.tldr: PINet estimates whole-person poses from visible body parts, improving crowded-scene pose estimation without bounding-box detection or keypoint grouping.

title: Robust Pose Estimation in Crowded Scenes with Direct Pose-Level Inference

abstract: Sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGP) methods are a common choice for non-conjugate Gaussian process inference because of their computational benefits. In this paper, we improve their computational efficiency by using a dual parameterization where each data example is assigned dual parameters, similarly to site parameters used in expectation propagation. Our dual parameterization speeds-up inference using natural gradient descent, and provides a tighter evidence lower bound for hyperparameter learning. The approach has the same memory cost as the current SVGP methods, but it is faster and more accurate.

paragraphs: Sparse variational Gaussian processes offer computational advantages for Gaussian process inference in non-conjugate settings. This paper aims to make that inference more efficient by changing how the variational approximation is parameterized. The central contribution is a dual representation that assigns parameters to individual training examples, resembling the site parameters used in expectation propagation.

This representation improves two parts of learning. It accelerates inference performed with natural gradient descent, and it supplies a tighter evidence lower bound for learning hyperparameters. These are distinct benefits: one concerns the process of computing the approximation, while the other concerns the bound used to fit the model’s hyperparameters. The proposed parameterization supports both within the sparse variational framework.

The abstract reports that the approach is faster and more accurate while retaining the memory cost of existing sparse variational Gaussian process methods. This makes the result relevant when computational efficiency motivates choosing a sparse approximation in the first place. The reported improvement comes from a different representation of the inference problem without an accompanying increase in memory cost.
summary.tldr: A dual parameterization speeds sparse variational Gaussian process inference and tightens hyperparameter learning bounds without increasing memory cost.

title: Dual Parameterization of Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes

abstract: Most existing imitation learning approaches assume the demonstrations are drawn from experts who are optimal, but relaxing this assumption enables us to use a wider range of data. Standard imitation learning may learn a suboptimal policy from demonstrations with varying optimality. Prior works use confidence scores or rankings to capture beneficial information from demonstrations with varying optimality, but they suffer from many limitations, e.g., manually annotated confidence scores or high average optimality of demonstrations. In this paper, we propose a general framework to learn from demonstrations with varying optimality that jointly learns the confidence score and a well-performing policy. Our approach, Confidence-Aware Imitation Learning (CAIL) learns a well-performing policy from confidence-reweighted demonstrations, while using an outer loss to track the performance of our model and to learn the confidence. We provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of CAIL and evaluate its performance in both simulated and real robot experiments.Our results show that CAIL significantly outperforms other imitation learning methods from demonstrations with varying optimality. We further show that even without access to any optimal demonstrations, CAIL can still learn a successful policy, and outperforms prior work.

paragraphs: Imitation learning often assumes that demonstrations come from optimal experts. When demonstration quality varies, copying the available behavior can produce a poor policy. Confidence-Aware Imitation Learning, or CAIL, addresses this problem by jointly learning a policy and confidence scores that determine how demonstrations contribute to its training.

CAIL trains the policy using demonstrations reweighted by confidence. An outer loss tracks model performance and guides the learning of those confidence values. This creates a connection between the usefulness of demonstration data and the policy being learned, addressing limitations of earlier approaches that require manually assigned confidence or highly optimal demonstrations on average.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and evaluates the framework in simulated and real robot experiments. It reports significant improvements over other imitation-learning methods for demonstrations of varying quality. It further demonstrates successful policy learning without any optimal demonstrations, outperforming prior work in that setting. These results show that, in the evaluated cases, useful behavior can be recovered by learning how much to trust imperfect demonstrations.
summary.tldr: CAIL jointly learns demonstration confidence and a policy, enabling successful imitation from mixed-quality data even without optimal demonstrations in the reported experiments.

title: Confidence-Aware Imitation Learning from Demonstrations with Varying Optimality

abstract: Imitation learning enables high-fidelity, vision-based learning of policies within rich, photorealistic environments. However, such techniques often rely on traditional discrete-time neural models and face difficulties in generalizing to domain shifts by failing to account for the causal relationships between the agent and the environment. In this paper, we propose a theoretical and experimental framework for learning causal representations using continuous-time neural networks, specifically over their discrete-time counterparts. We evaluate our method in the context of visual-control learning of drones over a series of complex tasks, ranging from short- and long-term navigation, to chasing static and dynamic objects through photorealistic environments. Our results demonstrate that causal continuous-time deep models can perform robust navigation tasks, where advanced recurrent models fail. These models learn complex causal control representations directly from raw visual inputs and scale to solve a variety of tasks using imitation learning.

paragraphs: Learning navigation from visual demonstrations can work well in rich environments yet struggle when the environment changes. The paper attributes part of this difficulty to discrete-time neural models failing to account for causal relationships between an agent and its surroundings. It investigates continuous-time networks as a way to learn those relationships.

The authors develop both a theoretical and an experimental framework for causal representation learning with continuous-time neural networks. Their application is drone control from raw visual inputs, trained through imitation learning. The evaluated tasks span short- and long-term navigation as well as pursuing static and moving objects in photorealistic environments.

The reported results show robust navigation in tested settings where advanced recurrent models fail. They also demonstrate that the continuous-time models can learn complex causal control representations directly from visual observations and handle a variety of tasks. The significance is that the model's treatment of temporal dynamics becomes part of the approach to generalization, alongside learning which control actions follow from the observed scene.
summary.tldr: Continuous-time neural networks learn causal visual-control representations that support robust drone navigation across the paper's evaluated tasks.

title: Causal Navigation by Continuous-time Neural Networks

abstract: This work introduces a dataset for large-scale instance-level recognition in the domain of artworks. The proposed benchmark exhibits a number of different challenges such as large inter-class similarity, long tail distribution, and many classes. We rely on the open access collection of The Met museum to form a large training set of about 224k classes, where each class corresponds to a museum exhibit with photos taken under studio conditions. Testing is primarily performed on photos taken by museum guests depicting exhibits, which introduces a distribution shift between training and testing. Testing is additionally performed on a set of images not related to Met exhibits making the task resemble an out-of-distribution detection problem. The proposed benchmark follows the paradigm of other recent datasets for instance level recognition on different domains to encourage research on domain independent approaches. A number of suitable approaches are evaluated to offer a testbed for future comparisons. Self-supervised and supervised contrastive learning are effectively combined to train the backbone which is used for non-parametric classification that is shown as a promising direction. Dataset webpage: http://cmp.felk.cvut.cz/met/

paragraphs: The Met Dataset studies recognition of individual artworks, with each museum exhibit treated as its own class. Built from the museum’s open collection, the training set covers about 224,000 classes using studio photographs. The challenge combines a large number of classes, uneven representation, and strong visual similarity between different exhibits.

Most testing uses photographs taken by museum visitors, introducing a shift from the controlled appearance of training images. Additional test images do not depict Met exhibits, adding a setting resembling out-of-distribution detection. Together, these tests examine recognition across photographic conditions and behavior when images fall outside the collection being recognized.

The authors evaluate several approaches to establish a comparison resource. They report that combining self-supervised and supervised contrastive learning effectively trains a visual backbone for non-parametric classification, identifying this as a promising direction. The benchmark also follows conventions from instance recognition in other domains to encourage methods whose usefulness can extend across different kinds of objects.
summary.tldr: The Met Dataset benchmarks recognition of individual artworks across studio and visitor photographs, with additional tests on images outside the collection.

title: The Met Dataset: Instance-level Recognition for Artworks

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success on a node classification task. Despite the broad interest in developing and evaluating GNNs, they have been assessed with limited benchmark datasets. As a result, the existing evaluation of GNNs lacks fine-grained analysis from various characteristics of graphs. Motivated by this, we conduct extensive experiments with a synthetic graph generator that can generate graphs having controlled characteristics for fine-grained analysis. Our empirical studies clarify the strengths and weaknesses of GNNs from four major characteristics of real-world graphs with class labels of nodes, i.e., 1) class size distributions (balanced vs. imbalanced), 2) edge connection proportions between classes (homophilic vs. heterophilic), 3) attribute values (biased vs. random), and 4) graph sizes (small vs. large). In addition, to foster future research on GNNs, we publicly release our codebase that allows users to evaluate various GNNs with various graphs. We hope this work offers interesting insights for future research.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are widely used to assign labels to nodes, but evaluation on a limited collection of benchmark graphs gives an incomplete picture of their behavior. This paper investigates performance through synthetic graphs whose characteristics can be controlled, allowing a finer-grained examination of where different GNNs succeed or struggle.

The study varies four properties: whether node classes are balanced, whether edges tend to connect nodes of the same or different classes, whether node attributes are biased or random, and whether graphs are small or large. Controlling these properties provides a way to examine particular aspects of a graph instead of relying only on comparisons between existing datasets.

The authors report that these experiments clarify GNN strengths and weaknesses across the studied characteristics. The contribution is an evaluation framework and empirical analysis, rather than a new node-classification architecture. A publicly released codebase lets researchers evaluate different GNNs on generated graphs, extending the same style of controlled investigation to future methods.
summary.tldr: Controlled synthetic graphs reveal how node-classification GNNs behave as class balance, connectivity, attributes, and graph size change.

title: Beyond Real-world Benchmark Datasets: An Empirical Study of Node Classification with GNNs

abstract:
Optimal transport (OT) theory describes general principles to define and select, among many possible choices, the most efficient way to map a probability measure onto another. That theory has been mostly used to estimate, given a pair of source and target probability measures $(\mu,
u)$, a parameterized map $T_	heta$ that can efficiently map $\mu$ onto $
u$. In many applications, such as predicting cell responses to treatments, pairs of input/output data measures $(\mu,
u)$ that define optimal transport problems do not arise in isolation but are associated with a context $c$, as for instance a treatment when comparing populations of untreated and treated cells. To account for that context in OT estimation, we introduce CondOT, a multi-task approach to estimate a family of OT maps conditioned on a context variable, using several pairs of measures $(\mu_i, 
u_i)$ tagged with a context label $c_i$. CondOT learns a global map $\mathcal{T}_{	heta}$ conditioned on context that is not only expected to fit all labeled pairs in the dataset $\{(c_i, (\mu_i, 
u_i))\}$, i.e., $\mathcal{T}_{	heta}(c_i) \sharp\mu_i \approx 
u_i$, but should also generalize to produce meaningful maps $\mathcal{T}_{	heta}(c_{	ext{new}})$ when conditioned on unseen contexts $c_{	ext{new}}$. Our approach harnesses and provides a novel usage for partially input convex neural networks, for which we introduce a robust and efficient initialization strategy inspired by Gaussian approximations. We demonstrate the ability of CondOT to infer the effect of an arbitrary combination of genetic or therapeutic perturbations on single cells, using only observations of the effects of said perturbations separately.

paragraphs: Optimal transport describes efficient ways to map one probability distribution onto another. Many applications involve related transport problems whose differences are explained by context, such as the treatment applied to a cell population. CondOT learns across these problems, using context-labeled pairs of input and output distributions.

The method trains a global, context-conditioned map rather than estimating each transport problem in isolation. It aims to fit the observed distribution pairs and produce meaningful maps for previously unseen contexts. Its architecture uses partially input convex neural networks, with a new initialization strategy inspired by Gaussian approximations that the authors describe as robust and efficient.

The demonstrated application predicts how single cells respond to combinations of genetic or therapeutic perturbations. CondOT infers combined effects using observations of the individual perturbations alone. This illustrates the value of sharing information across contextual transport problems: the learned family of maps can support predictions beyond the contexts directly observed during training. The stated generalization goal is supported by this application, rather than presented as a universal guarantee for arbitrary unseen contexts.
summary.tldr: CondOT learns context-conditioned transport maps and demonstrates prediction of combined cellular perturbations from observations of their individual effects.

title: Supervised Training of Conditional Monge Maps

abstract: Recently, significant progress has been made in masked image modeling to catch up to masked language modeling. However, unlike words in NLP, the lack of semantic decomposition of images still makes masked autoencoding (MAE) different between vision and language. In this paper, we explore a potential visual analogue of words, i.e., semantic parts, and we integrate semantic information into the training process of MAE by proposing a Semantic-Guided Masking strategy. Compared to widely adopted random masking, our masking strategy can gradually guide the network to learn various information, i.e., from intra-part patterns to inter-part relations. In particular, we achieve this in two steps. 1) Semantic part learning: we design a self-supervised part learning method to obtain semantic parts by leveraging and refining the multi-head attention of a ViT-based encoder. 2) Semantic-guided MAE (SemMAE) training: we design a masking strategy that varies from masking a portion of patches in each part to masking a portion of (whole) parts in an image. Extensive experiments on various vision tasks show that SemMAE can learn better image representation by integrating semantic information. In particular, SemMAE achieves 84.5% fine-tuning accuracy on ImageNet-1k, which outperforms the vanilla MAE by 1.4%. In the semantic segmentation and fine-grained recognition tasks, SemMAE also brings significant improvements and yields the state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Masked autoencoders learn image representations by reconstructing hidden content, but image patches do not naturally provide semantic units like words. SemMAE explores semantic parts as a possible visual counterpart. It uses those parts to organize which content is hidden, making the masking process reflect relationships within and between meaningful image regions.

The method first learns semantic parts without supervision by using and refining the multiple attention heads of a vision-transformer encoder. It then changes the masking strategy during training: initially, portions of patches within each part are hidden; later, entire parts are hidden. This progression is designed to guide learning from patterns inside parts toward relationships among parts.

Experiments report stronger image representations across several vision tasks. SemMAE achieves 84.5% fine-tuning accuracy on ImageNet-1k, exceeding vanilla MAE by the reported 1.4%. It also improves semantic segmentation and fine-grained recognition, reaching state-of-the-art performance in the reported evaluations. The findings support treating mask selection as a structured learning mechanism that can incorporate semantic organization.
summary.tldr: SemMAE learns semantic image parts and progressively masks them to teach representations that capture both within-part patterns and between-part relationships.

title: SemMAE: Semantic-Guided Masking for Learning Masked Autoencoders

abstract: While several types of post hoc explanation methods have been proposed in recent literature, there is very little work on systematically benchmarking these methods. Here, we introduce OpenXAI, a comprehensive and extensible open-source framework for evaluating and benchmarking post hoc explanation methods. OpenXAI comprises of the following key components: (i) a flexible synthetic data generator and a collection of diverse real-world datasets, pre-trained models, and state-of-the-art feature attribution methods, (ii) open-source implementations of twenty-two quantitative metrics for evaluating faithfulness, stability (robustness), and fairness of explanation methods, and (iii) the first ever public XAI leaderboards to readily compare several explanation methods across a wide variety of metrics, models, and datasets. OpenXAI is easily extensible, as users can readily evaluate custom explanation methods and incorporate them into our leaderboards. Overall, OpenXAI provides an automated end-to-end pipeline that not only simplifies and standardizes the evaluation of post hoc explanation methods, but also promotes transparency and reproducibility in benchmarking these methods. While the first release of OpenXAI supports only tabular datasets, the explanation methods and metrics that we consider are general enough to be applicable to other data modalities. OpenXAI datasets and data loaders, implementations of state-of-the-art explanation methods and evaluation metrics, as well as leaderboards are publicly available at https://open-xai.github.io/. OpenXAI will be regularly updated to incorporate text and image datasets, other new metrics and explanation methods, and welcomes inputs from the community.
