While the first release of OpenXAI supports only tabular datasets, the explanation methods and metrics that we consider are general enough to be applicable to other data modalities. OpenXAI datasets and data loaders, implementations of state-of-the-art explanation methods and evaluation metrics, as well as leaderboards are publicly available at https://open-xai.github.io/. OpenXAI will be regularly updated to incorporate text and image datasets, other new metrics and explanation methods, and welcomes inputs from the community.

paragraphs: Methods that explain a trained model's predictions are plentiful, but systematic comparisons between them have received less attention. OpenXAI provides an open-source framework for evaluating these post hoc explanations. Its purpose is to make benchmarking easier to reproduce and more transparent by putting data, models, explanation methods, and evaluation tools into a shared pipeline.

The framework includes a flexible synthetic-data generator, real-world datasets, pretrained models, and feature-attribution methods. It implements 22 quantitative metrics covering faithfulness, stability or robustness, and fairness. Public leaderboards compare explanation methods across metrics, models, and datasets, while users can evaluate their own methods and add them to the comparisons.

The first release supports tabular datasets only, although the authors describe the selected methods and metrics as general enough for other modalities. The framework's contribution is standardized, extensible evaluation across several dimensions of explanation quality. This makes it possible to examine how methods behave under different assessment criteria rather than relying on isolated demonstrations.
summary.tldr: OpenXAI standardizes explanation benchmarking with datasets, models, 22 evaluation metrics, and extensible public leaderboards.

title: OpenXAI: Towards a Transparent Evaluation of Model Explanations

abstract: The spectacular successes of recurrent neural network models where key parameters are adjusted via backpropagation-based gradient descent have inspired much thought as to how biological neuronal networks might solve the corresponding synaptic credit assignment problem [1, 2, 3]. There is so far little agreement, however, as to how biological networks could implement the necessary backpropagation through time, given widely recognized constraints of biological synaptic network signaling architectures. Here, we propose that extra-synaptic diffusion of local neuromodulators such as neuropeptides may afford an effective mode of backpropagation lying within the bounds of biological plausibility. Going beyond existing temporal truncation-based gradient approximations [4, 5, 6], our approximate gradient-based update rule, ModProp, propagates credit information through arbitrary time steps. ModProp suggests that modulatory signals can act on receiving cells by convolving their eligibility traces via causal, time-invariant and synapse-type-specific filter taps. Our mathematical analysis of ModProp learning, together with simulation results on benchmark temporal tasks, demonstrate the advantage of ModProp over existing biologically-plausible temporal credit assignment rules. These results suggest a potential neuronal mechanism for signaling credit information related to recurrent interactions over a longer time horizon. Finally, we derive an in-silico implementation of ModProp that could serve as a low-complexity and causal alternative to backpropagation through time.

paragraphs: Learning in recurrent networks requires assigning credit to earlier interactions that influenced later outcomes. Backpropagation through time performs this role in artificial networks, but implementing its signaling requirements in biological networks is difficult. This paper proposes that locally diffusing neuromodulators, such as neuropeptides, could provide a biologically plausible way to carry temporal credit information.

The proposed update rule, ModProp, approximates gradient-based learning while allowing credit to propagate across arbitrary numbers of time steps. It goes beyond approximations that explicitly truncate the temporal span. Its mechanism combines modulatory signals with receiving cells’ eligibility traces through causal filters whose behavior is time-invariant and specific to synapse type.

Mathematical analysis and simulations on benchmark temporal tasks show advantages over existing biologically plausible temporal credit-assignment rules. These results support a possible mechanism for communicating the consequences of recurrent interactions over longer horizons; they do not establish that biological networks actually implement it. The authors also derive a computational implementation that could offer a causal, low-complexity alternative to backpropagation through time, connecting the biological proposal to an artificial learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: ModProp proposes local neuromodulator signaling as a biologically plausible mechanism for approximate credit assignment across long temporal spans.

title: Biologically-plausible backpropagation through arbitrary timespans via local neuromodulators

abstract: Large neural networks trained in the overparameterized regime are able to fit noise to zero train error. Recent work of Nakkiran and Bansal has empirically observed that such networks behave as “conditional samplers” from the noisy distribution. That is, they replicate the noise in the train data to unseen examples. We give a theoretical framework for studying this conditional sampling behavior in the context of learning theory. We relate the notion of such samplers to knowledge distillation, where a student network imitates the outputs of a teacher on unlabeled data. We show that samplers, while being bad classifiers, can be good teachers. Concretely, we prove that distillation from samplers is guaranteed to produce a student which approximates the Bayes optimal classifier. Finally, we show that some common learning algorithms (e.g., Nearest-Neighbours and Kernel Machines) can often generate samplers when applied in the overparameterized regime.

paragraphs: A model that fits noisy training labels perfectly may reproduce that noise on unseen examples. The paper studies this behavior through conditional sampling: the model acts like a sampler from the noisy label distribution associated with an input. Such a model can be a poor classifier when judged by its individual predictions.

The authors develop a learning-theoretic framework for conditional samplers and connect it to knowledge distillation. In distillation, a student learns from a teacher’s outputs on unlabeled examples. They prove that distilling from samplers can produce a student that approximates the Bayes-optimal classifier, the best classification rule for the underlying distribution.

The result distinguishes a teacher’s classification quality from the usefulness of the information it supplies during learning. A noisy teacher can still provide a valuable training signal when it has the sampler behavior analyzed by the framework. The authors also show that familiar methods, including nearest-neighbor algorithms and kernel machines, can often generate such samplers in overparameterized settings.
summary.tldr: Models that sample noisy labels can be poor classifiers yet useful teachers, with distillation guarantees under the paper’s sampler framework.

title: Knowledge Distillation: Bad Models Can Be Good Role Models

abstract: We consider the problem of regret minimization in non-parametric stochastic bandits. When the rewards are known to be bounded from above, there exists asymptotically optimal algorithms, with asymptotic regret depending on an infimum of Kullback-Leibler divergences (KL). These algorithms are computationally expensive and require storing all past rewards, thus simpler but non-optimal algorithms are often used instead. We introduce several methods to approximate the infimum KL which reduce drastically the computational and memory costs of existing optimal algorithms, while keeping their regret guaranties. We apply our findings to design new variants of the MED and IMED algorithms, and demonstrate their interest with extensive numerical simulations.

When the rewards are known to be bounded from above, there exists asymptotically optimal algorithms, with asymptotic regret depending on an infimum of Kullback-Leibler divergences (KL). These algorithms are computationally expensive and require storing all past rewards, thus simpler but non-optimal algorithms are often used instead. We introduce several methods to approximate the infimum KL which reduce drastically the computational and memory costs of existing optimal algorithms, while keeping their regret guaranties. We apply our findings to design new variants of the MED and IMED algorithms, and demonstrate their interest with extensive numerical simulations.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit algorithm repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain rewards, trying to limit the reward lost through imperfect choices. This paper studies that regret-minimization problem without imposing a parametric reward model. Its setting assumes that rewards have a known upper bound, under which asymptotically optimal algorithms already exist.

The obstacle is their practical cost. Existing optimal methods depend on an infimum of Kullback–Leibler divergences, a distribution-comparison quantity that is expensive to compute. They also require storing all previous rewards. Consequently, simpler algorithms are often used even though they lack the same optimality guarantees.

The authors introduce several approximations to this KL-based quantity that substantially reduce computation and memory requirements while preserving the regret guarantees. They use the results to construct new versions of MED and IMED and examine them through extensive numerical simulations. The significance is that cheaper computation need not require giving up the established long-run regret guarantees in this setting. The stated optimality remains asymptotic and tied to the assumed reward bound.
summary.tldr: New KL approximations reduce the computation and memory costs of non-parametric bandit algorithms while preserving their asymptotic regret guarantees.

title: Fast Asymptotically Optimal Algorithms for Non-Parametric Stochastic Bandits

abstract: The marriage of Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) and Homomorphic Encryption (HE) enables the inference of graph data on the cloud with significantly enhanced client data privacy. However, the tremendous computation and memory overhead associated with HE operations challenges the practicality of HE-based GCN inference. GCN inference involves a sequence of expensive matrix-matrix multiplications, and we observe that directly applying the state-of-the-art HE-based secure matrix-matrix multiplication solutions to accelerate HE-GCN inference is far less efficient as it does not exploit the unique aggregation mechanism of two-dimension graph node-features in GCN layer computation. As a result, in this paper, we propose a novel HE-based ciphertext packing technique, i.e., Penguin, that can take advantage of the unique computation pattern during the HE-GCN inference to significantly reduce the computation and memory overhead associated with HE operations.Specifically, Penguin employs (i) an effective two-dimension parallel packing technique for feature ciphertext with optimal graph node partitioning and graph feature interleaving, and (ii) an interleaved assembly technique that can effectively make use of the blank slots to merge ciphertexts after feature reduction and significantly reduce the costly rotation operation.We provide theoretical analysis and experimental validation to demonstrate the speedup achieved by Penguin in accelerating GCN inference using popular GCN models and datasets. Our results show that Penguin can achieve up to $\sim10\times$ speedup and around $\sim79$% reduction in computational memory overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art solutions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that can ensure the protection of both graph structure and features when accelerating HE-GCN inference on encrypted data. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ranran0523/Penguin.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption lets graph convolutional networks process encrypted graph data in the cloud, but its computation and memory costs can be substantial. The paper observes that generic encrypted matrix-multiplication methods miss useful structure in how graph layers aggregate node features. Penguin reorganizes encrypted data to take advantage of that particular computation pattern.

Its packing scheme operates across the two dimensions of node-feature data, combining graph-node partitioning with feature interleaving. After feature reduction, an interleaved assembly step uses empty ciphertext slots to merge ciphertexts. This reduces costly rotation operations and makes more effective use of the encrypted representation as the network changes the feature dimensions.

Theoretical analysis and experiments with popular graph models and datasets support the efficiency gains. Reported improvements reach approximately tenfold speedup and around 79% lower computational memory overhead relative to state-of-the-art solutions. These figures describe the reported results rather than a uniform guarantee for every workload. The authors also identify protection of both graph structure and features during accelerated encrypted inference as a distinguishing contribution.
summary.tldr: Penguin packs encrypted graph features around GCN computation patterns, achieving reported speedups of up to roughly tenfold.

title: Penguin: Parallel-Packed Homomorphic Encryption for Fast Graph Convolutional Network Inference

abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is a method that enables language models to handle complex reasoning tasks by decomposing them into simpler steps. Despite its success, the underlying mechanics of CoT are not yet fully understood. In an attempt to shed light on this, our study investigates the impact of CoT on the ability of transformers to in-context learn a simple to study, yet general family of compositional functions: multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). In this setting, we find that the success of CoT can be attributed to breaking down in-context learning of a compositional function into two distinct phases: focusing on and filtering data related to each step of the composition and in-context learning the single-step composition function. Through both experimental and theoretical evidence, we demonstrate how CoT significantly reduces the sample complexity of in-context learning (ICL) and facilitates the learning of complex functions that non-CoT methods struggle with. Furthermore, we illustrate how transformers can transition from vanilla in-context learning to mastering a compositional function with CoT by simply incorporating additional layers that perform the necessary data-filtering for CoT via the attention mechanism. In addition to these test-time benefits, we show CoT helps accelerate pretraining by learning shortcuts to represent complex functions and filtering plays an important role in this process. These findings collectively provide insights into the mechanics of CoT, inviting further investigation of its role in complex reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting breaks a complex problem into intermediate steps, but its internal benefits remain incompletely understood. This paper investigates those benefits in a controlled setting: transformers learning compositional functions, represented by multilayer perceptrons, from examples in their context. The setting lets the authors study how step-by-step reasoning changes the learning problem.

They identify two interacting operations. First, the transformer focuses on and filters information relevant to the current step. Second, it learns that step's function from the selected context. Experimental and theoretical results show that this decomposition substantially reduces the number of examples needed for in-context learning and enables functions that methods without chain-of-thought struggle to learn.

The authors also show how additional transformer layers can supply the required filtering through attention, extending ordinary in-context learning to compositional learning. Benefits appear during pretraining as well: chain-of-thought supports shortcuts for representing complex functions, with filtering playing an important role. These findings explain mechanisms in the studied function-learning setting and motivate further investigation of their role in broader reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: In a compositional function-learning setting, chain-of-thought improves learning by filtering relevant context and learning one step at a time.

title: Dissecting Chain-of-Thought: Compositionality through In-Context Filtering and Learning

abstract: We study online meta-learning with bandit feedback, with the goal of improving performance across multiple tasks if they are similar according to some natural similarity measure. As the first to target the adversarial online-within-online partial-information setting, we design meta-algorithms that combine outer learners to simultaneously tune the initialization and other hyperparameters of an inner learner for two important cases: multi-armed bandits (MAB) and bandit linear optimization (BLO). For MAB, the meta-learners initialize and set hyperparameters of the Tsallis-entropy generalization of Exp3, with the task-averaged regret improving if the entropy of the optima-in-hindsight is small. For BLO, we learn to initialize and tune online mirror descent (OMD) with self-concordant barrier regularizers, showing that task-averaged regret varies directly with an action space-dependent measure they induce. Our guarantees rely on proving that unregularized follow-the-leader combined with two levels of low-dimensional hyperparameter tuning is enough to learn a sequence of affine functions of non-Lipschitz and sometimes non-convex Bregman divergences bounding the regret of OMD.

paragraphs: Bandit learners make decisions with feedback limited to the actions they take. This paper studies how a learner can improve across multiple adversarial tasks when those tasks share useful structure. An outer learning process adjusts the starting point and other hyperparameters of an inner learner that handles decisions within each task.

For multi-armed bandits, the method tunes a Tsallis-entropy generalization of Exp3. Its task-averaged regret improves when the best actions identified in hindsight have low entropy, capturing one form of similarity across tasks. For bandit linear optimization, the method tunes online mirror descent with self-concordant barrier regularizers, with guarantees tied to a measure determined by the action space.

The theoretical contribution shows that follow-the-leader, combined with two levels of low-dimensional hyperparameter tuning, can learn the quantities needed to control the inner learner's regret. This remains possible despite non-Lipschitz and sometimes non-convex Bregman divergences in the analysis. The resulting guarantees make the benefits of cross-task adaptation conditional on explicit measures of shared structure.
summary.tldr: Meta-learning tunes adversarial bandit algorithms across tasks, with regret improvements linked to explicit measures of task similarity.

title: Meta-Learning Adversarial Bandit Algorithms

abstract: This paper presents a collaborative implicit neural simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system with RGB-D image sequences, which consists of complete front-end and back-end modules including odometry, loop detection, sub-map fusion, and global refinement. In order to enable all these modules in a unified framework, we propose a novel neural point based 3D scene representation in which each point maintains a learnable neural feature for scene encoding and is associated with a certain keyframe. Moreover, a distributed-to-centralized learning strategy is proposed for the collaborative implicit SLAM to improve consistency and cooperation. A novel global optimization framework is also proposed to improve the system accuracy like traditional bundle adjustment. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in both camera tracking and mapping.

paragraphs: CP-SLAM builds a collaborative system for estimating camera motion and constructing a scene map from sequences containing both color and depth images. It brings together motion estimation, recognition of previously visited places, fusion of partial maps, and global refinement. The goal is to support these connected operations within one neural mapping framework.

The shared foundation is a three-dimensional point representation. Each point carries a learnable neural feature that encodes scene information and is associated with a selected keyframe. This gives the system a common representation for its mapping and tracking components. The method also uses a learning strategy that moves from distributed processing toward centralized learning to improve cooperation and consistency.

A global optimization framework further refines the system, serving an accuracy-improving role analogous to traditional bundle adjustment. Experiments on multiple datasets report better camera tracking and mapping than the compared approaches. The contribution is thus an integrated collaborative SLAM system whose representation, learning strategy, and refinement procedure are designed to work together.
summary.tldr: CP-SLAM combines neural scene points, collaborative learning, and global refinement to improve camera tracking and mapping from RGB-D sequences.

title: CP-SLAM: Collaborative Neural Point-based SLAM System

abstract: As societal awareness of climate change grows, corporate climate policy engagements are attracting attention.We propose a dataset to estimate corporate climate policy engagement from various PDF-formatted documents.Our dataset comes from LobbyMap (a platform operated by global think tank InfluenceMap) that provides engagement categories and stances on the documents.To convert the LobbyMap data into the structured dataset, we developed a pipeline using text extraction and OCR.Our contributions are: (i) Building an NLP dataset including 10K documents on corporate climate policy engagement. (ii) Analyzing the properties and challenges of the dataset. (iii) Providing experiments for the dataset using pre-trained language models.The results show that while Longformer outperforms baselines and other pre-trained models, there is still room for significant improvement.We hope our work begins to bridge research on NLP and climate change.

paragraphs: Understanding corporate involvement in climate policy requires interpreting documents that describe companies' engagement and positions. This paper creates a language-processing dataset for that task, drawing on LobbyMap, a platform operated by InfluenceMap. The source material supplies engagement categories and stances, giving the dataset a defined basis for assessing corporate policy activity.

The authors build a pipeline that converts PDF documents into structured data through text extraction and optical character recognition. The resulting collection contains 10,000 documents. Alongside assembling the data, they analyze its properties and challenges, making the contribution both a resource for modeling and an examination of the task that resource supports.

Experiments evaluate pretrained language models on the dataset. Longformer performs better than the tested baselines and other pretrained models, while the results still leave substantial room for improvement. The benchmark therefore provides a concrete starting point for comparing NLP approaches to corporate climate policy engagement, connecting document analysis with a specific climate-related research problem.
summary.tldr: A 10,000-document benchmark turns corporate climate policy records into an NLP task, with Longformer leading the reported comparisons.

title: An NLP Benchmark Dataset for Assessing Corporate Climate Policy Engagement

abstract: Memorization of training data is an active research area, yet our understanding of the inner workings of neural networks is still in its infancy.Recently, Haim et al. 2022 proposed a scheme to reconstruct training samples from multilayer perceptron binary classifiers, effectively demonstrating that a large portion of training samples are encoded in the parameters of such networks.In this work, we extend their findings in several directions, including reconstruction from multiclass and convolutional neural networks. We derive a more general reconstruction scheme which is applicable to a wider range of loss functions such as regression losses. Moreover, we study the various factors that contribute to networks' susceptibility to such reconstruction schemes. Intriguingly, we observe that using weight decay during training increases reconstructability both in terms of quantity and quality. Additionally, we examine the influence of the number of neurons relative to the number of training samples on the reconstructability.Code: https://github.com/gonbuzaglo/decoreco

paragraphs: A trained network’s parameters can retain enough information to reconstruct some of its training examples. Earlier work demonstrated this for multilayer perceptrons trained on binary classification. This paper broadens the investigation, asking how reconstruction extends to other model types and training objectives, and which training choices affect susceptibility.

The authors extend reconstruction to multiclass classifiers and convolutional neural networks. They also derive a more general reconstruction scheme that applies to a wider range of losses, including regression losses. These extensions show that the reconstruction phenomenon studied in earlier work reaches beyond a single architecture and a two-class prediction problem.

The study additionally examines weight decay and the number of neurons relative to the number of training samples. It observes that weight decay increases both the quantity and quality of reconstructed examples in the investigated settings. This finding makes the training procedure itself relevant to understanding what information remains recoverable from model parameters. The contribution combines broader reconstruction methods with an investigation of factors that influence their success.
summary.tldr: The paper extends training-data reconstruction to more models and losses, and observes increased reconstructability with weight decay.

title: Deconstructing Data Reconstruction: Multiclass, Weight Decay and General Losses

abstract: We study the problem of communication-efficient distributed vector mean estimation, which is a commonly used subroutine in distributed optimization and Federated Learning (FL). Rand-$k$ sparsification is a commonly used technique to reduce communication cost, where each client sends $k < d$ of its coordinates to the server. However, Rand-$k$ is agnostic to any correlations, that might exist between clients in practical scenarios. The recently proposed Rand-$k$-Spatial estimator leverages the cross-client correlation information at the server to improve Rand-$k$'s performance. Yet, the performance of Rand-$k$-Spatial is suboptimal, and improving mean estimation is key to a faster convergence in distributed optimization. We propose the Rand-Proj-Spatial estimator with a more flexible encoding-decoding procedure, which generalizes the encoding of Rand-$k$ by projecting the client vectors to a random $k$-dimensional subspace. We utilize Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform (SRHT) as the projection matrix, and show that Rand-Proj-Spatial with SRHT outperforms Rand-$k$-Spatial, using the correlation information more efficiently. Furthermore, we propose an approach to incorporate varying degrees of correlation, and suggest a practical variant of Rand-Proj-Spatial when the correlation information is not available to the server. Finally, experiments on real-world distributed optimization tasks showcase the superior performance of Rand-Proj-Spatial compared to Rand-$k$-Spatial and other more sophisticated sparsification techniques.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization often requires a server to average vectors held by multiple clients. Sending every coordinate is expensive, so Rand-k sparsification transmits only k coordinates from each d-dimensional vector. This saves communication but ignores relationships between clients. An existing correlation-aware estimator, Rand-k-Spatial, uses those relationships at the server, yet the paper identifies room to improve its estimation performance.

The proposed Rand-Proj-Spatial method changes what clients transmit. It projects each vector into a random k-dimensional subspace, generalizing the coordinate-selection approach. Using a Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform for this projection, the authors show improved performance over Rand-k-Spatial through more effective use of cross-client correlation information.

The paper also develops a way to handle different degrees of correlation and proposes a practical variant for servers without that information. Experiments on real-world distributed optimization tasks report improvements over Rand-k-Spatial and other sparsification methods. The contribution connects communication compression with the shared structure of client vectors, targeting better mean estimates within distributed learning.
summary.tldr: Rand-Proj-Spatial combines random projections with cross-client correlation information to improve communication-efficient distributed mean estimation.

title: Correlation Aware Sparsified Mean Estimation Using Random Projection

abstract: We propose DyGFormer, a new Transformer-based architecture for dynamic graph learning. DyGFormer is conceptually simple and only needs to learn from nodes' historical first-hop interactions by: (1) a neighbor co-occurrence encoding scheme that explores the correlations of the source node and destination node based on their historical sequences; (2) a patching technique that divides each sequence into multiple patches and feeds them to Transformer, allowing the model to effectively and efficiently benefit from longer histories. We also introduce DyGLib, a unified library with standard training pipelines, extensible coding interfaces, and comprehensive evaluating protocols to promote reproducible, scalable, and credible dynamic graph learning research. By performing exhaustive experiments on thirteen datasets for dynamic link prediction and dynamic node classification tasks, we find that DyGFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance on most of the datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing nodes' correlations and long-term temporal dependencies. Moreover, some results of baselines are inconsistent with previous reports, which may be caused by their diverse but less rigorous implementations, showing the importance of DyGLib. All the used resources are publicly available at https://github.com/yule-BUAA/DyGLib.

paragraphs: Dynamic graph learning uses histories of changing interactions to predict links or node properties. This paper introduces DyGFormer, a Transformer architecture that learns from nodes' historical first-hop interactions. It focuses on extracting relationships between two nodes and using longer histories effectively.

DyGFormer combines two mechanisms. Neighbor co-occurrence encoding captures correlations between source and destination nodes through their historical interaction sequences. A patching technique divides each sequence into chunks before sending it to the Transformer, enabling efficient use of longer histories. The paper also introduces DyGLib, a shared library with standardized training pipelines, extensible interfaces, and comprehensive evaluation protocols.

Across thirteen datasets for dynamic link prediction and node classification, DyGFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance on most datasets. Some baseline results differ from earlier reports; the authors suggest that less rigorous and varied implementations may explain those discrepancies. The work therefore contributes both an effective architecture and infrastructure intended to make comparisons more reproducible and credible, with public resources for the reported research.
summary.tldr: DyGFormer uses interaction histories for strong dynamic graph predictions, while DyGLib standardizes training and evaluation.

title: Towards Better Dynamic Graph Learning: New Architecture and Unified Library

abstract: This paper examines the issue of fairness in the estimation of graphical models (GMs), particularly Gaussian, Covariance, and Ising models. These models play a vital role in understanding complex relationships in high-dimensional data. However, standard GMs can result in biased outcomes, especially when the underlying data involves sensitive characteristics or protected groups. To address this, we introduce a comprehensive framework designed to reduce bias in the estimation of GMs related to protected attributes. Our approach involves the integration of the pairwise graph disparity error and a tailored loss function into a nonsmooth multi-objective optimization problem, striving to achieve fairness across different sensitive groups while maintaining the effectiveness of the GMs. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our framework effectively mitigates bias without undermining GMs' performance.

paragraphs: Graphical models describe relationships among variables and help researchers interpret high-dimensional data. However, estimating these relationships can produce biased outcomes when the data involve sensitive attributes or protected groups. This paper studies that issue across Gaussian, Covariance, and Ising models, placing fairness within the estimation problem itself.

The proposed framework combines a measure called pairwise graph disparity error with a tailored loss function. These components form a nonsmooth optimization problem with multiple objectives. The goal is to reduce disparities associated with protected attributes while retaining the model's ability to represent useful relationships in the data.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show reduced bias without undermining model performance in the reported evaluations. This matters because the framework addresses the structure being estimated, making fairness part of how relationships are learned. The evidence supports the compatibility of the chosen fairness objectives with effective graphical modeling in the tested settings. It does not establish that every possible definition of fairness can be satisfied simultaneously.
summary.tldr: The paper integrates disparity measures into graphical-model estimation to reduce protected-group bias while preserving empirical performance.

title: Fairness-Aware Estimation of Graphical Models

abstract: Current multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suffer from ''hallucination'', occasionally generating responses that are not grounded in the input images. To tackle this challenge, one promising path is to utilize reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), which steers MLLMs towards learning superior responses while avoiding inferior ones. We rethink the common practice of using binary preferences (*i.e.*, superior, inferior), and find that adopting multi-level preferences (*e.g.*, superior, medium, inferior) is better for two benefits: 1) It narrows the gap between adjacent levels, thereby encouraging MLLMs to discern subtle differences. 2) It further integrates cross-level comparisons (beyond adjacent-level comparisons), thus providing a broader range of comparisons with hallucination examples. To verify our viewpoint, we present the Automated Multi-level Preference (**AMP**) framework for MLLMs. To facilitate this framework, we first develop an automated dataset generation pipeline that provides high-quality multi-level preference datasets without any human annotators. Furthermore, we design the Multi-level Direct Preference Optimization (MDPO) algorithm to robustly conduct complex multi-level preference learning. Additionally, we propose a new hallucination benchmark, MRHal-Bench. Extensive experiments across public hallucination and general benchmarks, as well as our MRHal-Bench, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/takomc/amp.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models sometimes produce answers that are unsupported by the image they receive. Preference learning can discourage such hallucinations by teaching a model to favor better responses. This paper asks whether the usual division into preferred and rejected answers leaves useful distinctions unused.

The authors propose learning from several quality levels, such as strong, intermediate, and weak responses. Comparisons between neighboring levels ask the model to recognize subtle differences, while comparisons across more distant levels provide a wider range of examples involving hallucination. Their Automated Multi-level Preference framework includes a pipeline that creates these preference datasets without human annotators.

The framework also introduces Multi-level Direct Preference Optimization to handle the richer set of comparisons, alongside a new evaluation benchmark called MRHal-Bench. Experiments on that benchmark, public hallucination benchmarks, and general benchmarks support the method's effectiveness. The contribution combines automated supervision with a learning algorithm designed to use more detailed preference information than a binary ranking provides.
summary.tldr: AMP automatically creates multilevel response preferences and trains multimodal models to make finer distinctions that help reduce image-grounding errors.

title: Automated Multi-level Preference for MLLMs

abstract: Recently, foundation models, particularly large language models (LLMs), have demonstrated an impressive ability to adapt to various tasks by fine-tuning diverse instruction data. Notably, federated foundation models (FedFM) emerge as a privacy preservation method to fine-tune models collaboratively under federated learning (FL) settings by leveraging many distributed datasets with non-IID data. To alleviate communication and computation overhead, parameter-efficient methods are introduced for efficiency, and some research adapted personalization methods to FedFM for better user preferences alignment. However, a critical gap in existing research is the neglect of test-time distribution shifts in real-world applications, and conventional methods for test-time distribution shifts in personalized FL are less effective for FedFM due to their failure to adapt to complex distribution shift scenarios and the requirement to train all parameters. To bridge this gap, we refine the setting in FedFM, termed test-time personalization, which aims to learn personalized federated foundation models on clients while effectively handling test-time distribution shifts simultaneously. To address challenges in this setting, we explore a simple yet effective solution, a Federated Dual-Personalizing Adapter (FedDPA) architecture. By co-working with a foundation model, a global adapter and a local adapter jointly tackle the test-time distribution shifts and client-specific personalization. Additionally, we introduce an instance-wise dynamic weighting mechanism that dynamically integrates the global and local adapters for each test instance during inference, facilitating effective test-time personalization. The effectiveness of the proposed method has been evaluated on benchmark datasets across different NLP tasks.

paragraphs: Federated foundation models allow clients to collaborate on fine-tuning while their datasets remain distributed. Clients can have different data and preferences, creating a need for personalization. This paper adds another concern: the inputs a client encounters at test time may differ from the distribution used to personalize its model.

The authors formulate test-time personalization as handling client-specific preferences and test-time distribution shifts together. Their Federated Dual-Personalizing Adapter, or FedDPA, combines a foundation model with a global adapter and a local adapter. These components jointly address the two demands, using adapters within the parameter-efficient approach motivated by communication and computation costs.

At inference, an instance-wise weighting mechanism dynamically combines the global and local adapters for each example. The balance can therefore vary with the test input rather than being fixed for every client interaction. Evaluations across benchmark NLP tasks support the method's effectiveness. The central contribution is this input-dependent combination of shared and personalized adaptation, designed for settings where client differences and changing test distributions must be handled simultaneously.
summary.tldr: FedDPA dynamically combines global and local adapters to personalize federated foundation models under test-time distribution shifts.

title: Dual-Personalizing Adapter for Federated Foundation Models

abstract: Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) is a new cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) challenge that aims to train an ego agent to work with diverse, unseen partners during deployment. The significant difference between the deployment-time partners' distribution and the training partners' distribution determined by the training algorithm makes ZSC a unique out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization challenge. The potential distribution gap between evaluation and deployment-time partners leads to inadequate evaluation, which is exacerbated by the lack of appropriate evaluation metrics. In this paper, we present **ZSC-Eval**, the first evaluation toolkit and benchmark for ZSC algorithms. ZSC-Eval consists of: 1) Generation of evaluation partner candidates through behavior-preferring rewards to approximate deployment-time partners' distribution; 2) Selection of evaluation partners by Best-Response Diversity (BR-Div); 3) Measurement of generalization performance with various evaluation partners via the Best-Response Proximity (BR-Prox) metric. We use ZSC-Eval to benchmark ZSC algorithms in Overcooked and Google Research Football environments and get novel empirical findings. We also conduct a human experiment of current ZSC algorithms to verify the ZSC-Eval's consistency with human evaluation. ZSC-Eval is now available at https://github.com/sjtu-marl/ZSC-Eval.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination asks an agent to cooperate with partners it did not encounter during training. Evaluation is difficult because the partners selected for testing may differ from those encountered during deployment. A score against an unrepresentative partner population can therefore give an incomplete picture of the agent's ability to generalize.

ZSC-Eval addresses both partner selection and measurement. It first generates candidate partners using rewards that favor different behaviors, aiming to approximate the deployment partner distribution. It then selects evaluation partners using Best-Response Diversity and measures generalization across them with a metric called Best-Response Proximity.

The authors use the toolkit to benchmark coordination algorithms in Overcooked and Google Research Football. They also conduct a human experiment to verify consistency between the toolkit and human evaluation. The contribution is an evaluation process that explicitly considers whom an agent must cooperate with, rather than reducing assessment to performance against a single convenient partner set. It supplies a shared benchmark and metrics for studying generalization across unfamiliar collaborators.
summary.tldr: ZSC-Eval evaluates cooperation with unseen partners through behavior-based partner generation, diversity-based selection, and a dedicated generalization metric.

title: ZSC-Eval: An Evaluation Toolkit and Benchmark for Multi-agent Zero-shot Coordination

abstract: Simulation with realistic and interactive agents represents a key task for autonomous vehicle (AV) software development in order to test AV performance in prescribed, often long-tail scenarios. In this work, we propose SceneDiffuser, a scene-level diffusion prior for traffic simulation. We present a singular framework that unifies two key stages of simulation: scene initialization and scene rollout. Scene initialization refers to generating the initial layout for the traffic in a scene, and scene rollout refers to closed-loop simulation for the behaviors of the agents. While diffusion has been demonstrated to be effective in learning realistic, multimodal agent distributions, two open challenges remain: controllability and closed-loop inference efficiency and realism. To this end, to address controllability challenges, we propose generalized hard constraints, a generalized inference-time constraint mechanism that is simple yet effective. To improve closed-loop inference quality and efficiency, we propose amortized diffusion, a novel diffusion denoising paradigm that amortizes the physical cost of denoising over future simulation rollout steps, reducing the cost of per physical rollout step to a single denoising function evaluation, while dramatically reducing closed-loop errors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Waymo Open Dataset, where we are able to generate distributionally realistic scenes, while obtaining competitive performance in the Sim Agents Challenge, surpassing the state-of-the-art in many realism attributes.

paragraphs: Autonomous vehicle testing needs simulations with realistic traffic participants that interact over time, including in prescribed rare scenarios. SceneDiffuser uses a scene-level diffusion model to unify two parts of this process: generating the initial traffic layout and rolling the scene forward through closed-loop agent behavior. The paper focuses on controllability, realism, and inference cost.

For control, the authors introduce generalized hard constraints that operate during inference. For efficient rollout, they propose amortized diffusion, which spreads denoising work over future simulation steps. This reduces the cost per physical rollout step to one denoising function evaluation while also substantially reducing closed-loop errors. The method thus connects the denoising schedule to the simulation’s progression.

Evaluations on the Waymo Open Dataset show that the system generates scenes whose distributions resemble real traffic. It also achieves competitive performance in the Sim Agents Challenge and surpasses the state of the art on many realism attributes. These findings support a unified diffusion framework for controllable scene creation and efficient interactive rollout.
summary.tldr: SceneDiffuser unifies traffic initialization and rollout, using inference-time constraints and amortized denoising to improve control, efficiency, and realism.

title: SceneDiffuser: Efficient and Controllable Driving Simulation Initialization and Rollout

abstract: We propose Manifold Free-Form Flows (M-FFF), a simple new generative model for data on manifolds. The existing approaches to learning a distribution on arbitrary manifolds are expensive at inference time, since sampling requires solving a differential equation. Our method overcomes this limitation by sampling in a single function evaluation. The key innovation is to optimize a neural network via maximum likelihood on the manifold, possible by adapting the free-form flow framework to Riemannian manifolds. M-FFF is straightforwardly adapted to any manifold with a known projection. It consistently matches or outperforms previous single-step methods specialized to specific manifolds. It is typically two orders of magnitude faster than multi-step methods based on diffusion or flow matching, achieving better likelihoods in several experiments. We provide our code at https://github.com/vislearn/FFF.

paragraphs: Manifold Free-Form Flows, or M-FFF, model probability distributions on spaces with geometric constraints. Existing approaches that work on arbitrary manifolds can be expensive when generating samples because they must solve a differential equation. This paper develops a method that generates a sample with a single function evaluation, targeting that inference cost directly.

The approach adapts the free-form flow framework to Riemannian manifolds, enabling a neural network to be trained through maximum likelihood on the manifold itself. Its stated applicability depends on having a known projection onto the manifold. That condition provides a way to adapt the framework across different geometries while retaining a common modeling approach.

In the reported comparisons, M-FFF consistently matches or exceeds previous single-step methods designed for particular manifolds. It is typically about two orders of magnitude faster than multi-step diffusion or flow-matching methods and achieves better likelihoods in several experiments. These findings support the possibility of combining broadly adaptable geometric modeling with inexpensive sampling, without making the reported speed or likelihood advantage a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: M-FFF learns manifold-valued distributions through maximum likelihood and generates samples in a single function evaluation.

title: Learning Distributions on Manifolds with Free-Form Flows

abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection has recently attracted considerable attention due to its broad applications in autonomous driving and robotics, which aims to effectively recognize novel classes in previously unseen domains. However, existing point cloud-based open-vocabulary 3D detection models are limited by their high deployment costs. In this work, we propose a novel open-vocabulary monocular 3D object detection framework, dubbed OVM3D-Det, which trains detectors using only RGB images, making it both cost-effective and scalable to publicly available data. Unlike traditional methods, OVM3D-Det does not require high-precision LiDAR or 3D sensor data for either input or generating 3D bounding boxes. Instead, it employs open-vocabulary 2D models and pseudo-LiDAR to automatically label 3D objects in RGB images, fostering the learning of open-vocabulary monocular 3D detectors. However, training 3D models with labels directly derived from pseudo-LiDAR is inadequate due to imprecise boxes estimated from noisy point clouds and severely occluded objects. To address these issues, we introduce two innovative designs: adaptive pseudo-LiDAR erosion and bounding box refinement with prior knowledge from large language models. These techniques effectively calibrate the 3D labels and enable RGB-only training for 3D detectors. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of OVM3D-Det over baselines in both indoor and outdoor scenarios. The code will be released.

OVM3D-Det instead trains a detector from RGB images alone, avoiding high-precision LiDAR or other 3D sensor data for both inputs and the creation of training boxes.

The framework combines open-vocabulary 2D models with pseudo-LiDAR to automatically produce 3D object labels from images. The contribution is a training pipeline that makes use of widely available images while explicitly improving the quality of the automatically inferred 3D supervision.
summary.tldr: OVM3D-Det trains open-vocabulary 3D detectors from RGB images by generating and refining 3D labels without 3D sensor data.

title: Training an Open-Vocabulary Monocular 3D Detection Model without 3D Data

abstract: Binocular 3D human pose estimation (HPE), reconstructing a 3D pose from 2D poses of two views, offers practical advantages by combining multiview geometry with the convenience of a monocular setup. However, compared to a multiview setup, the reduction in the number of cameras increases uncertainty in 3D reconstruction. To address this issue, we leverage the diffusion model, which has shown success in monocular 3D HPE by recovering 3D poses from noisy data with high uncertainty. Yet, the uncertainty distribution of initial 3D poses remains unknown. Considering that 3D errors stem from 2D errors within geometric constraints, we recognize that the uncertainties of 3D and 2D are integrated in a binocular configuration, with the initial 2D uncertainty being well-defined. Based on this insight, we propose Dual-Diffusion specifically for Binocular 3D HPE, simultaneously denoising the uncertainties in 2D and 3D, and recovering plausible and accurate results. Additionally, we introduce Z-embedding as an additional condition for denoising and implement baseline-width-related pose normalization to enhance the model flexibility for various baseline settings. This is crucial as 3D error influence factors encompass depth and baseline width. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our Dual-Diffusion in 2D refinement and 3D estimation. The code and models are available at https://github.com/sherrywan/Dual-Diffusion.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a person's three-dimensional pose from two camera views provides geometric information without requiring a larger camera array. However, using fewer views leaves more uncertainty in the reconstructed pose. Dual-Diffusion addresses that uncertainty by considering errors in the original two-dimensional pose estimates together with errors in the three-dimensional reconstruction.

The key observation is that these errors are geometrically connected: uncertain image-plane locations contribute to uncertain spatial locations. Although the initial three-dimensional uncertainty distribution is unknown, the initial two-dimensional uncertainty is well-defined in the proposed setting. The method therefore denoises both representations simultaneously, using their connection to recover plausible and accurate poses.

The model also introduces Z-embedding as a denoising condition and normalizes poses according to the distance between cameras. These additions address the influence of depth and camera spacing on reconstruction errors and support flexibility across baseline settings. Experiments validate improvements in both two-dimensional refinement and three-dimensional estimation, supporting the value of treating the two sources of uncertainty jointly.
summary.tldr: Dual-Diffusion jointly denoises two-dimensional and three-dimensional pose uncertainty to improve human-pose reconstruction from two views.

title: Dual-Diffusion for Binocular 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: While 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently become popular for neural rendering, current methods rely on carefully engineered cloning and splitting strategies for placing Gaussians, which does not always generalize and may lead to poor-quality renderings. For many real-world scenes this leads to their heavy dependence on good initializations. In this work, we rethink the set of 3D Gaussians as a random sample drawn from an underlying probability distribution describing the physical representation of the scene—in other words, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. Under this view, we show that the 3D Gaussian updates can be converted as Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) update by simply introducing noise. We then rewrite the densification and pruning strategies in 3D Gaussian Splatting as simply a deterministic state transition of MCMC samples, removing these heuristics from the framework. To do so, we revise the ‘cloning’ of Gaussians into a relocalization scheme that approximately preserves sample probability. To encourage efficient use of Gaussians, we introduce an L1-regularizer on the Gaussians. On various standard evaluation scenes, we show that our method provides improved rendering quality, easy control over the number of Gaussians, and robustness to initialization. The project website is available at https://3dgs-mcmc.github.io/.
originalAbstract: While 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently become popular for neural rendering, current methods rely on carefully engineered cloning and splitting strategies for placing Gaussians, which does not always generalize and may lead to poor-quality renderings. For many real-world scenes this leads to their heavy dependence on good initializations. In this work, we rethink the set of 3D Gaussians as a random sample drawn from an underlying probability distribution describing the physical representation of the scene—in other words, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. Under this view, we show that the 3D Gaussian updates can be converted as Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) update by simply introducing noise. We then rewrite the densification and pruning strategies in 3D Gaussian Splatting as simply a deterministic state transition of MCMC samples, removing these heuristics from the framework. To do so, we revise the ‘cloning’ of Gaussians into a relocalization scheme that approximately preserves sample probability. To encourage efficient use of Gaussians, we introduce an L1-regularizer on the Gaussians. On various standard evaluation scenes, we show that our method provides improved rendering quality, easy control over the number of Gaussians, and robustness to initialization. The project website is available at https://3dgs-mcmc.github.io/.

paragraphs: This paper revisits how 3D Gaussian Splatting places and updates the Gaussians used to represent a scene. Existing approaches rely on carefully designed cloning and splitting rules, which can make rendering quality depend heavily on a good starting arrangement. The authors instead treat the Gaussians as samples from an underlying probability distribution representing the scene.

This perspective connects scene optimization to Markov Chain Monte Carlo. Adding noise converts the Gaussian updates into Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics updates. The authors also reformulate densification and pruning as deterministic transitions of the samples. Their replacement for cloning relocates Gaussians while approximately preserving sample probability, and an L1 regularizer encourages economical use of the available Gaussians.

On standard evaluation scenes, the method improves rendering quality, makes the number of Gaussians easier to control, and shows greater robustness to initialization. The contribution is a sampling-based account of both parameter updates and Gaussian placement, with practical benefits demonstrated in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Recasting 3D Gaussians as probability samples yields a rendering method with improved quality, controllable size, and greater robustness to initialization.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: Prod is a seminal algorithm in full-information online learning, which has been conjectured to be fundamentally sub-optimal for multi-armed bandits.By leveraging the interpretation of Prod as a first-order OMD approximation, we present the following surprising results:1. Variants of Prod can obtain optimal regret for adversarial multi-armed bandits. 2. There exists a simple and (arguably) importance-weighting free variant with optimal rate. 3. One can even achieve best-both-worlds guarantees with logarithmic regret in the stochastic regime.The bandit algorithms in this work use simple arithmetic update rules without the need of solving optimization problems typical in prior work. Finally, the results directly improve the state of the art of incentive-compatible bandits.

paragraphs: This paper revisits Prod, an online-learning algorithm originally associated with full-information feedback. In a multi-armed bandit problem, the learner observes feedback only for its chosen action, making learning more difficult. Prod had been conjectured to be fundamentally suboptimal in that setting. The authors show that appropriately designed variants can achieve optimal regret.

The analysis interprets Prod as a first-order approximation to online mirror descent. From that perspective, the authors derive variants with optimal guarantees against adversarial outcomes. They also identify a simple variant that they describe, with qualification, as importance-weighting free. Another result provides best-of-both-worlds guarantees, including logarithmic regret when outcomes follow the stochastic regime.

The algorithms use straightforward arithmetic updates instead of solving the optimization problems common in earlier approaches. Their significance is therefore both theoretical and computational: a seemingly unsuitable algorithm family can support strong bandit guarantees with simple update rules. The results also directly improve the state of the art for incentive-compatible bandits, extending the impact beyond the basic bandit setting.
summary.tldr: Simple Prod variants achieve optimal bandit regret, including a qualified importance-weighting-free variant and guarantees for both adversarial and stochastic settings.

title: PRODuctive bandits: Importance Weighting No More

abstract: We study the framework of a dynamic decision-making scenario with resource constraints.In this framework, an agent, whose target is to maximize the total reward under the initial inventory, selects an action in each round upon observing a random request, leading to a reward and resource consumptions that are further associated with an unknown random external factor.While previous research has already established an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ worst-case regret for this problem, this work offers two results that go beyond the worst-case perspective: one for the worst-case gap between benchmarks and another for logarithmic regret rates.We first show that an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ distance between the commonly used fluid benchmark and the online optimum is unavoidable when the former has a degenerate optimal solution.On the algorithmic side, we merge the re-solving heuristic with distribution estimation skills and propose an algorithm that achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1)$ regret as long as the fluid LP has a unique and non-degenerate solution.Furthermore, we prove that our algorithm maintains a near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret even in the worst cases and extend these results to the setting where the request and external factor are continuous.Regarding information structure, our regret results are obtained under two feedback models, respectively, where the algorithm accesses the external factor at the end of each round and at the end of a round only when a non-null action is executed.

paragraphs: The paper considers repeated decisions made with a limited inventory of resources. Each round brings a random request, and the chosen action generates rewards and resource consumption influenced by an unknown random external factor. The aim is to earn as much as possible before resources run out, while learning enough about uncertainty to make better decisions.

The authors first examine the benchmark used to judge performance. They show that when the fluid optimization benchmark has a degenerate optimum, its value can inevitably differ from the online optimum by an amount scaling at least as √T. This distinction matters because a gap to that benchmark can reflect the benchmark's advantage, rather than only an algorithm's shortcomings.

Their algorithm combines repeated re-solving with distribution estimation. When the fluid linear program has a unique, non-degenerate solution, regret is constant up to logarithmic factors; in worst cases it retains a near-optimal √T guarantee up to logarithmic factors. The results cover continuous requests and external factors, and two feedback settings: observing the external factor every round or only after a non-null action.
summary.tldr: A resource-constrained decision algorithm achieves much smaller regret under a unique, non-degenerate fluid optimum while retaining near-optimal worst-case guarantees.

title: Contextual Decision-Making with Knapsacks Beyond the Worst Case

abstract: Beyond estimating parameters of interest from data, one of the key goals of statistical inference is to properly quantify uncertainty in these estimates. In Bayesian inference, this uncertainty is provided by the posterior distribution, the computation of which typically involves an intractable high-dimensional integral. Among available approximation methods, sampling-based approaches come with strong theoretical guarantees but scale poorly to large problems, while variational approaches scale well but offer few theoretical guarantees. In particular, variational methods are known to produce overconfident estimates of posterior uncertainty and are typically non-identifiable, with many latent variable configurations generating equivalent predictions. Here, we address these challenges by showing how diffusion-based models (DBMs), which have recently produced state-of-the-art performance in generative modeling tasks, can be repurposed for performing calibrated, identifiable Bayesian inference. By exploiting a previously established connection between the stochastic and probability flow ordinary differential equations (pfODEs) underlying DBMs, we derive a class of models, \emph{inflationary flows,} that uniquely and deterministically map high-dimensional data to a lower-dimensional Gaussian distribution via ODE integration. This map is both invertible and neighborhood-preserving, with controllable numerical error, with the result that uncertainties in the data are correctly propagated to the latent space. We demonstrate how such maps can be learned via standard DBM training using a novel noise schedule and are effective at both preserving and reducing intrinsic data dimensionality. The result is a class of highly expressive generative models, uniquely defined on a low-dimensional latent space, that afford principled Bayesian inference.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference needs to describe uncertainty as well as estimate parameters. Computing the posterior distribution is often difficult, especially in high dimensions. The paper targets a tension between sampling methods, which have strong guarantees but scale poorly, and scalable variational methods, which can underestimate uncertainty and admit multiple equivalent latent descriptions.

The authors derive inflationary flows from a connection between the stochastic equations and probability-flow ordinary differential equations used in diffusion models. These flows deterministically map high-dimensional data to a lower-dimensional Gaussian distribution through numerical integration. The proposed mapping is unique, invertible, and neighborhood-preserving, with controllable numerical error, allowing uncertainty in the data to propagate correctly into the latent representation.

The flows can be learned with standard diffusion-model training using a new noise schedule. The authors demonstrate their effectiveness at preserving and reducing intrinsic data dimensionality. The resulting contribution is an expressive generative representation with a uniquely defined low-dimensional latent space, designed to support calibrated, identifiable Bayesian inference rather than generation alone.
summary.tldr: Inflationary flows adapt diffusion models into identifiable latent mappings that propagate uncertainty for calibrated Bayesian inference.

title: Inflationary Flows: Calibrated Bayesian Inference with Diffusion-Based Models

abstract: Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging allows for seeing hidden scenes around corners through active sensing.Most previous algorithms for NLOS reconstruction require dense transients acquired through regular scans over a large relay surface, which limits their applicability in realistic scenarios with irregular relay surfaces.In this paper, we propose an unsupervised learning-based framework for NLOS imaging from irregularly undersampled transients~(IUT).Our method learns implicit priors from noisy irregularly undersampled transients without requiring paired data, which is difficult and expensive to acquire and align. To overcome the ambiguity of the measurement consistency constraint in inferring the albedo volume, we design a virtual scanning process that enables the network to learn within both range and null spaces for high-quality reconstruction.We devise a physics-guided SURE-based denoiser to enhance robustness to ubiquitous noise in low-photon imaging conditions. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world data validate the performance and generalization of our method.Compared with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) method, our method achieves higher fidelity, greater robustness, and remarkably faster inference times by orders of magnitude.The code and model are available at https://github.com/XingyuCuii/Virtual-Scanning-NLOS.

paragraphs: Non-line-of-sight imaging reconstructs hidden scenes from active measurements taken through a relay surface. Many reconstruction methods expect dense measurements on a regular scan pattern, which can be difficult with realistic surfaces. This paper instead learns from noisy, irregularly undersampled transient measurements without requiring paired training data that are expensive to acquire and align.

The central challenge is ambiguity: multiple hidden-scene reconstructions can agree with the available measurements. The proposed virtual scanning process lets the network learn in both the range and null spaces, addressing aspects constrained by observations and those left unresolved. A physics-guided denoiser based on SURE further improves robustness to the noise common in low-photon conditions.

Experiments on simulated and real data validate reconstruction performance and generalization. Compared with the state-of-the-art method used in the evaluation, the authors report higher fidelity, greater robustness, and inference faster by orders of magnitude. The combined contribution targets practical acquisition constraints through unsupervised learning, measurement-aware reconstruction, and denoising designed for the sensing setting.
summary.tldr: Virtual Scanning reconstructs hidden scenes from sparse, irregular, noisy measurements without paired data, with reported gains in fidelity, robustness, and speed.

title: Virtual Scanning: Unsupervised Non-line-of-sight Imaging from Irregularly Undersampled Transients

abstract: In recent years, Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) has emerged as an alternative to post-training pruning for generating efficient models. In principle, DST allows for a much more memory efficient training process,as it maintains sparsity throughout the entire training run. However, current DST implementations fail to capitalize on this. Because sparse matrix multiplication is much less efficient than dense matrix multiplication on GPUs, mostimplementations simulate sparsity by masking weights. In this paper, we leverage recent advances in semi-structured sparse training to apply DST in the domain of classificationwith large output spaces, where memory-efficiency is paramount. With a label space of possibly millions of candidates,the classification layer alone will consume several gigabytes of memory. Switching from a dense to a fixed fan-in sparse layer updated with sparse evolutionary training (SET); however, severely hampers training convergence, especiallyat the largest label spaces. We find that the gradients fed back from the classifier into the text encoder make itmuch more difficult to learn good input representations, despite using a dense encoder.By employing an intermediate layer or adding an auxiliary training objective, we recover most of the generalisation performance of the dense model. Overall, we demonstrate the applicability of DST in a challenging domain, characterized by a highly skewed label distribution, that lies outside of DST's typical benchmark datasets, and enable end-to-end training with millions of labels on commodity hardware.

paragraphs: Classification with millions of possible labels can make the output layer alone consume several gigabytes of memory. Dynamic Sparse Training aims to reduce this burden by keeping weights sparse throughout training. However, many implementations merely mask dense weights because ordinary sparse multiplication performs poorly on GPUs, leaving the potential memory benefits unrealized.

The paper applies advances in semi-structured sparse training to this large-output setting. It replaces the dense classifier with a sparse layer that has a fixed number of incoming connections and updates those connections using sparse evolutionary training. This initially damages convergence, especially for the largest label spaces. The authors trace the problem to gradients from the sparse classifier making it harder for the dense text encoder to learn useful representations.

Adding an intermediate layer or an auxiliary training objective recovers most of the dense model's generalization performance. The resulting system enables end-to-end training with millions of labels on commodity hardware. The findings show that practical sparsity requires attention to how the sparse output layer trains the rest of the network, especially with highly uneven label frequencies.
summary.tldr: Dynamic sparse classifiers enable training with millions of labels when changes to representation learning address their convergence problems.

title: Navigating Extremes: Dynamic Sparsity in Large Output Spaces

abstract: Visual grounding is a common vision task that involves grounding descriptive sentences to the corresponding regions of an image. Most existing methods use independent image-text encoding and apply complex hand-crafted modules or encoder-decoder architectures for modal interaction and query reasoning. However, their performance significantly drops when dealing with complex textual expressions. This is because the former paradigm only utilizes limited downstream data to fit the multi-modal feature fusion. Therefore, it is only effective when the textual expressions are relatively simple. In contrast, given the wide diversity of textual expressions and the uniqueness of downstream training data, the existing fusion module, which extracts multimodal content from a visual-linguistic context, has not been fully investigated. In this paper, we present a simple yet robust transformer-based framework, SimVG, for visual grounding. Specifically, we decouple visual-linguistic feature fusion from downstream tasks by leveraging existing multimodal pre-trained models and incorporating additional object tokens to facilitate deep integration of downstream and pre-training tasks. Furthermore, we design a dynamic weight-balance distillation method in the multi-branch synchronous learning process to enhance the representation capability of the simpler branch. This branch only consists of a lightweight MLP, which simplifies the structure and improves reasoning speed. Experiments on six widely used VG datasets, i.e., RefCOCO/+/g, ReferIt, Flickr30K, and GRefCOCO, demonstrate the superiority of SimVG. Finally, the proposed method not only achieves improvements in efficiency and convergence speed but also attains new state-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/Dmmm1997/SimVG.

paragraphs: Visual grounding identifies the image region described by a sentence. The paper argues that methods learning image-text fusion mainly from limited downstream data struggle with complex expressions. SimVG addresses this by drawing on multimodal pretraining, allowing the grounding system to use visual-language interactions learned beyond its task-specific training examples.

The framework separates visual-language feature fusion from the downstream grounding task. It uses existing multimodal pretrained models and adds object tokens to connect pretrained representations with task-specific learning. During joint training of multiple branches, a dynamic weighting scheme distills information into a simpler branch. That branch consists only of a lightweight multilayer perceptron, reducing structural complexity and improving inference speed.

Experiments on six visual grounding datasets report new state-of-the-art performance alongside improvements in efficiency and convergence speed. The findings support combining broadly pretrained multimodal features with a compact downstream predictor. The distillation component is central to that combination: it is designed to strengthen the lightweight branch's representations while retaining the simpler structure used for faster reasoning.
summary.tldr: SimVG combines pretrained image-text fusion with distillation into a lightweight grounding branch, improving reported accuracy, efficiency, and convergence speed.

title: SimVG: A Simple Framework for Visual Grounding with Decoupled Multi-modal Fusion

abstract: Radiation therapy, treating over half of all cancer patients, involves using specialized machines to direct high-energy beams at tumors, aiming to damage cancer cells while minimizing harm to nearby healthy tissues. Customizing the shape and intensity of radiation beams for each patient leads to solving large-scale constrained optimization problems that need to be solved within tight clinical time-frame. At the core of these challenges is a large matrix that is commonly sparsified for computational efficiency by neglecting small elements. Such a crude approximation can degrade the quality of treatment, potentially causing unnecessary radiation exposure to healthy tissues—this may lead to significant radiation-induced side effects—or delivering inadequate radiation to the tumor, which is crucial for effective tumor treatment. In this work, we demonstrate, for the first time, that randomized sketch tools can effectively sparsify this matrix without sacrificing treatment quality. We also develop a novel randomized sketch method with desirable theoretical guarantees that outperforms existing techniques in practical application. Beyond developing a novel randomized sketch method, this work emphasizes the potential of harnessing scientific computing tools, crucial in today's big data analysis, to tackle computationally intensive challenges in healthcare. The application of these tools could have a profound impact on the lives of numerous cancer patients. Code and sample data available at https://github.com/PortPy-Project/CompressRTP
