paragraphs: Radiotherapy planning adjusts radiation beam shapes and intensities to treat a tumor while limiting exposure to healthy tissue. This requires solving large constrained optimization problems within clinical time limits. A large matrix sits at the center of the computation, making its storage and processing important practical concerns.

A common shortcut removes small matrix entries to make the matrix sparse. The paper explains that this approximation can reduce treatment-plan quality, potentially increasing healthy-tissue exposure or leaving the tumor inadequately irradiated. The authors investigate randomized sketching as a way to obtain a sparse representation while preserving the information needed for planning.

They demonstrate that randomized sketch tools can sparsify the matrix without sacrificing treatment quality in their study. They also develop a new randomized sketch method with theoretical guarantees that outperforms existing techniques in practical application. The contribution connects a matrix-compression method to a concrete planning requirement: reducing computational burden while retaining the quality of the resulting treatment plan.
summary.tldr: Randomized matrix sparsification reduces the computational burden of radiotherapy optimization while preserving treatment quality in the reported study.

title: Randomized Sparse Matrix Compression for Large-Scale Constrained Optimization in Cancer Radiotherapy

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is critical when deploying machine learning models in the real world. Outlier exposure methods, which incorporate auxiliary outlier data in the training process, can drastically improve OOD detection performance compared to approaches without advanced training strategies. We introduce Hopfield Boosting, a boosting approach, which leverages modern Hopfield energy to sharpen the decision boundary between the in-distribution and OOD data. Hopfield Boosting encourages the model to focus on hard-to-distinguish auxiliary outlier examples that lie close to the decision boundary between in-distribution and auxiliary outlier data. Our method achieves a new state-of-the-art in OOD detection with outlier exposure, improving the FPR95 from 2.28 to 0.92 on CIFAR-10, from 11.76 to 7.94 on CIFAR-100, and from 50.74 to 36.60 on ImageNet-1K.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is intended to handle. One training strategy, outlier exposure, provides auxiliary examples of unfamiliar data so the detector can learn to distinguish them from ordinary inputs. This paper studies how to make better use of those auxiliary examples.

Hopfield Boosting uses modern Hopfield energy to sharpen the boundary between in-distribution data and auxiliary outliers. Its central idea is to emphasize outliers that are difficult to distinguish from familiar examples. These boundary-adjacent cases provide the training process with a focused challenge: improving separation where the distinction is currently weakest.

The authors report state-of-the-art detection performance within the outlier-exposure setting. FPR95 falls from 2.28 to 0.92 on CIFAR-10, from 11.76 to 7.94 on CIFAR-100, and from 50.74 to 36.60 on ImageNet-1K. These results support the value of directing training toward difficult auxiliary outliers. The method's stated setting includes access to auxiliary outlier data during training.
summary.tldr: Hopfield Boosting improves outlier-exposure training by emphasizing auxiliary outliers near the detector's decision boundary.

title: Energy-based Hopfield Boosting for Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: The human capacity to envision possible futures fundamentally shapes who we become. Yet for many, especially those without access to mentorship or resources, imagining vivid career futures remains abstract and distant. We present ``Possible You,'' a creative AI system that transforms career exploration into an intimate dialogue with one's future selves. Through personalized narratives and AI-generated portraits, the system makes abstract futures tangible and emotionally resonant. In our mixed-methods study (N=209), we discovered that the perceived authenticity of these AI-created futures influenced participants' sense of connection to their future selves. While viewing multiple possible selves expanded participants' sense of possibility, exploring a single future self fostered deeper commitment. This tension reveals a fundamental aspect of human future-making: we need both breadth to discover and depth to commit. Our work demonstrates how creative AI can serve not as predictor or prescriber of futures, but as a mirror that helps humans see and shape their own becoming—contributing to a more equitable landscape where all people can vividly imagine and pursue meaningful futures.

paragraphs: Possible You uses personalized stories and AI-generated portraits to help people imagine future career identities. The motivating problem is that possible careers can feel distant or abstract, especially when mentorship and resources are limited. The system turns career exploration into an encounter with representations of one’s possible future selves.

A mixed-methods study with 209 participants examines how people respond to these representations. The researchers find that perceived authenticity influences participants’ connection to their future selves. They also identify a difference between exploring several possibilities and concentrating on one: multiple selves broaden participants’ sense of possibility, while a single self encourages deeper commitment.

The findings highlight two different needs within career imagination: having room to discover alternatives and developing enough connection to commit to a direction. The system is framed as a reflective aid for shaping futures, rather than a means of predicting them. Its contribution is to make potential identities tangible and to show how the breadth of an AI-supported exploration relates to the depth of a participant’s engagement.
summary.tldr: Possible You uses AI-generated future identities to support career reflection, revealing a trade-off between exploring possibilities and deepening commitment.

title: Possible You: AI-Generated Digital Twins as Creative Mirrors for Future Self Modeling

abstract: We introduce BO4Mob, a new benchmark framework for high-dimensional Bayesian Optimization (BO), driven by the challenge of origin-destination (OD) travel demand estimation in large urban road networks. Estimating OD travel demand from limited traffic sensor data is a difficult inverse optimization problem, particularly in real-world, large-scale transportation networks. This problem involves optimizing over high-dimensional continuous spaces where each objective evaluation is computationally expensive, stochastic, and non-differentiable. BO4Mob comprises five scenarios based on real-world San Jose, CA road networks, with input dimensions scaling up to 10,100. These scenarios utilize high-resolution, open-source traffic simulations that incorporate realistic nonlinear and stochastic dynamics. We demonstrate the benchmark's utility by evaluating five optimization methods: three state-of-the-art BO algorithms and two non-BO baselines. This benchmark is designed to support both the development of scalable optimization algorithms and their application for the design of data-driven urban mobility models, including high-resolution digital twins of metropolitan road networks. Code and documentation are available at https://github.com/UMN-Choi-Lab/BO4Mob.

paragraphs: BO4Mob turns an urban transportation problem into a benchmark for optimization methods: estimating how much travel occurs between different origins and destinations using limited traffic sensor observations. This is an inverse problem because the desired travel demand must be inferred from its effects on the road network, rather than observed directly.

The benchmark contains five scenarios built around real road networks in San Jose, California, with as many as 10,100 input dimensions. High-resolution, open-source traffic simulations provide realistic nonlinear and stochastic behavior. Each candidate evaluation is computationally expensive, can vary because of randomness, and does not supply derivatives. Together, these properties make the scenarios challenging tests for Bayesian optimization at large scale.

The authors demonstrate the framework by evaluating three state-of-the-art Bayesian optimization algorithms and two other optimization baselines. The contribution is a realistic testing environment, with no particular winner stated in the abstract. It is intended to support scalable optimization research and transportation modeling, including detailed digital representations of metropolitan road networks.
summary.tldr: BO4Mob provides five realistic traffic-demand estimation scenarios for testing optimization methods in spaces with up to 10,100 dimensions.

title: BO4Mob: Bayesian Optimization Benchmarks for High-Dimensional Urban Mobility Problem

abstract: While energy-based models have recently proven to be a powerful framework for learning to reason with neural networks, their practical application is still limited by computational cost. That is, existing methods for energy-based iterative reasoning suffer from computational bottlenecks by relying on expensive optimization routines during training and especially during inference. Furthermore, these routines may not always converge to minimal energy states, potentially leading to suboptimal reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose a novel and efficient algorithm for energy-based iterative reasoning based on a difference-of-convex (DC) functions approach. Our algorithm achieves a significant speedup compared to prior methods while offering theoretical convergence guarantees ensuring locally minimal energy states. In addition, we achieve state-of-the-art or superior performance on continuous reasoning tasks, as demonstrated by our experiments on multiple benchmark datasets from continuous algorithmic reasoning. As such, our method offers a leap in computational efficiency, enabling faster inference with theoretical guarantees, and hence unlocking the potential of energy-based models for iterative reasoning applications.

paragraphs: Energy-based iterative reasoning improves a candidate solution by searching for a state with lower energy. This makes the optimization procedure central to both the quality and speed of reasoning. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: their optimization routines are expensive during training and especially inference, and those routines may fail to reach an energy minimum.

The authors introduce an algorithm based on a difference-of-convex functions approach. This mathematical structure provides a different way to organize the optimization underlying successive reasoning steps. The proposed algorithm combines a significant reported speedup over prior methods with theoretical guarantees of convergence to locally minimal energy states. The local qualification matters: the guarantee concerns a nearby minimum rather than a globally best solution.

Experiments on multiple continuous algorithmic reasoning benchmarks report performance matching or exceeding the state of the art. Together, the findings connect computational savings with stronger control over the optimization process. For these reasoning tasks, faster inference comes with both competitive empirical results and a stated convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: A difference-of-convex optimization approach speeds up energy-based reasoning while guaranteeing convergence to local energy minima.

title: A Difference-of-Convex Functions Approach to Energy-Based Iterative Reasoning

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been shown to memorize their training data, but similar analyses for graph neural networks (GNNs) remain under-explored. We introduce NCMemo (Node Classification Memorization), the first framework to quantify label memorization in semi-supervised node classification. We establish an inverse relationship between memorization and graph homophily, i.e the tendency of connected nodes to share labels or features. Lower homophily significantly increases memorization, indicating that GNNs rely on label memorization when learning less homophilic graphs. We then analyze GNN training dynamics and find that increased memorization in low-homophily graphs is tightly coupled to GNNs' implicit bias toward using graph structure. When structure is less informative, models instead memorize node labels to minimize training loss. Finally, we show that nodes with higher label inconsistency in their feature-space neighborhood are more prone to memorization. Based on these insights, we investigate graph rewiring as a mitigation strategy. Our results show that rewiring reduces memorization without harming model performance, while also lowering the privacy risk for previously memorized data points. Thus, our work advances understanding of GNN learning and supports more privacy-preserving GNN deployment.

In the reported results, changing graph connections reduces memorization without harming predictive performance and lowers privacy risk for previously memorized data points. The work therefore connects graph structure, training behavior, and privacy: the usefulness of relationships between nodes influences how much the model depends on memorizing particular labels.
summary.tldr: NCMemo links graph-network label memorization to low homophily and shows that graph rewiring can reduce memorization and associated privacy risk.

title: Memorization in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Accurately estimating *semantic* aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties in large language models (LLMs) is particularly challenging in free-form question answering (QA), where obtaining stable estimates often requires many expensive generations. We introduce a **diversity-steered sampler** that discourages semantically redundant outputs during decoding, covers both autoregressive and masked diffusion paradigms, and yields substantial sample-efficiency gains. The key idea is to inject a continuous semantic-similarity penalty into the model’s proposal distribution using a natural language inference (NLI) model lightly finetuned on partial prefixes or intermediate diffusion states. We debias downstream uncertainty estimates with importance reweighting and shrink their variance with control variates. Across four QA benchmarks, our method matches or surpasses baselines while covering more semantic clusters with the same number of samples. Being modular and requiring no gradient access to the base LLM, the framework promises to serve as a drop-in enhancement for uncertainty estimation in risk-sensitive model deployments.

paragraphs: Estimating uncertainty in free-form answers requires comparing meanings, because differently worded responses can express the same answer. Repeatedly generating semantically redundant responses can make stable uncertainty estimates expensive. This paper proposes steering sampling toward a broader range of meanings to obtain more useful information from a fixed generation budget.

The sampler applies a continuous semantic-similarity penalty during decoding. A natural language inference model, lightly fine-tuned on partial outputs, supplies the semantic signal. The approach accommodates both autoregressive generation and masked diffusion. Because steering changes the sampling distribution, the method uses importance reweighting to debias uncertainty estimates and control variates to reduce their variance.

Across four question-answering benchmarks, the method matches or exceeds baseline performance while reaching more semantic clusters with the same number of samples. It requires no gradient access to the underlying language model. The findings support a modular approach to more efficient semantic uncertainty estimation, with statistical corrections allowing deliberate diversity in generation to remain useful for measuring uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A diversity-steered sampler explores more answer meanings and statistically corrects its estimates to measure uncertainty with fewer redundant generations.

title: Efficient semantic uncertainty quantification in language models via diversity-steered sampling

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning in mixed-motive settings presents a fundamental challenge: agents must balance individual interests with collective goals, which are neither fully aligned nor strictly opposed. To address this, reward restructuring methods such as gifting and intrinsic motivation have been proposed. However, these approaches primarily focus on promoting cooperation by managing the trade-off between individual and collective returns, without explicitly addressing fairness with respect to agents’ task-specific rewards. In this paper, we propose an adaptive conflict-aware gradient adjustment method that promotes cooperation while ensuring fairness in individual rewards. The proposed method dynamically balances policy gradients derived from individual and collective objectives in situations where the two objectives are in conflict. By explicitly resolving such conflicts, our method improves collective performance while preserving fairness across agents. We provide theoretical results that guarantee monotonic non-decreasing improvement in both the collective and individual objectives and ensure fairness. Empirical results in sequential social dilemma environments demonstrate that our approach outperforms baselines in terms of social welfare, while maintaining fairness.

paragraphs: In mixed-motive games, agents have reasons to cooperate but also pursue their own rewards. Improving the group's total return does not by itself resolve whether individual agents benefit fairly. This paper addresses both concerns within multi-agent reinforcement learning, focusing on fairness in the rewards associated with each agent's task.

The method adjusts policy gradients when the individual and collective objectives conflict. These gradients indicate how learning would change behavior to improve the respective objectives. Dynamically balancing them lets the method respond directly to conflicting learning directions. This places fairness and cooperation within the policy update process, beyond the tradeoffs managed by reward restructuring methods such as gifting or intrinsic motivation.

The authors provide theoretical results guaranteeing non-decreasing improvement in both individual and collective objectives, together with fairness. Experiments in sequential social dilemma environments report higher social welfare than the compared baselines while maintaining fairness. The theoretical and empirical contributions jointly support the approach's aim: improving cooperation while preserving attention to the rewards of the individual agents involved.
summary.tldr: Conflict-aware policy gradient adjustments promote cooperation while supporting fairness and non-decreasing individual and collective objectives.

title: Fair Cooperation in Mixed-Motive Games via Conflict-Aware Gradient Adjustment

abstract: Drug recommendation systems aim to identify optimal drug combinations for patient care, balancing therapeutic efficacy and safety. Advances in large-scale longitudinal EHRs have enabled learning-based approaches that leverage patient histories such as diagnoses, procedures, and previously prescribed drugs, to model complex patient-drug relationships. Yet, many existing solutions overlook standard clinical practices that favor certain drugs for specific conditions and fail to fully integrate the influence of molecular substructures on drug efficacy and safety. In response, we propose \textbf{SubRec}, a unified framework that integrates representation learning across both patient and drug spaces. Specifically, SubRec introduces a conditional information bottleneck to extract core drug substructures most relevant to patient conditions, thereby enhancing interpretability and clinical alignment. Meanwhile, an adaptive vector quantization mechanism is designed to generate patient–drug interaction patterns into a condition-aware codebook which reuses clinically meaningful patterns, reduces training overhead, and provides a controllable latent space for recommendation. Crucially, the synergy between condition-specific substructure learning and discrete patient prototypes allows SubRec to make accurate and personalized drug recommendations. Experimental results on the real-world MIMIC III and IV demonstrate our model's advantages. The source code is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DrugRecommendation-5173}{https://anonymous.4open.science/}.

paragraphs: Drug recommendation systems use patient histories to suggest combinations that balance therapeutic benefit and safety. This paper argues that existing approaches often underuse two sources of structure: clinical preferences for particular drugs under particular conditions, and molecular substructures that influence drug effects. SubRec combines representations of patients and drugs to bring these sources together.

A conditional information bottleneck extracts drug substructures most relevant to a patient's condition. The goal is to concentrate the representation on clinically meaningful molecular information and improve interpretability. An adaptive vector-quantization mechanism also organizes patient–drug interaction patterns into a condition-aware codebook. This supplies reusable discrete patterns and a controllable representation space while reducing training overhead.

Experiments on the MIMIC III and IV datasets demonstrate advantages for the model. The stated findings concern recommendation performance on these records; the approach's contribution is integrating molecular detail and longitudinal patient information in a representation designed to reflect clinical patterns.
summary.tldr: SubRec combines condition-relevant drug substructures with reusable patient–drug patterns to improve personalized drug recommendations.

title: Integrating Drug Substructures and Longitudinal Electronic Health Records for Personalized Drug Recommendation

abstract: Measuring parameter importance is crucial for understanding and optimizing large language models (LLMs). Existing work predominantly focuses on pruning or probing at neuron/feature levels without fully considering the cooperative behaviors of model parameters. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach--Model Shapley to quantify parameter importance based on the Shapley value, a principled method from cooperative game theory that captures both individual and synergistic contributions among parameters, via only one gradient backpropagation. We derive a scalable second-order approximation to compute Shapley values at the parameter level, leveraging blockwise Fisher information for tractability in large-scale settings. Our method enables fine-grained differentiation of parameter importance, facilitating targeted knowledge injection and model compression. Through mini-batch Monte Carlo updates and efficient approximation of the Hessian structure, we achieve robust Shapley-based attribution with only modest computational overhead. Experimental results indicate that this cooperative game perspective enhances interpretability, guides more effective parameter-specific fine-tuning and model compressing, and paves the way for continuous model improvement in various downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Model Shapley measures the importance of individual language-model parameters while accounting for cooperation among them. Its starting point is that a parameter's contribution can depend on other parameters, so importance measures should capture both individual effects and synergy. The paper draws on Shapley values from cooperative game theory to express that idea.

To make parameter-level attribution scalable, the authors derive a second-order approximation using blockwise Fisher information. The approach obtains importance information through one gradient backpropagation, with mini-batch Monte Carlo updates and an efficient approximation of Hessian structure supporting the computation. The resulting scores are approximate Shapley-based attributions rather than an exhaustive accounting of every possible parameter coalition.

Experiments indicate that these attributions improve interpretability and guide more effective parameter-specific fine-tuning and compression with modest computational overhead. They also support targeted knowledge injection. The contribution is a practical way to bring cooperative parameter behavior into decisions about which parts of a large model to modify or retain.
summary.tldr: Model Shapley approximates parameter importance while accounting for cooperation, guiding targeted fine-tuning and compression.

title: MODEL SHAPLEY: Find Your Ideal Parameter Player via One Gradient Backpropagation

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved significant success in various real-world applications, including social networks, finance systems, and traffic management. Recent researches highlight their vulnerability to backdoor attacks in node classification, where GNNs trained on a poisoned graph misclassify a test node only when specific triggers are attached. These studies typically focus on single attack categories and use adaptive trigger generators to create node-specific triggers. However, adaptive trigger generators typically have a simple structure, limited parameters, and lack category-aware graph knowledge, which makes them struggle to handle backdoor attacks across multiple categories as the number of target categories increases. We address this gap by proposing a novel approach for Effective and Unnoticeable Multi-Category (EUMC) graph backdoor attacks, leveraging subgraph from the attacked graph as category-aware triggers to precisely control the target category. To ensure the effectiveness of our method, we construct a Multi-Category Subgraph Triggers Pool (MC-STP) using the subgraphs of the attacked graph as triggers. We then exploit the attachment probability shifts of each subgraph trigger as category-aware priors for target category determination. Moreover, we develop a ``select then attach'' strategy that connects suitable category-aware trigger to attacked nodes for unnoticeability. Extensive experiments across different real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of our method in conducting multi-category graph backdoor attacks on various GNN models and defense strategies.

paragraphs: This paper studies backdoor attacks against graph neural networks that classify nodes. A poisoned training graph can cause a model to assign an attacker-chosen category when a trigger is attached to a test node. The authors focus on attacks involving multiple target categories, where existing trigger generators struggle as the number of categories increases.

Their EUMC approach draws trigger subgraphs from the graph being attacked. This provides a source of existing graph structure with category-related information. The method organizes these subgraphs into a pool and uses changes in attachment probabilities as evidence about their target categories. A selection-and-attachment strategy then chooses suitable triggers with the aim of making the modifications less noticeable.

Experiments across real-world datasets, several graph neural networks, and defense strategies support the effectiveness of the approach. The central finding is that the attacked graph itself can supply useful category-aware triggers. This broadens the demonstrated backdoor threat beyond methods centered on a single target category.
summary.tldr: EUMC uses subgraphs from an attacked graph to create less noticeable backdoor triggers for multiple target categories.

title: Attack by Yourself: Effective and Unnoticeable Multi-Category Graph Backdoor Attacks with Subgraph Triggers Pool

abstract: Open-world reinforcement learning challenges agents to develop intelligent behavior in vast exploration spaces. Recent approaches like LS-Imagine have advanced the field by extending imagination horizons through jumpy state transitions, yet remain limited by fixed exploration mechanisms and static jump thresholds that cannot adapt across changing task phases, resulting in inefficient exploration and lower completion rates. Humans demonstrate remarkable capabilities in open-world decision-making through a chain-like process of task decomposition, selective memory utilization, and adaptive uncertainty regulation. Inspired by human decision-making processes, we present Cognitive Predictive Processing (CPP), a novel framework that integrates three neurologically-inspired systems: a phase-adaptive cognitive controller that dynamically decomposes tasks into exploration, approach, and completion phases with adaptive parameters; a dual-memory integration system implementing dual-modal memory that balances immediate context with selective long-term storage; and an uncertainty-modulated prediction regulator that continuously updates environmental predictions to modulate exploration behavior. Comprehensive experiments in MineDojo demonstrate that these human-inspired decision-making strategies enhance performance over recent techniques, with success rates improving by an average of 4.6\% across resource collection tasks while reducing task completion steps by an average of 7.1\%. Our approach bridges cognitive neuroscience and reinforcement learning, excelling in complex scenarios that require sustained exploration and strategic adaptation while demonstrating how neural-inspired models can solve key challenges in open-world AI systems.

paragraphs: Exploration in an open world requires an agent to change its behavior as a task progresses. A strategy useful while searching may become inefficient once the goal is nearby. Cognitive Predictive Processing addresses the fixed exploration mechanisms and static transition thresholds that the authors identify as limitations of recent approaches.

The framework combines three systems inspired by human decision-making. A cognitive controller separates activity into exploration, approach, and completion phases and adjusts its parameters accordingly. A memory system balances immediate context with selectively retained long-term information. An uncertainty-sensitive prediction regulator continually revises expectations about the environment and uses them to adjust exploration. Together, these components connect task progress, remembered information, and uncertainty to action selection.

These findings support the usefulness of adaptive exploration and selective memory in the evaluated tasks. The human-inspired structure functions as a practical design for sustained exploration and strategic adjustment.
summary.tldr: CPP coordinates task phases, selective memory, and uncertainty-aware predictions to improve exploration efficiency and success in MineDojo.

title: Cognitive Predictive Processing: A Human-inspired Framework for Adaptive Exploration in Open-World Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Mean field games (MFGs) have emerged as a powerful framework for modeling interactions in large-scale multi-agent systems. Despite recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) for MFGs, existing methods are typically limited to finite spaces or stationary models, hindering their applicability to real-world problems. This paper introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm specifically designed for non-stationary continuous MFGs. The proposed approach builds upon a Fictitious Play (FP) methodology, leveraging DRL for best-response computation and supervised learning for average policy representation. Furthermore, it learns a representation of the time-dependent population distribution using a Conditional Normalizing Flow. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we evaluate it on three different examples of increasing complexity. By addressing critical limitations in scalability and density approximation, this work represents a significant advancement in applying DRL techniques to complex MFG problems, bringing the field closer to real-world multi-agent systems.

paragraphs: Mean field games model interactions within large populations of agents. The paper targets cases with continuous spaces and population behavior that changes over time. These features exceed the finite-space or stationary settings that typically constrain existing reinforcement learning approaches, motivating a method that explicitly represents the evolving population.

The algorithm builds on fictitious play. Deep reinforcement learning computes best responses, while supervised learning represents the average policy. A conditional normalizing flow learns the time-dependent population distribution. These components address different parts of the problem: choosing an agent's response, retaining an average policy, and representing how the population is distributed as time passes.

The authors evaluate the approach on three examples of increasing complexity. They present the results as evidence that it addresses scalability and density-approximation difficulties in non-stationary continuous games. The contribution is an integrated learning procedure for a broader class of mean field problems, bringing reinforcement learning methods closer to the changing, continuous interactions found in large multi-agent systems.
summary.tldr: A fictitious-play algorithm combines deep reinforcement learning, policy averaging, and conditional flows to solve continuous mean field games with changing population dynamics.

title: Solving Continuous Mean Field Games: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Non-Stationary Dynamics

abstract: The ability to actively acquire information is essential for open-world planning under partial observability and incomplete knowledge. However, most existing embodied AI systems either assume a known object category or rely on passive perception strategies that exhaustively gather object and relational information from the environment. Such a strategy becomes insufficient in visually complex open-world settings. For instance, a typical household may contain thousands of novel and uniquely configured objects, most of which are irrelevant to the agent’s current task. Consequently, open-world agents must be capable of actively identifying and prioritizing task-relevant objects to enable efficient and goal-directed knowledge acquisition. In this work, we introduce ActiveVOO, a novel zero-shot framework for open-world embodied planning that emphasizes object-centric active knowledge acquisition. ActiveVOO employs lifted regression to generate compact, first-order subgoal descriptions that identify task-relevant objects, and provides a principled mechanism to quantify the utility of sensing actions based on commonsense priors derived from LLMs and VLMs. We evaluate ActiveVOO on the visual ALFWorld benchmark, where it achieves substantial improvements over existing LLM- and VLM-based planning approaches, notably outperforming VLMs fine-tuned on ALFWorld data. This work establishes a principled foundation for developing embodied agents capable of actively and efficiently acquiring knowledge to plan and act in open-world environments.
originalAbstract: The ability to actively acquire information is essential for open-world planning under partial observability and incomplete knowledge. However, most existing embodied AI systems either assume a known object category or rely on passive perception strategies that exhaustively gather object and relational information from the environment. Such a strategy becomes insufficient in visually complex open-world settings. For instance, a typical household may contain thousands of novel and uniquely configured objects, most of which are irrelevant to the agent’s current task. Consequently, open-world agents must be capable of actively identifying and prioritizing task-relevant objects to enable efficient and goal-directed knowledge acquisition. In this work, we introduce ActiveVOO, a novel zero-shot framework for open-world embodied planning that emphasizes object-centric active knowledge acquisition. ActiveVOO employs lifted regression to generate compact, first-order subgoal descriptions that identify task-relevant objects, and provides a principled mechanism to quantify the utility of sensing actions based on commonsense priors derived from LLMs and VLMs. We evaluate ActiveVOO on the visual ALFWorld benchmark, where it achieves substantial improvements over existing LLM- and VLM-based planning approaches, notably outperforming VLMs fine-tuned on ALFWorld data. This work establishes a principled foundation for developing embodied agents capable of actively and efficiently acquiring knowledge to plan and act in open-world environments.

paragraphs: An embodied agent often needs more information before it can act, but inspecting everything in its surroundings can waste effort. ActiveVOO addresses planning when the agent cannot fully observe the environment and lacks complete knowledge. Its central question is which objects and observations matter for the current goal.

The framework uses lifted regression to work backward from a task and form compact subgoal descriptions. These descriptions identify relevant objects without requiring a complete account of every object in the scene. It then estimates the usefulness of sensing actions using commonsense expectations supplied by language and vision-language models. Observation becomes a decision guided by the plan, with attention directed toward information that could help achieve a subgoal.

On visual ALFWorld, the authors report substantial improvements over existing language- and vision-language-based planners, including vision-language models fine-tuned on that benchmark. These results support the usefulness of the zero-shot framework in the evaluated setting: selecting what to learn about can improve planning when exhaustive perception would involve many irrelevant objects.
summary.tldr: ActiveVOO guides embodied agents toward task-relevant observations by combining backward planning with estimates of sensing utility.

title: ActiveVOO: Value of Observation Guided Active Knowledge Acquisition for Open-World Embodied Lifted Regression Planning

abstract: Recent advancements in large multimodal models (LMMs) have significantly enhanced performance across diverse tasks, with ongoing efforts to further integrate additional modalities such as video and audio. However, most existing LMMs remain vulnerable to hallucinations, the discrepancy between the factual multimodal input and the generated textual output, which has limited their applicability in various real-world scenarios. This paper presents the first systematic investigation of hallucinations in LMMs involving the three most common modalities: language, visual, and audio. Our study reveals two key contributors to hallucinations: overreliance on unimodal priors and spurious inter-modality correlations. To address these challenges, we introduce the benchmark The Curse of Multi-Modalities (CMM), which comprehensively evaluates hallucinations in LMMs, providing a detailed analysis of their underlying issues. Our findings highlight key vulnerabilities, including imbalances in modality integration and biases from training data, underscoring the need for balanced cross-modal learning and enhanced hallucination mitigation strategies. Based on our observations and findings, we suggest potential research directions that could enhance the reliability of LMMs.

Such hallucinations remain a reliability problem even as these models improve across tasks. This paper systematically investigates hallucinations involving all three modalities, examining how a model's use of different kinds of information contributes to its errors.

The study identifies two key contributors: excessive reliance on priors associated with a single modality and misleading correlations between modalities. Both can lead a model away from the factual input. The authors introduce The Curse of Multi-Modalities benchmark to evaluate these failures and support detailed analysis of their underlying causes.

The findings expose uneven integration of modalities and biases associated with training data. They motivate more balanced cross-modal learning and further work on reducing hallucinations. The paper's main contribution is diagnostic: it provides an evaluation resource and evidence about recurring vulnerabilities, alongside possible research directions. The abstract presents those directions as opportunities to improve reliability, rather than as remedies already shown to solve the problem.
summary.tldr: The CMM benchmark investigates multimodal hallucinations linked to overreliance on single-modality priors and misleading cross-modality correlations.

title: The Curse of Multi-Modalities: Evaluating Hallucinations of Large Multimodal Models across Language, Visual, and Audio

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are predominantly evaluated on Standard American English (SAE), often overlooking the diversity of global English varieties.This narrow focus may raise fairness concerns as degraded performance on non-standard varieties can lead to unequal benefits for users worldwide.Therefore, it is critical to extensively evaluate the linguistic robustness of LLMs on multiple non-standard English varieties.We introduce Trans-EnV, a framework that automatically transforms SAE datasets into multiple English varieties to evaluate the linguistic robustness. Our framework combines (1) linguistics expert knowledge to curate variety-specific features and transformation guidelines from linguistic literature and corpora, and (2) LLM-based transformations to ensure both linguistic validity and scalability.Using Trans-EnV, we transform six benchmark datasets into 38 English varieties and evaluate seven state-of-the-art LLMs.Our results reveal significant performance disparities, with accuracy decreasing by up to 46.3% on non-standard varieties.These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive linguistic robustness evaluation across diverse English varieties. Each construction of Trans-EnV was validated through rigorous statistical testing and consultation with a researcher in the field of second language acquisition, ensuring its linguistic validity.Our code and datasets are publicly available.

paragraphs: Language models are often evaluated using Standard American English, leaving their performance across other English varieties less visible. This matters because lower performance for particular varieties can distribute the benefits of these systems unevenly. Trans-EnV provides a way to expand existing evaluations across a broader range of English usage.

The framework combines linguistic expertise with language-model-based transformation. Variety-specific features and conversion guidelines are curated from linguistic literature and corpora, then used to transform benchmark text. This combination is intended to support both linguistic validity and scale. The authors validate the constructions through statistical testing and consultation with a researcher in second language acquisition.

Using Trans-EnV, the authors transform six benchmark datasets into 38 English varieties and evaluate seven leading language models. They find substantial disparities, with accuracy decreasing by up to 46.3% on non-standard varieties. That maximum describes the reported evaluations, rather than a uniform decline across all varieties. The findings show why evaluation centered on one English variety can miss consequential differences in model performance, and the released code and datasets support broader testing.
summary.tldr: Trans-EnV transforms benchmarks into diverse English varieties and reveals substantial model-performance disparities beyond Standard American English.

title: Trans-EnV: A Framework for Evaluating the Linguistic Robustness of LLMs Against English Varieties

abstract: We propose Heterogeneous Swarms, an algorithm to design multi-LLM systems by jointly optimizing model roles and weights. We represent multi-LLM systems as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of LLMs with topological message passing for collaborative generation. Given a pool of LLM experts and a utility function, Heterogeneous Swarms employs two iterative steps: role-step and weight-step. For role-step, we interpret model roles as learning a DAG that specifies the flow of inputs and outputs between LLMs. Starting from a swarm of random continuous adjacency matrices, we decode them into discrete DAGs, call the LLMs in topological order, evaluate on the utility function (e.g. accuracy on a task), and optimize the adjacency matrices with particle swarm optimization based on the utility score. For weight-step, we assess the contribution of individual LLMs in the multi-LLM systems and optimize model weights with swarm intelligence. We propose JFK-score to quantify the individual contribution of each LLM in the best-found DAG of the role-step, then optimize model weights with particle swarm optimization based on the JFK-score. Experiments demonstrate that Heterogeneous Swarms outperforms 17 role- and/or weight-based baselines by 18.5% on average across 12 tasks. Further analysis reveals that Heterogeneous Swarms discovers multi-LLM systems with heterogeneous model roles and substantial collaborative gains, and benefits from the diversity of language models.

paragraphs: Designing a group of collaborating language models involves deciding both how they interact and how their model weights should be adapted. Heterogeneous Swarms searches over these decisions together. It represents a system as a directed acyclic graph, where connections determine how inputs and generated outputs move between models.

Across 12 tasks, the authors report an average 18.5% advantage over 17 baselines that optimize roles, weights, or both. Further analysis finds varied model roles and substantial benefits from collaboration. The results also indicate that diversity among the available language models helps the search discover effective systems.
summary.tldr: Heterogeneous Swarms jointly searches collaboration graphs and model weights to build more effective multi-LLM systems.

title: Heterogeneous Swarms: Jointly Optimizing Model Roles and Weights for Multi-LLM Systems

abstract: Visual generative and understanding models typically rely on distinct tokenizers to process images, presenting a key challenge for unifying them within a single framework. Recent studies attempt to address this by connecting the training of VQVAE (for autoregressive generation) and CLIP (for understanding) to build a unified tokenizer. However, directly combining these training objectives has been observed to cause severe loss conflicts. In this paper, we show that reconstruction and semantic supervision do not inherently conflict. Instead, the underlying bottleneck stems from limited representational capacity of discrete token space. Building on these insights, we introduce UniTok, a unified tokenizer featuring a novel multi-codebook quantization mechanism that effectively scales up the vocabulary size and bottleneck dimension. In terms of final performance, UniTok sets a new record of 0.38 rFID and 78.6\% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet. Besides, UniTok can be seamlessly integrated into MLLMs to unlock native visual generation capability, without compromising the understanding performance. Additionally, we show that UniTok favors cfg-free generation, reducing gFID from 14.6 to 2.5 on ImageNet 256$\times$256 benchmark. All codes and models have been made publicly available.

paragraphs: Visual generation and visual understanding typically use different image tokenizers. Efforts to combine reconstruction-oriented and semantic training have encountered severe loss conflicts. This paper argues that the objectives are not inherently incompatible: the underlying problem is insufficient representational capacity in the discrete tokens used to describe images.

UniTok addresses that bottleneck with multi-codebook quantization, increasing both vocabulary size and bottleneck dimension. This expands what the token representation can express while serving reconstruction and semantic supervision together. The design therefore targets the shared representation rather than assuming that generation and understanding must remain separated.

The authors report 0.38 reconstruction FID and 78.6% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy, presenting these as record results. They also show integration into multimodal language models that adds native visual generation without compromising understanding performance. For generation without classifier-free guidance, UniTok reduces generation FID from 14.6 to 2.5 on ImageNet at 256 × 256 resolution. These results support increased token capacity as a route to unifying the two capabilities.
summary.tldr: UniTok expands discrete image-token capacity to support strong visual reconstruction, understanding, and generation within a unified tokenizer.

title: UniTok: a Unified Tokenizer for Visual Generation and Understanding

abstract: Object–context shortcuts remain a persistent challenge in vision‑language models, undermining zero‑shot reliability when test-time scenes diverge from familiar training co-occurrences. We recast this issue as a causal inference problem and ask: Would the prediction remain if the object appeared in a different environment? To answer it at inference time, we estimate object and background expectations within CLIP’s representation space, and synthesize counterfactual embeddings by recombining object features with diverse alternative contexts sampled from external datasets, batch neighbors, or text-derived descriptions. By estimating the Total Direct Effect and simulating intervention, we further subtract background‑only activation, preserving beneficial object–context interactions while mitigating hallucinated scores. Without retraining or prompt design, our method substantially improves both worst-group and average accuracy on context-sensitive benchmarks, establishing a new zero‑shot state of the art. Beyond performance, our framework provides a lightweight representation-level counterfactual approach, offering a practical causal avenue for debiased and reliable multimodal reasoning.

paragraphs: This paper targets object–context shortcuts in vision-language models: predictions can depend too heavily on familiar backgrounds rather than the object itself. Such shortcuts undermine zero-shot recognition when test scenes differ from training co-occurrences. The method asks whether a prediction would persist if the same object appeared in a different environment.

At inference time, it estimates object and background expectations in CLIP’s representation space. It then constructs counterfactual embeddings by combining object features with alternative contexts from external datasets, neighboring batch examples, or text descriptions. Using a Total Direct Effect estimate and simulated intervention, it subtracts background-only activation while preserving useful interactions between objects and their surroundings.

The method requires neither retraining nor prompt design. On context-sensitive benchmarks, the authors report substantial improvements in both average and worst-group accuracy, reaching a new zero-shot state of the art. The contribution is a lightweight representation-level calibration procedure that uses counterfactual context changes to reduce misleading scores associated with background shortcuts.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual recombination of object and context embeddings improves zero-shot recognition by reducing background-driven scores without retraining.

title: Representation-Level Counterfactual Calibration for Debiased Zero-Shot Recognition

abstract: A key task in Artificial Intelligence is learning effective policies for controlling agents in unknown environments to optimize performance measures. Off-policy learning methods, like Q-learning, allow learners to make optimal decisions based on past experiences. This paper studies off-policy learning from biased data in complex and high-dimensional domains where \emph{unobserved confounding} cannot be ruled out a priori. Building on the well-celebrated Deep Q-Network (DQN), we propose a novel deep reinforcement learning algorithm robust to confounding biases in observed data. Specifically, our algorithm attempts to find a safe policy for the worst-case environment compatible with the observations. We apply our method to twelve confounded Atari games, and find that it consistently dominates the standard DQN in all games where the observed input to the behavioral and target policies mismatch and unobserved confounders exist.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from past experience becomes difficult when the recorded data contain hidden sources of bias. This paper studies off-policy reinforcement learning in complex, high-dimensional environments where unobserved confounding cannot be ruled out. The concern is that the observations may support misleading conclusions about which actions produce good outcomes.

The authors build on the Deep Q-Network approach and introduce an algorithm intended to withstand confounding in the available experience. It attempts to find a safe policy for the worst-case environment compatible with the observations. This explicitly incorporates uncertainty about the environment that generated the data into policy learning.

The method is evaluated on twelve Atari games with confounding. The authors report that it consistently outperforms standard DQN in all games where the behavioral and target policies receive mismatched observed inputs and unobserved confounders exist. That qualification matters: the stated empirical advantage concerns these confounded, mismatched-input settings. The contribution connects causal concerns about biased experience with a practical deep reinforcement-learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: A DQN-based method seeks policies robust to hidden confounding and outperforms standard DQN in the reported confounded, mismatched-input Atari settings.

title: Confounding Robust Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Causal Approach

abstract: We study the mediation analysis under the distributed framework, where data are stored and processed across different worker machines due to storage limitations or privacy concerns. Building upon the classic Sobel's test and MaxP test, we introduce the distributed Sobel's test and distributed MaxP test, respectively. These tests are both communication-efficient and easy to implement. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments show that, compared to the global test obtained by pooling all data together, the proposed tests achieve nearly identical power, independent of the number of machines. Furthermore, based on these two distributed test statistics, many enhanced mediation tests derived from the Sobel's or MaxP tests can be easily adapted to the distributed system. We apply our method to an educational study, testing whether the effect of high school mathematics on college-level Probability and Mathematical Statistics courses is mediated by Calculus. Our method successfully detects the mediation effect, which would not be identifiable using data from only the first or second class, highlighting the advantage of our approach.

paragraphs: Mediation analysis examines whether an effect passes through an intermediate variable. This paper considers performing that analysis when data are stored and processed on separate machines because of storage constraints or privacy concerns. The challenge is to combine evidence across those machines with little communication while retaining the sensitivity of an analysis using all the data together.

The authors develop distributed versions of Sobel’s test and the MaxP test. The methods are described as easy to implement and communication-efficient. Theory and numerical experiments show nearly the same statistical power as the corresponding pooled-data test, independent of the number of machines. Their distributed statistics also provide a basis for adapting enhanced tests derived from either original procedure.

An educational application examines whether Calculus mediates the relationship between high school mathematics and college Probability and Mathematical Statistics courses. The distributed method detects a mediation effect that data from either the first or second class alone would not identify. This illustrates the value of combining distributed evidence without requiring a pooled analysis.
summary.tldr: Distributed mediation tests combine evidence across machines with little communication and nearly the statistical power of pooled-data tests.

title: Distributed mediation analysis with communication efficiency

abstract: A major challenge in using diffusion models is aligning outputs with user-defined conditions. Existing conditional generation methods fall into two major categories: classifier-based guidance, which requires differentiable target models and gradient-based correction; and classifier-free guidance, which embeds conditions directly into the diffusion model but demands expensive joint training and architectural coupling. In this work, we introduce a third paradigm: DISCrete nOise (DISCO) guidance, which replaces the continuous conditional correction term with a finite codebook of discrete noise vectors sampled from a Gaussian prior. Conditional generation is reformulated as a code selection task, and we train prediction network to choose the optimal code given the intermediate diffusion state and the conditioning input. Our approach is differentiability-free, and training-efficient, avoiding the gradient computation and architectural redundancy of prior methods. Empirical results demonstrate that DISCO achieves competitive controllability while substantially reducing resource demands, positioning it as a scalable and effective alternative for conditional diffusion generation.

paragraphs: DISCO tackles the problem of steering a diffusion model toward user-specified conditions. The paper contrasts two established approaches: guidance using gradients from a differentiable target model, and guidance built into the diffusion model through joint training. These approaches introduce requirements on either the target model or the training and architecture.

DISCO turns conditional guidance into a discrete selection problem. It constructs a finite collection of noise vectors sampled from a Gaussian prior, then trains a prediction network to choose a code using the current diffusion state and the conditioning input. The selected vector takes the role of the continuous conditional correction used in other guidance approaches.

This design avoids requiring differentiable target models and the gradient computations associated with their guidance. The authors also describe it as training-efficient and less architecturally redundant. Empirical results show competitive control over outputs with substantially lower resource demands. The stated result is a practical alternative for conditional generation, with controllability maintained competitively rather than a claim of universally superior image generation.
summary.tldr: DISCO steers diffusion generation by selecting discrete noise codes, achieving competitive conditional control with reduced resource demands.

title: DISCO: DISCrete nOise for Conditional Control in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: Given i.i.d.~samples from an unknown distribution $P$, the goal of distribution learning is to recover the parameters of a distribution that is close to $P$. When $P$ belongs to the class of product distributions on the Boolean hypercube $\{0,1\}^d$, it is known that $\Omega(d/\epsilon^2)$ samples are necessary to learn $P$ within total variation (TV) distance $\epsilon$. We revisit this problem when the learner is also given as advice the parameters of a product distribution $Q$. We show that there is an efficient algorithm to learn $P$ within TV distance $\epsilon$ that has sample complexity $\tilde{O}(d^{1-\eta}/\epsilon^2)$, if $\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_1<\epsilon d^{0.5 - \Omega(\eta)}$. Here, $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are the mean vectors of $P$ and $Q$ respectively, and no bound on $\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_1$ is known to the algorithm a priori.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning an unknown distribution over binary vectors whose coordinates are independent. Given independent samples, the learner must recover a distribution close to the original in total variation distance. Without additional advice, learning to accuracy epsilon requires at least order d divided by epsilon squared samples, where d is the number of coordinates.

The authors give the learner another product distribution as advice. Its coordinate means may be imperfect estimates of the target means. They provide an efficient algorithm whose sample complexity is approximately d to the power of one minus eta, divided by epsilon squared, with logarithmic factors suppressed, when the advice meets a specified closeness condition.

Specifically, the sum of absolute differences between the two mean vectors must be below epsilon times d raised to one-half minus an order-eta term. The algorithm does not need an advance bound on this discrepancy. The result shows that sufficiently accurate advice can reduce the dimensional dependence of sample requirements even when its accuracy is not known beforehand.
summary.tldr: Sufficiently close product-distribution advice reduces learning sample complexity without requiring the learner to know the advice's accuracy beforehand.

title: Product Distribution Learning with Imperfect Advice

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used preference optimization algorithm in large language model (LLM) alignment, which reparameterizes the reward function in reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) without requiring a separate reward model. However, during the DPO training process, when a large negative gradient is applied to low-confidence samples, LLMs with a softmax output head tend to squeeze the confidence in the model's output distribution towards the highest-confidence sentence, which may lead to a decrease in the confidence of both preference and non-preference samples, while increasing the confidence of unrelated tokens. This phenomenon becomes more complex in reasoning tasks. In this work, focusing on reasoning tasks, we propose VPO, a negative gradient constraint method for human non-preference samples based on $\mathcal{V}$-usable information. By using $\mathcal{V}$-usable information to measure the similarity between preference pairs and selectively constrain the negative gradient, VPO can alleviate the squeezing effect of DPO, enhance alignment with the generation objective, and maintain the model's ability to distinguish between preference and non-preference samples. We compare VPO with DPO and its latest variants on mathematical reasoning tasks using the LLama 3.1 and Qwen 2.5 series, including both Base and Instruct models. Our results demonstrate that VPO consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods. Specifically, on Qwen2.5-7B-Base, VPO achieves 7.80\% and 13.25\% improvement over DPO on MATH500 and AMC23, respectively. We also conduct ablation experiments and in-depth analysis on VPO to explain its effectiveness and rationale.

In this work, focusing on reasoning tasks, we propose VPO, a negative gradient constraint method for human non-preference samples based on $\mathcal{V}$-usable information. We compare VPO with DPO and its latest variants on mathematical reasoning tasks using the LLama 3.1 and Qwen 2.5 series, including both Base and Instruct models. Our results demonstrate that VPO consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods. Specifically, on Qwen2.5-7B-Base, VPO achieves 7.80\% and 13.25\% improvement over DPO on MATH500 and AMC23, respectively. We also conduct ablation experiments and in-depth analysis on VPO to explain its effectiveness and rationale.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization trains a language model to favor preferred responses without requiring a separate reward model. This paper examines a problematic training effect: strongly reducing the probability of an already unlikely rejected response can shift probability toward the model’s most confident output. Both preferred and rejected responses may lose confidence while unrelated tokens gain it.

VPO addresses this effect for reasoning tasks by selectively constraining negative gradients on rejected examples. It uses V-usable information to measure similarity between preference pairs and guide those constraints. The aim is to reduce undesirable probability shifts while preserving the model’s ability to distinguish preferred reasoning from rejected reasoning and better aligning training with generation.

The authors compare VPO with DPO and recent variants on mathematical reasoning using Base and Instruct models from the Llama 3.1 and Qwen 2.5 families. They report consistent, significant improvements. For Qwen2.5-7B-Base, the reported gains over DPO are 7.80% on MATH500 and 13.25% on AMC23, with ablations and further analysis examining the method’s effectiveness.
summary.tldr: VPO selectively limits negative preference-training gradients to reduce harmful probability shifts and improve mathematical reasoning performance.

title: VPO: Reasoning Preferences Optimization Based on $\mathcal{V}$-Usable Information

abstract: In this paper, we analyze the performance of a semiparametric principal component analysis named Copula Component Analysis (COCA) (Han & Liu, 2012) when the data are dependent. The semiparametric model assumes that, after unspecified marginally monotone transformations, the distributions are multivariate Gaussian. We study the scenario where the observations are drawn from non-i.i.d. processes ($m$-dependency or a more general $\phi$-mixing case). We show that COCA can allow weak dependence. In particular, we provide the generalization bounds of convergence for both support recovery and parameter estimation of COCA for the dependent data. We provide explicit sufficient conditions on the degree of dependence, under which the parametric rate can be maintained. To our knowledge, this is the first work analyzing the theoretical performance of PCA for the dependent data in high dimensional settings. Our results strictly generalize the analysis in Han & Liu (2012) and the techniques we used have the separate interest for analyzing a variety of other multivariate statistical methods.

The authors also identify their proof techniques as potentially useful for studying other multivariate statistical methods, beyond this particular principal-component procedure.
summary.tldr: COCA retains theoretical recovery guarantees under weak dependence, with sufficient conditions for maintaining the parametric convergence rate.

title: Principal Component Analysis on non-Gaussian Dependent Data

abstract: In this paper, we analyze the task of inferring rare links between pairs of entities that seem too similar to have occurred by chance. Variations of this task appear in such diverse areas as social network analysis, security, fraud detection, and entity resolution. To address the task in a general form, we propose a simple, flexible mixture model in which most entities are generated independently from a distribution but a small number of pairs are constrained to be similar. We predict the true pairs using a likelihood ratio that trades off the entities’ similarity with their rarity. This method always outperforms using only similarity; however, with certain parameter settings, similarity turns out to be surprisingly competitive. Using real data, we apply the model to detect twins given their birth weights and to re-identify cell phone users based on distinctive usage patterns.

paragraphs: When two entities look alike, their resemblance may reflect a real connection or an ordinary coincidence. This paper studies how to detect rare connected pairs across settings such as social analysis, fraud detection, and entity resolution. The central question is whether a similarity is surprising given how common the entities' characteristics are.

The authors propose a mixture model in which most entities arise independently, while a small number of pairs are constrained to resemble one another. A likelihood ratio identifies candidate links by balancing similarity against rarity. Consequently, the method can distinguish resemblance that is common in the population from resemblance that provides stronger evidence of a connection.

Within the proposed analysis, the likelihood-ratio method outperforms using similarity alone, although similarity remains surprisingly competitive for some parameter settings. Real-data applications detect twins from birth weights and re-identify phone users through distinctive usage patterns. These examples demonstrate how the same modeling idea can support different tasks involving unusually similar pairs.
summary.tldr: A mixture model detects rare linked pairs by weighing both their similarity and how unusual that similarity is.

title: Copy or Coincidence? A Model for Detecting Social Influence and Duplication Events

abstract: The analysis and characterization of correlated point process data has wide applications, ranging from biomedical research to network analysis. In this work, we model such data as generated by a latent collection of continuous-time binary semi-Markov processes, corresponding to external events appearing and disappearing. A continuous-time modeling framework is more appropriate for multichannel point process data than a binning approach requiring time discretization, and we show connections between our model and recent ideas from the discrete-time literature. We describe an efficient MCMC algorithm for posterior inference, and apply our ideas to both synthetic data and a real-world biometrics application.

paragraphs: Point-process data describe events through their arrival times, and arrivals across multiple channels can be correlated. The paper models those relationships using hidden external events that appear and disappear over time. This provides a probabilistic account of observed arrivals in terms of underlying activity that is not directly observed.

The hidden activity is represented by a collection of continuous-time binary semi-Markov processes. Each process captures an external event's presence or absence. Working in continuous time avoids the need to divide observations into time bins, an approach the authors argue is less appropriate for multichannel point-process data. They also establish connections to related ideas developed in discrete time.

An efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm performs posterior inference for the model. The authors apply the framework to synthetic data and a real-world biometrics problem. These applications illustrate how correlated arrival data can be analyzed through latent event dynamics while preserving a continuous-time representation. The abstract presents a modeling and inference contribution without claiming a particular comparative performance improvement.
summary.tldr: Latent continuous-time semi-Markov processes explain correlated arrivals through hidden events that switch between presence and absence.

title: Modeling Correlated Arrival Events with Latent Semi-Markov Processes

abstract: We introduce a method for actively learning parameterized skills. Parameterized skills are flexible behaviors that can solve any task drawn from a distribution of parameterized reinforcement learning problems. Approaches to learning such skills have been proposed, but limited attention has been given to identifying which training tasks allow for rapid skill acquisition. We construct a non-parametric Bayesian model of skill performance and derive analytical expressions for a novel acquisition criterion capable of identifying tasks that maximize expected improvement in skill performance. We also introduce a spatiotemporal kernel tailored for non-stationary skill performance models. The proposed method is agnostic to policy and skill representation and scales independently of task dimensionality. We evaluate it on a non-linear simulated catapult control problem over arbitrarily mountainous terrains.

paragraphs: A parameterized skill is a flexible behavior intended to handle tasks drawn from a distribution of reinforcement learning problems. Learning such a skill involves deciding not only how to improve behavior, but also which tasks to practice. This paper focuses on selecting training tasks that are expected to produce useful improvements in the skill.

The method builds a nonparametric Bayesian model of skill performance. It then derives analytical expressions for an acquisition criterion that identifies tasks maximizing expected improvement. Because skill performance changes during training, the authors also introduce a spatiotemporal kernel tailored to nonstationary performance models. This makes changes over training part of the task-selection machinery.

The approach does not depend on a particular policy or skill representation, and the authors state that its scaling is independent of task dimensionality. They evaluate it using simulated nonlinear catapult control over arbitrarily mountainous terrain. The contribution is therefore a general method for deciding what to practice next, supported by an evaluation in a challenging control setting.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian performance model selects training tasks that maximize expected improvement when learning flexible reinforcement learning skills.

title: Active Learning of Parameterized Skills

abstract: Statistical models for manifold-valued data permit capturing the intrinsic nature of the curved spaces in which the data lie and have been a topic of research for several decades. Typically, these formulations use geodesic curves and distances defined locally for most cases - this makes it hard to design parametric models globally on smooth manifolds. Thus, most (manifold specific) parametric models available today assume that the data lie in a small neighborhood on the manifold. To address this ’locality’ problem, we propose a novel nonparametric model which unifies multivariate general linear models (MGLMs) using multiple tangent spaces. Our framework generalizes existing work on (both Euclidean and non-Euclidean) general linear models providing a recipe to globally extend the locally-defined parametric models (using a mixture of local models). By grouping observations into sub-populations at multiple tangent spaces, our method provides insights into the hidden structure (geodesic relationships) in the data. This yields a framework to group observations and discover geodesic relationships between covariates X and manifold-valued responses Y, which we call Dirichlet process mixtures of multivariate general linear models (DP-MGLM) on Riemannian manifolds. Finally, we present proof of concept experiments to validate our model.

Many existing parametric models on manifolds work within a small neighborhood because their geometric ingredients are locally defined. This paper addresses the resulting difficulty of describing observations that extend beyond a single local region.

The proposed framework combines multivariate general linear models across multiple tangent spaces. Each local model handles a neighborhood, and their mixture extends the description across the manifold. The authors formulate this as a Dirichlet process mixture, providing a nonparametric framework that generalizes existing linear-model approaches in both Euclidean and non-Euclidean settings.

The main contribution is therefore a recipe for combining locally meaningful statistical relationships into a broader model, together with an initial demonstration of that recipe.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture combines local linear models across tangent spaces to model manifold-valued responses beyond a single neighborhood.

title: Manifold-valued Dirichlet Processes

abstract: Recent progress in deep latent variable models has largely been driven by the development of flexible and scalable variational inference methods. Variational training of this type involves maximizing a lower bound on the log-likelihood, using samples from the variational posterior to compute the required gradients. Recently, Burda et al. (2016) have derived a tighter lower bound using a multi-sample importance sampling estimate of the likelihood and showed that optimizing it yields models that use more of their capacity and achieve higher likelihoods. This development showed the importance of such multi-sample objectives and explained the success of several related approaches. We extend the multi-sample approach to discrete latent variables and analyze the difficulty encountered when estimating the gradients involved. We then develop the first unbiased gradient estimator designed for importance-sampled objectives and evaluate it at training generative and structured output prediction models. The resulting estimator, which is based on low-variance per-sample learning signals, is both simpler and more effective than the NVIL estimator proposed for the single-sample variational objective, and is competitive with the currently used biased estimators.
