paragraphs: Variational training of latent-variable models optimizes a lower bound on log-likelihood using sampled gradient estimates. Multi-sample importance-sampling objectives can provide tighter bounds, but extending this approach to discrete latent variables creates difficulties in gradient estimation. This paper analyzes those difficulties and develops a method designed for that setting.

The authors introduce what they identify as the first unbiased gradient estimator specifically for importance-sampled objectives. It uses low-variance learning signals for individual samples. Unbiasedness concerns whether the estimator targets the desired gradient on average; reducing variance addresses how much its individual estimates fluctuate.

The estimator is evaluated in training generative models and structured-output prediction models. It is reported to be simpler and more effective than NVIL, an estimator developed for a single-sample variational objective, and competitive with biased estimators in current use. The contribution makes multi-sample objectives more usable with discrete latent variables by addressing the gradient-estimation problem directly, combining an unbiased construction with encouraging empirical training results.
summary.tldr: An unbiased, low-variance gradient estimator enables multi-sample variational training with discrete latent variables and performs competitively in reported evaluations.

title: Variational Inference for Monte Carlo Objectives

abstract: Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT) is a class of projected gradient descent methods for optimizing sparsity-constrained minimization models, with the best known efficiency and scalability in practice. As far as we know, the existing IHT-style methods are designed for sparse minimization in primal form. It remains open to explore duality theory and algorithms in such a non-convex and NP-hard setting. In this article, we bridge the gap by establishing a duality theory for sparsity-constrained minimization with $\ell_2$-regularized objective and proposing an IHT-style algorithm for dual maximization. Our sparse duality theory provides a set of sufficient and necessary conditions under which the original NP-hard/non-convex problem can be equivalently solved in a dual space. The proposed dual IHT algorithm is a super-gradient method for maximizing the non-smooth dual objective. An interesting finding is that the sparse recovery performance of dual IHT is invariant to the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP), which is required by all the existing primal IHT without sparsity relaxation. Moreover, a stochastic variant of dual IHT is proposed for large-scale stochastic optimization. Numerical results demonstrate that dual IHT algorithms can achieve more accurate model estimation given small number of training data and have higher computational efficiency than the state-of-the-art primal IHT-style algorithms.

Existing methods discussed in this paper operate on the primal minimization problem. The authors investigate whether a dual formulation can provide another route through a setting that is nonconvex and NP-hard.

For sparsity-constrained objectives with squared-norm regularization, they establish a duality theory giving necessary and sufficient conditions for equivalent solution in dual space. They then propose dual iterative hard thresholding, a supergradient method for maximizing the nonsmooth dual objective. summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional sparse duality and develops dual hard-thresholding algorithms with favorable recovery and computational results.

title: Dual Iterative Hard Thresholding: From Non-convex Sparse Minimization to Non-smooth Concave Maximization

abstract: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects from observational data is a central problem in many domains. Because counterfactual data is inaccessible, the problem differs fundamentally from supervised learning, and entails a more complex set of modeling choices. Despite a variety of recently proposed algorithmic solutions, a principled guideline for building estimators of treatment effects using machine learning algorithms is still lacking. In this paper, we provide such a guideline by characterizing the fundamental limits of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects, and establishing conditions under which these limits can be achieved. Our analysis reveals that the relative importance of the different aspects of observational data vary with the sample size. For instance, we show that selection bias matters only in small-sample regimes, whereas with a large sample size, the way an algorithm models the control and treated outcomes is what bottlenecks its performance. Guided by our analysis, we build a practical algorithm for estimating treatment effects using a non-stationary Gaussian processes with doubly-robust hyperparameters. Using a standard semi-synthetic simulation setup, we show that our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art, and that the behavior of existing algorithms conforms with our analysis.

paragraphs: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects means learning how a treatment’s effect varies across cases. Observational data make this difficult because the counterfactual outcome is unavailable: the data do not reveal both outcomes for the same case. The paper develops guidance for estimator design by characterizing fundamental estimation limits and conditions under which they can be reached.

The analysis finds that the relative importance of modeling choices changes with sample size. Within the setting analyzed, selection bias matters in small-sample regimes, while modeling treated and control outcomes becomes the performance bottleneck with large samples. This identifies a changing allocation of modeling effort rather than a single concern that dominates every data regime.

The contribution joins theoretical limits with a practical estimator designed around the sources of difficulty those limits reveal.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes treatment-effect estimation limits across sample sizes and uses them to design a successful Gaussian-process estimator.

title: Limits of Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects: Guidelines for Practical Algorithm Design

abstract: Deep multitask learning boosts performance by sharing learned structure across related tasks. This paper adapts ideas from deep multitask learning to the setting where only a single task is available. The method is formalized as pseudo-task augmentation, in which models are trained with multiple decoders for each task. Pseudo-tasks simulate the effect of training towards closely-related tasks drawn from the same universe. In a suite of experiments, pseudo-task augmentation is shown to improve performance on single-task learning problems. When combined with multitask learning, further improvements are achieved, including state-of-the-art performance on the CelebA dataset, showing that pseudo-task augmentation and multitask learning have complementary value. All in all, pseudo-task augmentation is a broadly applicable and efficient way to boost performance in deep learning systems.

paragraphs: Multitask learning can improve performance by sharing learned structure across related tasks. This paper asks whether some of that benefit can be obtained when only one task is available. Its answer is pseudo-task augmentation, a method that introduces multiple decoders for each task during training.

These decoders create pseudo-tasks intended to simulate training on closely related tasks from the same underlying universe. The method brings the idea of sharing within a task, making multiple decoders part of learning from the available task. The same construction can also be applied when several actual tasks are already being learned together.

Experiments show improvements on single-task learning problems. Combining pseudo-task augmentation with multitask learning yields further improvements, including reported state-of-the-art performance on CelebA. Those results support complementary value: the benefit of multiple decoders remains useful alongside sharing across actual tasks. The authors present the method as an efficient, broadly applicable way to improve deep learning systems through the organization of their training.
summary.tldr: Training multiple decoders per task improves single-task learning and provides complementary gains when combined with multitask learning.

title: Pseudo-task Augmentation: From Deep Multitask Learning to Intratask Sharing—and Back

abstract: As machine learning black boxes are increasingly being deployed in real-world applications, there has been a growing interest in developing post hoc explanations that summarize the behaviors of these black boxes. However, existing algorithms for generating such explanations have been shown to lack stability and robustness to distribution shifts. We propose a novel framework for generating robust and stable explanations of black box models based on adversarial training. Our framework optimizes a minimax objective that aims to construct the highest fidelity explanation with respect to the worst-case over a set of adversarial perturbations. We instantiate this algorithm for explanations in the form of linear models and decision sets by devising the required optimization procedures. To the best of our knowledge, this work makes the first attempt at generating post hoc explanations that are robust to a general class of adversarial perturbations that are of practical interest. Experimental evaluation with real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrates that our approach substantially improves robustness of explanations without sacrificing their fidelity on the original data distribution.

paragraphs: Post hoc explanations summarize how an already trained black-box model behaves. The paper addresses a weakness of existing explanation methods: their summaries can be unstable or fail under distribution shifts. It proposes using adversarial training to make explanations more robust while keeping them faithful to the model.

The framework optimizes a minimax objective. It seeks an explanation with the best fidelity under the worst perturbation in a specified adversarial set. This builds robustness directly into explanation construction. The authors instantiate the framework for linear explanations and decision sets, developing the optimization procedures needed for both forms.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show substantial improvements in explanation robustness without sacrificing fidelity on the original data distribution. The result concerns the explanation's ability to continue representing the black box under the considered perturbations. The authors also position the framework as, to their knowledge, the first attempt to construct post hoc explanations robust to a general class of practically relevant adversarial perturbations.
summary.tldr: Adversarially trained explanations improve robustness in experiments while preserving fidelity to the black-box model on the original data distribution.

title: Robust and Stable Black Box Explanations

abstract: We study the problem of constructing black-box adversarial attacks, where no model information is revealed except for the feedback knowledge of the given inputs. To obtain sufficient knowledge for crafting adversarial examples, previous methods query the target model with inputs that are perturbed with different searching directions. However, these methods suffer from poor query efficiency since the employed searching directions are sampled randomly. To mitigate this issue, we formulate the goal of mounting efficient attacks as an optimization problem in which the adversary tries to fool the target model with a limited number of queries. Under such settings, the adversary has to select appropriate searching directions to reduce the number of model queries. By solving the efficient-attack problem, we find that we need to distill the knowledge in both the path of the adversarial examples and the path of the searching directions. Therefore, we propose a novel framework, dual-path distillation, that utilizes the feedback knowledge not only to craft adversarial examples but also to alter the searching directions to achieve efficient attacks. Experimental results suggest that our framework can significantly increase the query efficiency.

paragraphs: In a black-box adversarial attack, the attacker can submit inputs and observe feedback but cannot inspect the target model. Each query must therefore supply information useful for finding an input that fools the model. This paper focuses on query efficiency, identifying randomly sampled search directions as a source of wasted queries in previous approaches.

The authors formulate attack construction as an optimization problem with a limited query budget. Their analysis motivates learning along two paths: the sequence of adversarial examples and the sequence of directions used to search for them. Feedback from the target informs both how the candidate input changes and where the attack searches next.

The resulting dual-path distillation framework makes search direction selection responsive to knowledge already collected. Its importance lies in treating the search process itself as something to improve with feedback, alongside the adversarial example. Experiments suggest that this combined use of feedback can significantly improve query efficiency in the evaluated attacks.
summary.tldr: Dual-path distillation uses target-model feedback to refine both adversarial examples and search directions, improving query efficiency experimentally.

title: Dual-Path Distillation: A Unified Framework to Improve Black-Box Attacks

abstract: We consider stochastic convex optimization problems, where several machines act asynchronously in parallel while sharing a common memory. We propose a robust training method for the constrained setting and derive non asymptotic convergence guarantees that do not depend on prior knowledge of update delays, objective smoothness, and gradient variance. Conversely, existing methods for this setting crucially rely on this prior knowledge, which render them unsuitable for essentially all shared-resources computational environments, such as clouds and data centers. Concretely, existing approaches are unable to accommodate changes in the delays which result from dynamic allocation of the machines, while our method implicitly adapts to such changes.

paragraphs: When several machines train a shared model asynchronously, their updates can arrive with different delays. Those delays can change as computing resources are reassigned. This paper studies stochastic convex optimization in that shared-memory setting, focusing on constrained problems and the difficulty of designing a method without reliable advance information about the computation.

The proposed training method does not require prior knowledge of update delays, objective smoothness, or gradient variance. This is the central adaptation advantage: the method can accommodate changes in delays implicitly, rather than depending on information fixed before training. The motivating environments are clouds and data centers, where machine availability and resource allocation can vary.

The authors derive non-asymptotic convergence guarantees, providing a finite-stage theoretical account of learning progress. Their claim concerns a method that works without advance knowledge of these quantities; it does not say that delays or gradient variability have no effect on training. The contribution is a robust approach to asynchronous optimization when the information required by existing methods is unavailable or becomes outdated.
summary.tldr: A constrained stochastic convex optimization method adapts to asynchronous update delays without requiring prior knowledge of delays, smoothness, or gradient variance.

title: Asynchronous Distributed Learning : Adapting to Gradient Delays without Prior Knowledge

abstract: There is growing awareness and concern about fairness in machine learning and algorithm design. This is particularly true in online selection problems where decisions are often biased, for example, when assessing credit risks or hiring staff. We address the issues of fairness and bias in online selection by introducing multi-color versions of the classic secretary and prophet problem. Interestingly, existing algorithms for these problems are either very unfair or very inefficient, so we develop optimal fair algorithms for these new problems and provide tight bounds on their competitiveness. We validate our theoretical findings on real-world data.

paragraphs: Online selection concerns decisions made as candidates or opportunities arrive, rather than after all options are available. Fairness becomes especially consequential when these decisions concern people, as in hiring or credit assessment. This paper studies how fairness requirements interact with selection quality through extensions of two classical models: the secretary problem and the prophet problem.

The authors introduce versions with multiple colors, providing a way to represent distinctions among groups within these mathematical selection problems. They find that existing algorithms can be very unfair or very inefficient in the resulting settings. This motivates designing algorithms around the fairness requirement from the outset, rather than relying on the existing selection procedures.

The paper develops optimal fair algorithms for the new problems and gives tight bounds on their competitiveness. These bounds characterize performance within the formal models, making the cost and achievable quality of fair selection explicit. Evaluation on real-world data supports the theoretical findings. The contribution connects fairness-aware algorithm design with precise performance guarantees for sequential selection.
summary.tldr: Group-aware versions of classical online selection problems admit optimal fair algorithms with tight competitiveness bounds.

title: Fairness and Bias in Online Selection

abstract: Density ratio estimation (DRE) is at the core of various machine learning tasks such as anomaly detection and domain adaptation. In the DRE literature, existing studies have extensively studied methods based on Bregman divergence (BD) minimization. However, when we apply the BD minimization with highly flexible models, such as deep neural networks, it tends to suffer from what we call train-loss hacking, which is a source of over-fitting caused by a typical characteristic of empirical BD estimators. In this paper, to mitigate train-loss hacking, we propose non-negative correction for empirical BD estimators. Theoretically, we confirm the soundness of the proposed method through a generalization error bound. In our experiments, the proposed methods show favorable performances in inlier-based outlier detection.

paragraphs: Density ratio estimation measures how two probability distributions compare and supports applications including anomaly detection and domain adaptation. A common approach fits a model by minimizing a Bregman divergence objective. The paper examines what happens when this established approach is paired with highly flexible models such as deep neural networks.

The authors identify a failure they call train-loss hacking. A characteristic of empirical Bregman divergence estimators lets flexible models drive the training objective in a way that causes overfitting. They propose a non-negative correction to these empirical estimators, designed to mitigate this behavior at the level of the learning objective.

The paper supports the correction with a generalization error bound and reports favorable experimental performance in inlier-based outlier detection. These contributions link a specific source of overfitting to a targeted objective modification and then examine its theoretical and practical consequences. The proposed correction is presented as a way to mitigate train-loss hacking, with the experimental evidence focused on the stated outlier-detection application.
summary.tldr: A non-negative correction mitigates objective-driven overfitting in deep density ratio estimation and performs favorably in outlier detection.

title: Non-Negative Bregman Divergence Minimization for Deep Direct Density Ratio Estimation

abstract: Saliency methods can make deep neural network predictions more interpretable by identifying a set of critical features in an input sample, such as pixels that contribute most strongly to a prediction made by an image classifier. Unfortunately, recent evidence suggests that many saliency methods poorly perform, especially in situations where gradients are saturated, inputs contain adversarial perturbations, or predictions rely upon inter-feature dependence. To address these issues, we propose a framework, DANCE, which improves the robustness of saliency methods by following a two-step procedure. First, we introduce a perturbation mechanism that subtly varies the input sample without changing its intermediate representations. Using this approach, we can gather a corpus of perturbed ("decoy") data samples while ensuring that the perturbed and original input samples follow similar distributions. Second, we compute saliency maps for the decoy samples and propose a new method to aggregate saliency maps. With this design, we offset influence of gradient saturation. From a theoretical perspective, we show that the aggregated saliency map not only captures inter-feature dependence but, more importantly, is robust against previously described adversarial perturbation methods. Our empirical results suggest that, both qualitatively and quantitatively, DANCE outperforms existing methods in a variety of application domains.

paragraphs: Saliency maps identify input features that contribute strongly to a neural network’s prediction. Their usefulness can deteriorate when gradients saturate, when inputs contain adversarial perturbations, or when predictions depend on interactions between features. DANCE addresses these issues by constructing and combining explanations across carefully perturbed versions of the same input.

Its first step generates decoy samples through subtle input changes that preserve intermediate representations. The construction also keeps the perturbed samples distributed similarly to the original inputs. Its second step computes saliency maps for these decoys and combines them using a new aggregation method. This design offsets the influence of gradient saturation on the resulting explanation.

The theoretical analysis shows that the aggregated map captures dependence between features and is robust to the previously described adversarial perturbation methods considered by the paper. Empirical results suggest improvements over existing methods both visually and quantitatively across several application domains. The significance is that explanation quality can improve through structured input variation and aggregation, while preserving the model representations used to construct the decoys.
summary.tldr: DANCE aggregates saliency maps from carefully constructed decoy inputs to improve explanation robustness and capture feature interactions.

title: DANCE: Enhancing saliency maps using decoys

abstract: Deep learning has recently achieved initial success in program analysis tasks such as bug detection. Lacking real bugs, most existing works construct training and test data by injecting synthetic bugs into correct programs. Despite achieving high test accuracy (e.g., >90%), the resulting bug detectors are found to be surprisingly unusable in practice, i.e., <10% precision when used to scan real software repositories. In this work, we argue that this massive performance difference is caused by a distribution shift, i.e., a fundamental mismatch between the real bug distribution and the synthetic bug distribution used to train and evaluate the detectors. To address this key challenge, we propose to train a bug detector in two phases, first on a synthetic bug distribution to adapt the model to the bug detection domain, and then on a real bug distribution to drive the model towards the real distribution. During these two phases, we leverage a multi-task hierarchy, focal loss, and contrastive learning to further boost performance. We evaluate our approach extensively on three widely studied bug types, for which we construct new datasets carefully designed to capture the real bug distribution. The results demonstrate that our approach is practically effective and successfully mitigates the distribution shift: our learned detectors are highly performant on both our test set and the latest version of open source repositories. Our code, datasets, and models are publicly available at https://github.com/eth-sri/learning-real-bug-detector.

The paper cites synthetic test accuracy above 90% alongside real-world precision below 10%. These are different evaluation measures, but the contrast motivates investigating whether the training examples represent real bugs.

The authors attribute the deployment problem to a mismatch between synthetic and real bug distributions. Their solution trains a detector in two phases: synthetic bugs first introduce the detection task, and real bugs then move the model toward the distribution it will encounter in practice. A multi-task hierarchy, focal loss, and contrastive learning further support training.

The evaluation covers three widely studied bug types and introduces datasets designed to reflect real bug distributions. The resulting detectors perform well on both these test sets and the open-source repository versions evaluated. The findings support matching training and evaluation data to deployment conditions, while showing how synthetic examples can remain useful as an initial stage of a more realistic training process.
summary.tldr: Training first on synthetic bugs and then on real bugs helps bridge the distribution shift that undermines practical bug detection.

title: On Distribution Shift in Learning-based Bug Detectors

abstract: We consider transfer learning approaches that fine-tune a pretrained deep neural network on a target task. We investigate generalization properties of fine-tuning to understand the problem of overfitting, which often happens in practice. Previous works have shown that constraining the distance from the initialization of fine-tuning improves generalization. Using a PAC-Bayesian analysis, we observe that besides distance from initialization, Hessians affect generalization through the noise stability of deep neural networks against noise injections. Motivated by the observation, we develop Hessian distance-based generalization bounds for a wide range of fine-tuning methods. Next, we investigate the robustness of fine-tuning with noisy labels. We design an algorithm that incorporates consistent losses and distance-based regularization for fine-tuning. Additionally, we prove a generalization error bound of our algorithm under class conditional independent noise in the training dataset labels. We perform a detailed empirical study of our algorithm on various noisy environments and architectures. For example, on six image classification tasks whose training labels are generated with programmatic labeling, we show a 3.26% accuracy improvement over prior methods. Meanwhile, the Hessian distance measure of the fine-tuned network using our algorithm decreases by six times more than existing approaches.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained neural network to a new task, but it can overfit the target data. Keeping the adapted parameters close to their initial values is one known way to improve generalization. This paper investigates how the curvature of the loss, represented by Hessians, adds to that explanation.

Using PAC-Bayesian analysis, the authors connect generalization to both parameter movement and stability under injected noise. They derive Hessian distance-based bounds for a broad range of fine-tuning methods. They then design an algorithm combining consistent losses with distance-based regularization to address noisy labels, and prove a generalization bound under a class-conditional independent label-noise assumption.

The empirical study spans multiple architectures and noisy environments. On six image classification tasks with programmatically generated training labels, the authors report a 3.26% accuracy improvement over prior methods. They also report a six-times-greater decrease in the Hessian distance measure than existing approaches. These findings connect the proposed theoretical measure with improved fine-tuning behavior in the evaluated noisy-label settings.
summary.tldr: Hessian-based analysis motivates a regularized fine-tuning method with conditional noisy-label guarantees and improved accuracy in reported experiments.

title: Robust Fine-Tuning of Deep Neural Networks with Hessian-based Generalization Guarantees

abstract: Cutting planes are essential for solving mixed-integer linear problems (MILPs), because they facilitate bound improvements on the optimal solution value. For selecting cuts, modern solvers rely on manually designed heuristics that are tuned to gauge the potential effectiveness of cuts. We show that a greedy selection rule explicitly looking ahead to select cuts that yield the best bound improvement delivers strong decisions for cut selection – but is too expensive to be deployed in practice. In response, we propose a new neural architecture (NeuralCut) for imitation learning on the lookahead expert. Our model outperforms standard baselines for cut selection on several synthetic MILP benchmarks. Experiments on a realistic B&C solver further validate our approach, and exhibit the potential of learning methods in this setting.

paragraphs: Mixed-integer linear optimization solvers use cutting planes to improve bounds on the best achievable solution. Choosing useful cuts is therefore an important solver decision. Existing solvers commonly rely on manually designed heuristics to estimate which candidates will help. This paper investigates learning those choices from an expert that explicitly checks their immediate consequences.

The expert uses a greedy lookahead rule: it selects cuts according to the bound improvement they would produce. The authors find that this yields strong decisions, but the computation required makes direct use impractical. They introduce NeuralCut, a neural architecture trained through imitation learning to reproduce the lookahead expert's selection behavior.

NeuralCut outperforms standard cut-selection baselines on several synthetic mixed-integer linear programming benchmarks. Experiments within a realistic branch-and-cut solver provide further support for the approach. The central idea is to use expensive decision evaluation as a source of training guidance, then learn a selection model from it. The reported results demonstrate the potential of this strategy for an important component of optimization solvers.
summary.tldr: NeuralCut learns to select cutting planes by imitating an effective but computationally expensive lookahead expert.

title: Learning to Cut by Looking Ahead: Cutting Plane Selection via Imitation Learning

abstract: Domain adversarial training has been ubiquitous for achieving invariant representations and is used widely for various domain adaptation tasks. In recent times, methods converging to smooth optima have shown improved generalization for supervised learning tasks like classification. In this work, we analyze the effect of smoothness enhancing formulations on domain adversarial training, the objective of which is a combination of task loss (eg. classification, regression etc.) and adversarial terms. We find that converging to a smooth minima with respect to (w.r.t.) task loss stabilizes the adversarial training leading to better performance on target domain. In contrast to task loss, our analysis shows that converging to smooth minima w.r.t. adversarial loss leads to sub-optimal generalization on the target domain. Based on the analysis, we introduce the Smooth Domain Adversarial Training (SDAT) procedure, which effectively enhances the performance of existing domain adversarial methods for both classification and object detection tasks. Our analysis also provides insight into the extensive usage of SGD over Adam in the community for domain adversarial training.

paragraphs: Domain adversarial training learns representations intended to remain useful across different data distributions. Its training objective combines a task component, such as classification, with an adversarial component. This paper asks how encouraging smooth solutions affects that combination, motivated by results connecting smooth optima with better generalization in supervised learning.

The central finding is that the two components respond differently. Reaching a smooth minimum of the task loss stabilizes adversarial training and improves performance on the target domain. Encouraging smoothness of the adversarial loss instead leads to suboptimal target generalization in the authors’ analysis. Smoothness therefore needs to be considered in relation to a particular part of the objective, rather than treated as a single property to improve everywhere.

The authors use this distinction to develop Smooth Domain Adversarial Training, or SDAT. They report improvements when applying it to existing domain adversarial methods for classification and object detection. Their analysis also offers insight into why practitioners often use SGD instead of Adam for these methods, connecting optimizer choices with the behavior of the combined objective.
summary.tldr: SDAT improves domain adversarial training by encouraging smooth task-loss solutions, while the analysis finds that smoothing the adversarial loss can hurt target generalization.

title: A Closer Look at Smoothness in Domain Adversarial Training

abstract: Black-box model-based optimization (MBO) problems, where the goal is to find a design input that maximizes an unknown objective function, are ubiquitous in a wide range of domains, such as the design of proteins, DNA sequences, aircraft, and robots. Solving model-based optimization problems typically requires actively querying the unknown objective function on design proposals, which means physically building the candidate molecule, aircraft, or robot, testing it, and storing the result. This process can be expensive and time consuming, and one might instead prefer to optimize for the best design using only the data one already has. This setting—called offline MBO—poses substantial and different algorithmic challenges than more commonly studied online techniques. A number of recent works have demonstrated success with offline MBO for high-dimensional optimization problems using high-capacity deep neural networks. However, the lack of standardized benchmarks in this emerging field is making progress difficult to track. To address this, we present Design-Bench, a benchmark for offline MBO with a unified evaluation protocol and reference implementations of recent methods. Our benchmark includes a suite of diverse and realistic tasks derived from real-world optimization problems in biology, materials science, and robotics that present distinct challenges for offline MBO. Our benchmark and reference implementations are released at github.com/rail-berkeley/design-bench and github.com/rail-berkeley/design-baselines.

paragraphs: Design optimization seeks an input, such as a molecule or robot design, that scores highly under an unknown objective. Usually, optimization proceeds by proposing designs and measuring their performance. Those measurements can require physically building and testing candidates, making repeated evaluation expensive and slow. Offline model-based optimization instead seeks good designs using only measurements already available.

This restriction creates algorithmic challenges distinct from those faced by methods that can request new measurements during optimization. Although recent approaches using large neural networks had shown success, inconsistent evaluation made progress difficult to assess. Design-Bench addresses that problem with a shared benchmark, a unified evaluation protocol, and reference implementations of recent methods.

The benchmark contains diverse tasks derived from real optimization problems in biology, materials science, and robotics. Their differing challenges provide a broader basis for assessing offline optimization methods. The paper’s contribution is evaluation infrastructure: shared tasks and implementations make comparisons more consistent and help researchers track progress in learning to design from fixed datasets.
summary.tldr: Design-Bench standardizes evaluation of methods that optimize designs using existing data without collecting new measurements.

title: Design-Bench: Benchmarks for Data-Driven Offline Model-Based Optimization

abstract: Bayesian structure learning allows one to capture uncertainty over the causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) responsible for generating given data. In this work, we present Tractable Uncertainty for STructure learning (TRUST), a framework for approximate posterior inference that relies on probabilistic circuits as a representation of our posterior belief. In contrast to sample-based posterior approximations, our representation can capture a much richer space of DAGs, while being able to tractably answer a range of useful inference queries. We empirically demonstrate how probabilistic circuits can be used to as an augmented representation for structure learning methods, leading to improvement in both the quality of inferred structures and posterior uncertainty. Experimental results also demonstrate the improved representational capacity of TRUST, outperforming competing methods on conditional query answering.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph from data involves uncertainty about which directed connections generated the observations. Bayesian structure learning represents that uncertainty with a posterior distribution over directed acyclic graphs. The challenge addressed here is how to represent this distribution richly enough while still being able to answer useful questions about it efficiently.

TRUST uses probabilistic circuits as an approximate representation of posterior belief. Compared with approximations based on graph samples, the circuit representation can capture a much richer space of candidate graphs while supporting tractable inference queries. The emphasis is therefore on both representation and computation: uncertainty should remain accessible for questions beyond simply selecting a single inferred structure.

Experiments show that probabilistic circuits can augment structure-learning methods and improve both inferred graph quality and posterior uncertainty. TRUST also outperforms competing methods on conditional query answering, supporting the claimed benefit of its richer representation. These are empirical findings for an approximate-inference framework. The contribution is a way to preserve and query more of the uncertainty over possible causal structures without relying solely on a collection of sampled graphs.
summary.tldr: TRUST represents uncertainty over causal graphs with probabilistic circuits, enabling richer approximate posteriors and efficient queries.

title: Tractable Uncertainty for Structure Learning

abstract: Learning to predict missing links is important for many graph-based applications. Existing methods were designed to learn the association between observed graph structure and existence of link between a pair of nodes. However, the causal relationship between the two variables was largely ignored for learning to predict links on a graph. In this work, we visit this factor by asking a counterfactual question: "would the link still exist if the graph structure became different from observation?" Its answer, counterfactual links, will be able to augment the graph data for representation learning. To create these links, we employ causal models that consider the information (i.e., learned representations) of node pairs as context, global graph structural properties as treatment, and link existence as outcome. We propose a novel data augmentation-based link prediction method that creates counterfactual links and learns representations from both the observed and counterfactual links. Experiments on benchmark data show that our graph learning method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the task of link prediction.

paragraphs: Link prediction estimates which connections are missing from a graph. Existing approaches commonly learn associations between observed graph structure and whether two nodes are connected. This paper adds a causal perspective by asking whether a connection would still exist under a different graph structure, using the resulting counterfactual links as additional training information.

The proposed causal model assigns distinct roles to the available information. Learned representations of node pairs provide context, global structural properties of the graph serve as the treatment, and link existence is the outcome. This formulation gives the method a way to create counterfactual examples about connections under altered structural conditions.

The prediction method then learns representations from both observed and generated counterfactual links. Its contribution is therefore a data augmentation strategy that incorporates the causal model into graph representation learning. Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art link prediction performance. Those findings support the usefulness of the augmented training data for prediction in the tested settings, with the counterfactual links supplied by the proposed modeling framework.
summary.tldr: A causal data augmentation method generates counterfactual links and combines them with observed links to improve graph link prediction.

title: Learning from Counterfactual Links for Link Prediction

abstract: Optimal transport aligns samples across distributions by minimizing the transportation cost between them, e.g., the geometric distances. Yet, it ignores coherence structure in the data such as clusters, does not handle outliers well, and cannot integrate new data points. To address these drawbacks, we propose InfoOT, an information-theoretic extension of optimal transport that maximizes the mutual information between domains while minimizing geometric distances. The resulting objective can still be formulated as a (generalized) optimal transport problem, and can be efficiently solved by projected gradient descent. This formulation yields a new projection method that is robust to outliers and generalizes to unseen samples. Empirically, InfoOT improves the quality of alignments across benchmarks in domain adaptation, cross-domain retrieval, and single-cell alignment.

paragraphs: Optimal transport aligns samples from different distributions by minimizing the cost of moving between them, often measured geometrically. This paper addresses shortcomings of that formulation: it can overlook coherent structures such as clusters, handle outliers poorly, and lack a way to integrate new samples. These issues matter when an alignment should preserve more than proximity between individual points.

InfoOT adds an information-theoretic objective to the transport problem. It seeks high mutual information between the domains while also keeping geometric distances small. The combined objective remains expressible as a generalized optimal transport problem and can be solved efficiently with projected gradient descent. This connects structural information across domains to the familiar transport optimization framework.

The formulation also produces a projection method that is robust to outliers and generalizes to previously unseen samples. Experiments report improved alignment quality on benchmarks for domain adaptation, cross-domain retrieval, and single-cell alignment. The findings support using information shared across domains alongside geometric cost when constructing alignments that must handle both existing and new data.
summary.tldr: InfoOT combines mutual information with geometric transport cost to improve cross-domain alignments and support robust projection of unseen samples.

title: InfoOT: Information Maximizing Optimal Transport

abstract: Integer Linear Programs (ILPs) are powerful tools for modeling and solving a large number of combinatorial optimization problems. Recently, it has been shown that Large Neighborhood Search (LNS), as a heuristic algorithm, can find high-quality solutions to ILPs faster than Branch and Bound. However, how to find the right heuristics to maximize the performance of LNS remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose a novel approach, CL-LNS, that delivers state-of-the-art anytime performance on several ILP benchmarks measured by metrics including the primal gap, the primal integral, survival rates and the best performing rate. Specifically, CL-LNS collects positive and negative solution samples from an expert heuristic that is slow to compute and learns a more efficient one with contrastive learning. We use graph attention networks and a richer set of features to further improve its performance.

paragraphs: Integer linear programs express many combinatorial optimization problems, but finding strong solutions quickly depends on the search strategy. Large Neighborhood Search improves solutions by exploring substantial changes around a current candidate. Its effectiveness depends on the heuristic guiding that exploration, and choosing such heuristics remains a central challenge.

CL-LNS learns a faster heuristic from an expert heuristic that is expensive to compute. It gathers both positive and negative solution samples and uses contrastive learning to distinguish useful examples from less useful ones. Graph attention networks and a richer feature set further improve the learned method’s performance.

The authors report state-of-the-art anytime performance on several integer programming benchmarks. Anytime performance concerns the quality of solutions available as computation proceeds, making it relevant when optimization may be stopped at different times. The reported evaluation includes primal gap, primal integral, survival rates, and best-performing rate. The contribution is an empirical demonstration that guidance from a costly expert can be converted into a more efficient learned search heuristic with strong performance across those benchmarks.
summary.tldr: CL-LNS learns an efficient integer-program search heuristic from positive and negative examples supplied by a costly expert.

title: Searching Large Neighborhoods for Integer Linear Programs with Contrastive Learning

abstract: Adversarial imitation learning (AIL) is a popular method that has recently achieved much success. However, the performance of AIL is still unsatisfactory on the more challenging tasks. We find that one of the major reasons is due to the low quality of AIL discriminator representation. Since the AIL discriminator is trained via binary classification that does not necessarily discriminate the policy from the expert in a meaningful way, the resulting reward might not be meaningful either. We propose a new method called Policy Contrastive Imitation Learning (PCIL) to resolve this issue. PCIL learns a contrastive representation space by anchoring on different policies and uses a smooth cosine-similarity-based reward to encourage imitation learning. Our proposed representation learning objective can be viewed as a stronger version of the AIL objective and provide a more meaningful comparison between the agent and the policy. From a theoretical perspective, we show the validity of our method using the apprenticeship learning framework. Furthermore, our empirical evaluation on the DeepMind Control suite demonstrates that PCIL can achieve state-of-the-art performance. Finally, qualitative results suggest that PCIL builds a smoother and more meaningful representation space for imitation learning.

paragraphs: Adversarial imitation learning uses a discriminator to distinguish an agent’s behavior from expert behavior, then uses that distinction to guide learning. This paper identifies poor discriminator representations as a major source of difficulty on challenging tasks. Binary classification can separate examples without providing a meaningful measure of how behavior should improve.

Policy Contrastive Imitation Learning, or PCIL, learns a representation space anchored on different policies. It then defines a smooth reward using cosine similarity within that space. The aim is to make behavioral comparisons more informative, so that the reward encourages imitation through the learned structure of policies rather than relying solely on a binary decision.

The authors interpret the representation objective as a stronger version of the adversarial imitation objective and establish its validity through the apprenticeship learning framework. Experiments on the DeepMind Control suite show that PCIL can reach state-of-the-art performance. Qualitative results additionally suggest a smoother, more meaningful representation space. Those visual or qualitative findings support the proposed explanation of the method’s behavior without establishing it as a universal outcome.
summary.tldr: PCIL uses policy-based contrastive representations and a smooth similarity reward to improve imitation learning.

title: Policy Contrastive Imitation Learning

abstract: The advent of large language models trained on code (code LLMs) has led to significant progress in language-to-code generation. State-of-the-art approaches in this area combine LLM decoding with sample pruning and reranking using test cases or heuristics based on the execution results. However, it is challenging to obtain test cases for many real-world language-to-code applications, and heuristics cannot well capture the semantic features of the execution results, such as data type and value range, which often indicates the correctness of the program. In this work, we propose LEVER, a simple approach to improve language-to-code generation by learning to verify the generated programs with their execution results. Specifically, we train verifiers to determine whether a program sampled from the LLMs is correct or not based on the natural language input, the program itself and its execution results. The sampled programs are reranked by combining the verification score with the LLM generation probability, and marginalizing over programs with the same execution results. On four datasets across the domains of table QA, math QA and basic Python programming, LEVER consistently improves over the base code LLMs (4.6% to 10.9% with code-davinci-002) and achieves new state-of-the-art results on all of them.

paragraphs: Code-generating language models can produce several candidate programs for a natural-language request, leaving the problem of selecting the correct one. Test cases are often difficult to obtain, while simple execution-based heuristics may overlook meaningful clues such as an output's type or value range. LEVER learns to interpret these clues through a verifier.

The verifier considers the original request, a generated program, and that program's execution results when estimating correctness. LEVER combines this verification score with the language model's generation probability to rerank candidates. It also aggregates evidence across programs that produce the same execution result, allowing different candidate implementations to contribute to the selection process.

Evaluation covers four datasets spanning table question answering, mathematical question answering, and basic Python programming. LEVER consistently improves the underlying code language models, with reported gains of 4.6% to 10.9% for code-davinci-002, and achieves state-of-the-art results on all four datasets. These findings support learned execution-aware selection as a way to improve the usefulness of programs already sampled from a code model.
summary.tldr: LEVER improves code generation by learning to verify candidate programs using their execution results and combining verification with generation probabilities.

title: LEVER: Learning to Verify Language-to-Code Generation with Execution

abstract: A complex system with cluttered observations may be a coupled mixture of multiple simple sub-systems corresponding to latent entities. Such sub-systems may hold distinct dynamics in the continuous-time domain; therein, complicated interactions between sub-systems also evolve over time. This setting is fairly common in the real world but has been less considered. In this paper, we propose a sequential learning approach under this setting by decoupling a complex system for handling irregularly sampled and cluttered sequential observations. Such decoupling brings about not only subsystems describing the dynamics of each latent entity but also a meta-system capturing the interaction between entities over time. Specifically, we argue that the meta-system evolving within a simplex is governed by projected differential equations (ProjDEs). We further analyze and provide neural-friendly projection operators in the context of Bregman divergence. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show the advantages of our approach when facing complex and cluttered sequential data compared to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: A cluttered sequence of observations may combine several hidden entities, each following its own dynamics while interacting with the others. This paper develops a sequential-learning approach for that setting, including observations collected at irregular times. It represents the complex system through separate subsystems and an additional model of their changing interactions.

Each subsystem describes the continuous-time dynamics of a latent entity. A meta-system captures how those entities interact over time. The authors argue that this meta-system evolves within a simplex and is governed by projected differential equations. They also analyze projection operators through Bregman divergence and provide versions suitable for use with neural models.

The separation matters because entity behavior and interaction behavior are represented as distinct parts of the overall model. That structure gives the method a way to address clutter without treating all observed change as one undifferentiated process. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report advantages over state-of-the-art approaches when handling the complex, cluttered sequential data considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: The method models cluttered sequences by separating latent-entity dynamics from a continuous-time meta-system describing their interactions.

title: Learning to Decouple Complex Systems

abstract: Large language models are increasingly integrated with external environments, tools, and agents like ChatGPT plugins to extend their capability beyond language-centric tasks. However, today’s LLM inference systems are designed for standalone LLMs. They treat each external interaction as the end of LLM generation and form a new request when the interaction finishes, causing unnecessary recomputation of already computed contexts, which accounts for 37-40% of total model forwarding time. This paper presents InferCept, the first LLM inference framework targeting augmented LLMs and supporting the efficient interception of LLM generation. InferCept minimizes the GPU resource waste caused by LLM interceptions and dedicates saved memory for serving more requests.InferCept improves the overall serving throughput by 1.6x-2x and completes 2x more requests per second compared to the state-of-the-art LLM inference systems.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly pause generation to interact with tools, external environments, or other agents. Inference systems designed for standalone models commonly treat that pause as the end of a request. When the external interaction finishes, they start a new request and recompute context that was already processed. The paper attributes 37–40% of total model forwarding time to this redundant work.

InferCept is an inference framework designed to support these interruptions directly. It targets GPU resource waste caused by intercepted generation and uses saved memory to serve additional requests. The system contribution is to make external interactions part of the serving workflow rather than handling every return from an interaction as a fresh generation request.

The authors report overall serving throughput improvements of 1.6–2 times and twice as many completed requests per second compared with leading inference systems. These findings show that supporting the interaction pattern of augmented language models can materially improve serving efficiency. The gains concern how requests are executed and resources are managed, rather than changes to the model’s language capabilities.
summary.tldr: InferCept reduces wasted GPU work around external tool interactions, increasing reported language-model serving throughput by 1.6–2 times.

title: InferCept: Efficient Intercept Support for Augmented Large Language Model Inference

abstract: We propose a generalization of the classical G-optimal design concept to non-linear function classes. The criterion, termed F -design, coincides with G-design in the linear case. We compute the value of the optimal design, termed the F-condition number, for several non-linear function classes. We further provide algorithms to construct designs with a bounded F -condition number. Finally, we employ the F-design in a variety of interactive machine learning tasks, where the design is naturally useful for data collection or exploration. We show that in four diverse settings of confidence band construction, contextual bandits, model-free reinforcement learning, and active learning, F-design can be combined with existing approaches in a black-box manner to yield state-of-the-art results in known problem settings as well as to generalize to novel ones.

paragraphs: Interactive learning methods must decide what data to collect or where to explore. This paper develops F-design, a criterion for guiding those choices with nonlinear function classes. It generalizes classical G-optimal design and agrees with that established criterion when the function class is linear, providing a connection between the two settings.

The authors call the value of an optimal design its F-condition number. They calculate this value for several nonlinear function classes and give algorithms for constructing designs with a bounded condition number. The work therefore provides both a measure of design quality and procedures for obtaining designs with controlled values of that measure.

The paper applies F-design to confidence-band construction, contextual bandits, model-free reinforcement learning, and active learning. In these four settings, it can be combined with existing approaches as a black-box component. The authors report state-of-the-art results for established problem settings and extensions to new ones. Its broader significance is a reusable design framework that links data collection and exploration across several interactive learning tasks.
summary.tldr: F-design extends optimal experimental design to nonlinear function classes and supports data collection and exploration across interactive learning tasks.

title: The Non-linear $F$-Design and Applications to Interactive Learning

abstract: In this work, we investigate the interplay between memorization and learning in the context of stochastic convex optimization (SCO). We define memorization via the information a learning algorithm reveals about its training data points. We then quantify this information using the framework of conditional mutual information (CMI) proposed by Steinke and Zakynthinou (2020). Our main result is a precise characterization of the tradeoff between the accuracy of a learning algorithm and its CMI, answering an open question posed by Livni (2023). We show that, in the $L^2$ Lipschitz–bounded setting and under strong convexity, every learner with an excess error $\epsilon$ has CMI bounded below by $\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)$ and $\Omega(1/\epsilon)$, respectively. We further demonstrate the essential role of memorization in learning problems in SCO by designing an adversary capable of accurately identifying a significant fraction of the training samples in specific SCO problems. Finally, we enumerate several implications of our results, such as a limitation of generalization bounds based on CMI and the incompressibility of samples in SCO problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much information a learning algorithm must reveal about its training examples to solve stochastic convex optimization accurately. It treats memorization as information disclosure, measured through conditional mutual information, rather than simply as reproducing a training example verbatim.

The main result precisely characterizes a tradeoff between learning accuracy and this information measure. In the L2 Lipschitz–bounded setting, a learner with excess error epsilon must have conditional mutual information at least on the order of one over epsilon squared. Under strong convexity, the corresponding lower bound is on the order of one over epsilon. Greater accuracy therefore carries unavoidable information requirements in the settings studied.

The authors also construct an adversary that can accurately identify a significant fraction of training samples for specific stochastic convex optimization problems. This gives a tracing interpretation to the information-theoretic results. Further implications include limits on generalization bounds based on conditional mutual information and on sample compressibility. The findings establish an essential role for memorization in these problems without claiming that every learning task exposes its training examples in the same way.
summary.tldr: Accuracy in studied stochastic convex optimization settings requires measurable training-data information, with consequences for tracing, compression, and generalization bounds.

title: Information Complexity of Stochastic Convex Optimization: Applications to Generalization, Memorization, and Tracing

abstract: We propose a novel regression adjustment method designed for estimating distributional treatment effect parameters in randomized experiments. Randomized experiments have been extensively used to estimate treatment effects in various scientific fields. However, to gain deeper insights, it is essential to estimate distributional treatment effects rather than relying solely on average effects. Our approach incorporates pre-treatment covariates into a distributional regression framework, utilizing machine learning techniques to improve the precision of distributional treatment effect estimators. The proposed approach can be readily implemented with off-the-shelf machine learning methods and remains valid as long as the nuisance components are reasonably well estimated. Also, we establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator and present a uniformly valid inference method. Through simulation results and real data analysis, we demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating machine learning techniques in reducing the variance of distributional treatment effect estimators in finite samples.

paragraphs: An average treatment effect summarizes an intervention with one number, but researchers may also want to understand how it changes the distribution of outcomes. This paper develops a regression adjustment method for estimating such distributional effects in randomized experiments. Its goal is to improve precision by using information measured before treatment.

The method incorporates these pre-treatment covariates into distributional regression and allows standard machine learning tools to estimate the supporting components. Those components help adjust the treatment-effect estimator. The validity claim is conditional: the nuisance components must be estimated reasonably well. The approach therefore combines flexible prediction with a statistical requirement on the quality of those estimates.

The authors establish large-sample properties and a uniformly valid inference method, supporting uncertainty assessment as well as point estimation. Simulations and a real-data analysis show reduced estimator variance in finite samples. The stated practical benefit is more precise distributional treatment-effect estimation from randomized data, extending attention beyond mean effects while making use of readily available machine learning methods.
summary.tldr: Machine learning regression adjustment improves precision for distributional treatment effects, with validity depending on adequate nuisance estimation.

title: Estimating Distributional Treatment Effects in Randomized Experiments: Machine Learning for Variance Reduction

abstract: The unsupervised outlier detection (UOD) problem refers to a task to identify inliers given training data which contain outliers as well as inliers, without any labeled information about inliers and outliers. It has been widely recognized that using fully-trained likelihood-based deep generative models (DGMs) often results in poor performance in distinguishing inliers from outliers. In this study, we claim that the likelihood itself could serve as powerful evidence for identifying inliers in UOD tasks, provided that DGMs are carefully under-fitted. Our approach begins with a novel observation called the inlier-memorization (IM) effect–when training a deep generative model with data including outliers, the model initially memorizes inliers before outliers. Based on this finding, we develop a new method called the outlier detection via the IM effect (ODIM). Remarkably, the ODIM requires only a few updates, making it computationally efficient–at least tens of times faster than other deep-learning-based algorithms. Also, the ODIM filters out outliers excellently, regardless of the data type, including tabular, image, and text data. To validate the superiority and efficiency of our method, we provide extensive empirical analyses on close to 60 datasets.

paragraphs: Unsupervised outlier detection starts with data containing both ordinary examples and outliers, without labels identifying either group. Fully trained likelihood-based deep generative models often struggle to distinguish them. This paper argues that likelihood can nevertheless be useful when the model is deliberately kept under-fitted.

The method rests on an observed inlier-memorization effect: early in training, the generative model memorizes inliers before outliers. ODIM uses this early training behavior to identify inliers and filter outliers. The timing is central to the approach because the useful separation appears before the model has fully fitted the mixed training data.

ODIM requires only a few updates, and the authors report that it is at least tens of times faster than other deep-learning-based algorithms. They evaluate it on close to 60 datasets spanning tables, images, and text, reporting strong detection performance across these data types. The findings show how an intermediate stage of generative-model training can provide a useful detection signal that is often ineffective after full training.
summary.tldr: ODIM detects outliers using the early training period when generative models memorize inliers first, requiring only a few updates.

title: ODIM: Outlier Detection via Likelihood of Under-Fitted Generative Models

abstract: Augmenting large language models (LLMs) to understand audio – including non-speech sounds and non-verbal speech – is critically important for diverse real-world applications of LLMs. In this paper, we propose Audio Flamingo, a novel audio language model with 1) strong audio understanding abilities, 2) the ability to quickly adapt to unseen tasks via in-context learning and retrieval, and 3) strong multi-turn dialogue abilities. We introduce a series of training techniques, architecture design, and data strategies to enhance our model with these abilities. Extensive evaluations across various audio understanding tasks confirm the efficacy of our method, setting new state-of-the-art benchmarks. Our demo website is https://audioflamingo.github.io/ and the code is open-sourced at https://github.com/NVIDIA/audio-flamingo.

paragraphs: Audio Flamingo addresses how to give a language model useful understanding of audio, including sounds that are not spoken words and nonverbal aspects of speech. The intended capability extends beyond extracting text from a recording. The model must also use audio information when responding to a user, adapting to a task, and participating in an ongoing conversation.

The paper combines architecture choices, training techniques, and data strategies to develop three abilities: audio understanding, adaptation to unseen tasks, and mult turn dialogue. Adaptation uses in-context learning and retrieval, allowing examples and retrieved information to help guide the model on tasks it has not previously encountered. Dialogue capability makes audio understanding part of a continuing exchange.

Evaluations across multiple audio-understanding tasks report state-of-the-art results and support the effectiveness of the overall approach. The contribution is the combination of these capabilities within an audio-language model. Its findings support the tested methods for connecting audio understanding, task adaptation, and conversation, without establishing that every unfamiliar audio task will be handled equally well.
summary.tldr: Audio Flamingo combines audio understanding, adaptation through examples and retrieval, and ongoing dialogue, with state-of-the-art results across evaluated audio tasks.

title: Audio Flamingo: A Novel Audio Language Model with Few-Shot Learning and Dialogue Abilities

abstract: The partially observable generalized linear model (POGLM) is a powerful tool for understanding neural connectivities under the assumption of existing hidden neurons. With spike trains only recorded from visible neurons, existing works use variational inference to learn POGLM meanwhile presenting the difficulty of learning this latent variable model. There are two main issues: (1) the sampled Poisson hidden spike count hinders the use of the pathwise gradient estimator in VI; and (2) the existing design of the variational model is neither expressive nor time-efficient, which further affects the performance. For (1), we propose a new differentiable POGLM, which enables the pathwise gradient estimator, better than the score function gradient estimator used in existing works. For (2), we propose the forward-backward message-passing sampling scheme for the variational model. Comprehensive experiments show that our differentiable POGLMs with our forward-backward message passing produce a better performance on one synthetic and two real-world datasets. Furthermore, our new method yields more interpretable parameters, underscoring its significance in neuroscience.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer connections among neurons when recordings capture only some of them. Its starting point is a partially observable generalized linear model, which accounts for hidden neurons alongside visible ones. Learning this model requires estimating unobserved activity, making the inference procedure central to both predictive performance and the interpretation of connections.

The authors address two obstacles in existing variational inference methods. First, discrete samples of hidden spike counts make it difficult to differentiate through the sampling process. They introduce a differentiable model that permits a pathwise gradient estimator. Second, they develop a forward-backward message-passing sampling scheme to improve the variational model, addressing shortcomings in its expressiveness and computational efficiency.

Experiments on one synthetic dataset and two real datasets report better performance from combining these changes. The resulting parameters are also described as more interpretable. The contribution therefore concerns both learning the hidden-neuron model more effectively and making its fitted parameters more useful for understanding neural connectivity under the assumption that hidden neurons exist.
summary.tldr: A differentiable neural connectivity model combines pathwise gradients with forward-backward sampling to improve inference when some neurons are unobserved.

title: A Differentiable Partially Observable Generalized Linear Model with Forward-Backward Message Passing

abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful technique for discovering the underlying mathematical expressions from observed data. Inspired by the success of deep learning, recent deep generative SR methods have shown promising results. However, these methods face difficulties in processing high-dimensional problems and learning constants due to the large search space, and they don’t scale well to unseen problems. In this work, we propose DySymNet, a novel neural-guided Dynamic Symbolic Network for SR. Instead of searching for expressions within a large search space, we explore symbolic networks with various structures, guided by reinforcement learning, and optimize them to identify expressions that better-fitting the data. Based on extensive numerical experiments on low-dimensional public standard benchmarks and the well-known SRBench with more variables, DySymNet shows clear superiority over several representative baseline models. Open source code is available at https://github.com/AILWQ/DySymNet.

The paper focuses on difficulties faced by deep generative approaches: searching among many possible expressions, learning constants, handling more input variables, and transferring effectively to unseen problems.

DySymNet changes the object being explored during that search. It considers symbolic networks with different structures and uses reinforcement learning to guide their exploration. The candidate networks are then optimized to identify expressions that fit the data better. This connects the choice of mathematical structure with the process of improving its fit to observations.

The authors evaluate DySymNet on public benchmarks with relatively few variables and on SRBench problems with more variables. They report clear advantages over several representative baseline models across these numerical experiments. Those findings support the proposed network-based search strategy across the tested problem sizes. The contribution is a way to organize expression discovery around adaptable symbolic structures, addressing the search difficulties that motivate the work.
summary.tldr: DySymNet uses reinforcement learning to explore and optimize symbolic network structures for discovering mathematical expressions from data.

title: A Neural-Guided Dynamic Symbolic Network for Exploring Mathematical Expressions from Data

abstract: Questions of fair use of copyright-protected content to train Large Language Models (LLMs) are being actively debated. Document-level inference has been proposed as a new task: inferring from black-box access to the trained model whether a piece of content has been seen during training. SOTA methods however rely on naturally occurring memorization of (part of) the content. While very effective against models that memorize significantly, we hypothesize - and later confirm - that they will not work against models that do not naturally memorize, e.g. medium-size 1B models. We here propose to use copyright traps, the inclusion of fictitious entries in original content, to detect the use of copyrighted materials in LLMs with a focus on models where memorization does not naturally occur. We carefully design a randomized controlled experimental setup, inserting traps into original content (books) and train a 1.3B LLM from scratch. We first validate that the use of content in our target model would be undetectable using existing methods. We then show, contrary to intuition, that even medium-length trap sentences repeated a significant number of times (100) are not detectable using existing methods. However, we show that longer sequences repeated a large number of times can be reliably detected (AUC=0.75) and used as copyright traps. Beyond copyright applications, our findings contribute to the study of LLM memorization: the randomized controlled setup enables us to draw causal relationships between memorization and certain sequence properties such as repetition in model training data and perplexity.

This paper investigates copyright traps: deliberately inserted fictitious passages intended to make training-data use detectable even when ordinary content leaves little detectable trace.

summary.tldr: Controlled experiments show that long, heavily repeated fictitious passages can reveal training-data use where ordinary content and shorter repeated traps remain undetectable.

title: Copyright Traps for Large Language Models

abstract: Generating rich and controllable motion is a pivotal challenge in video synthesis. We propose Boximator, a new approach for fine-grained motion control. Boximator introduces two constraint types: hard box and soft box. Users select objects in the conditional frame using hard boxes and then use either type of boxes to roughly or rigorously define the object’s position, shape, or motion path in future frames. Boximator functions as a plug-in for existing video diffusion models. Its training process preserves the base model’s knowledge by freezing the original weights and training only the control module. To address training challenges, we introduce a novel self-tracking technique that greatly simplifies the learning of box-object correlations. Empirically, Boximator achieves state-of-the-art video quality (FVD) scores, improving on two base models, and further enhanced after incorporating box constraints. Its robust motion controllability is validated by drastic increases in the bounding box alignment metric. Human evaluation also shows that users favor Boximator generation results over the base model.

paragraphs: Boximator gives users a spatial way to control movement in generated videos. Users first select objects in a conditioning frame with hard boxes.
