This enables self-supervised pretraining on 49,497 fMRI sessions from nine datasets. The contribution combines an atlas-free representation with a mechanism intended to make training at that resolution scalable.

The authors also establish a benchmark covering 11 datasets and a range of resting-state and task-based fMRI tasks. This provides a shared basis for reproducibility and comparison. Across the reported experiments, Omni-fMRI consistently outperforms existing foundation models. The findings support direct voxel-level learning as a useful alternative to atlas-based representations, with the benchmark providing a framework for evaluating that approach across different fMRI tasks.
summary.tldr: Omni-fMRI uses dynamic patching to learn directly from voxel-level brain signals and outperforms existing foundation models in the reported evaluations.

title: Omni-fMRI: A Universal Atlas-Free fMRI Foundation Model

abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for robots to achieve human-like gentle manipulation. However, existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle to exploit tactile feedback for gentle manipulation due to scarce aligned vision-tactile-language data and the lack of effective closed-loop force feedback mechanisms. To address these challenges, we introduce Tabero, a benchmark and model suite for gentle, language-conditioned robotic manipulation that demands fine-grained contact force perception. First, the Tabero benchmark addresses the scarcity of tactile data by presenting a data-efficient pipeline that repurposes open-source robot manipulation trajectories to generate diverse vision-tactile-language tasks, and establishes a multidimensional evaluation protocol that measures task success alongside physical interaction quality. Second, we propose Tabero-VTLA, an architecture with a decoupled force-position command interface; the resulting force-position commands are executed by a fixed hybrid controller to enable real-time, force-aware manipulation. Evaluated on Tabero, our model maintains high task success while reducing average grip force by over 70% under gentle instructions, demonstrating its ability to modulate interaction forces based on multimodal experience.

paragraphs: A robot can complete a manipulation task while applying more force than intended. Tabero focuses on gentle manipulation guided by language, vision, and touch. It addresses both the scarcity of aligned multimodal training data and the need for a feedback mechanism that adjusts contact forces during execution.

The benchmark uses a data-efficient pipeline to repurpose open-source robot trajectories into varied vision–tactile–language tasks. Its evaluation considers physical interaction quality alongside task completion. The accompanying Tabero-VTLA model produces separate force and position commands, which a fixed hybrid controller executes. This interface connects the model's multimodal decisions to real-time force-aware control.

On the Tabero benchmark, the model maintains high task success while reducing average grip force by more than 70% under gentle instructions. The finding demonstrates that language-conditioned behavior can include modulation of physical contact, rather than task completion being the sole evaluation target. The benchmark and model together provide a setting for learning and measuring how successfully robots follow instructions about the quality of their interactions.
summary.tldr: Tabero combines a tactile manipulation benchmark with force-aware control, reporting over 70% lower average grip force under gentle instructions.

title: Tabero: Learning Gentle Manipulation with Closed-Loop Force Feedback from Vision, Touch, and Language

abstract: Long-form video understanding remains a formidable challenge due to the complexity of modeling long-range temporal dependencies and multi-event narratives. Existing methods often rely on static reasoning or external Visual-Language Models (VLMs), resulting in high computational complexity and sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we propose Video-MTR, a reinforced multi-turn reasoning framework that operates solely through data-efficient, pure RL post-training. Video-MTR reformulates video understanding as a dynamic decision-making process, where the agent iteratively selects key segments conditioned on the evolving context of previously processed frames and the query. To ensure effective intermediate reasoning and training stability, we introduce a novel gated bi-level reward system, which synergizes trajectory-level rewards (answer correctness) with turn-level rewards (frame-query relevance). This mechanism eliminates the need for data-intensive supervised fine-tuning, thereby substantially reducing reliance on large-scale datasets. Remarkably, Video-MTR achieves competitive or superior performance using only $\sim$8K training samples, compared to existing approaches that require 257K to 4.4M examples. Extensive experiments on benchmarks including VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench, LVBench, and EgoSchema demonstrate that Video-MTR surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/Xyuan13/Video-MTR.

The agent repeatedly chooses key video segments using both the query and the evolving context of frames it has already processed.

Training uses reinforcement-learning post-training with a gated reward system operating at two levels. A trajectory-level reward evaluates answer correctness, while turn-level rewards evaluate frame relevance to the query. title: Video-MTR: Reinforced Multi-Turn Reasoning for Long Video Understanding

abstract: Adversarial imitation learning (AIL) achieves high-quality imitation compared to behavioral cloning (BC), but demands substantial online environment interaction. Recent empirical work has explored initializing AIL algorithms with BC-pretrained policies to address this limitation, yet a rigorous theoretical understanding of pretraining’s role in AIL remains elusive. This paper provides a systematic theoretical analysis and introduces principled pretraining algorithms for accelerating AIL. We begin by analyzing AIL with policy pretraining alone, identifying reward error as the dominant source of suboptimality. This reveals a critical and previously overlooked gap: the absence of reward pretraining. Motivated by this finding, we develop a principled policy–reward co-pretraining approach grounded in a reward-shaping analysis. Our analysis uncovers a fundamental connection between expert policies and shaping rewards, which naturally gives rise to CoPT-AIL, an approach that jointly pretrains both policy and reward through a single BC procedure. We prove that CoPT-AIL achieves an improved imitation gap bound over standard AIL, establishing the first theoretical guarantee for the benefits of pretraining in AIL. Experimental results confirm CoPT-AIL’s superior performance over existing AIL methods.

title: Provably Efficient Policy-Reward Co-Pretraining for Adversarial Imitation Learning

abstract: Controllable diffusion generation often relies on various heuristics that are seemingly disconnected without a unified understanding. We bridge this gap with Diffusion Controller (DiffCon), a unified control-theoretic view that casts reverse diffusion sampling as state-only stochastic control within (generalized) linearly-solvable Markov Decision Processes (LS-MDPs). Under this framework, control acts by reweighting the pretrained reverse-time transition kernels, balancing terminal objectives against an $f$-divergence cost. From the resulting optimality conditions, we derive practical reinforcement learning methods for diffusion fine-tuning: (i) $f$-divergence-regularized policy-gradient updates, including a PPO-style rule, and (ii) a regularizer-determined reward-weighted regression objective with a minimizer-preservation guarantee under the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. The LS-MDP framework further implies a principled model form: the optimal score decomposes into a fixed pretrained baseline plus a lightweight control correction, motivating a side-network parameterization conditioned on exposed intermediate denoising outputs, enabling effective gray-box adaptation with a frozen backbone. Experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.4 across supervised and reward-driven finetuning show consistent gains in preference-alignment win rates and improved quality–efficiency trade-offs versus gray-box baselines and even the parameter-efficient white-box adapter LoRA.

It treats reverse diffusion as stochastic control within generalized linearly-solvable Markov decision processes. Control reweights a pretrained model’s reverse-time transitions, balancing the desired final outcome against an f-divergence cost that measures departure from the original transition behavior.

From the framework’s optimality conditions, the authors derive reinforcement learning updates and reward-weighted regression objectives. The former include an f-divergence-regularized, PPO-style rule. The latter include a minimizer-preservation guarantee specifically under KL divergence. This connects practical fine-tuning objectives to a shared mathematical construction while retaining the stated condition on that guarantee.

The theory also motivates an implementation: express the optimal score as a fixed pretrained component plus a lightweight control correction. A side network learns that correction from exposed intermediate denoising outputs while the backbone remains frozen. On Stable Diffusion v1.4, supervised and reward-driven experiments report better preference-alignment win rates and quality–efficiency trade-offs than gray-box baselines and LoRA. The results support adapting generation through a limited interface to the pretrained model.
summary.tldr: DiffCon derives diffusion fine-tuning algorithms and a frozen-backbone side network from a unified stochastic-control formulation.

title: Diffusion Controller: Framework, Algorithms and Parameterization

abstract: Model robustness against natural image corruptions is essential for safety-critical applications. While existing methods primarily focus on implicit representation learning, we provide the first systematic exploration of computational pathways to explicitly characterize internal robustness. We identify a progressive decay of robust features across network layers and establish a functional dependency between the prevalence of these features and model performance. To exploit these insights, we propose Suppress and Diversify (S&D), a non-intrusive refinement approach that enhances robustness by dynamically selecting robust pathways and diversifying them through symmetry-preserving transformations. S&D is architecture-agnostic, parameter-free, and incurs zero test-time overhead. Extensive evaluations across eight benchmarks demonstrate that S&D consistently improves performance across multiple vision tasks, diverse backbones, and complex real-world scenarios, highlighting its broad efficacy and scalability.

The authors identify a progressive decline in robust features through those layers and establish a functional relationship between their prevalence and model performance.

They also show that explicitly refining those routes can improve evaluated performance across varied settings, rather than relying only on implicit representation learning.
summary.tldr: Suppress and Diversify improves corruption robustness by selecting and diversifying robust computational pathways without extra parameters or test-time overhead.

title: Suppress and Diversify: Refining Robust Pathways for Corruption Robustness

abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that learned representations from models trained on different modalities converge to a shared latent structure of the world. However, this hypothesis has largely been examined in vision and language, and it remains unclear whether time series participate in such convergence. We first examine this in a trimodal setting and find that independently pretrained time series, vision, and language encoders exhibit near-orthogonal geometry in the absence of explicit coupling. We then apply post-hoc alignment by training projection heads over frozen encoders using contrastive learning, and analyze the resulting representations with respect to geometry, scaling behavior, and dependence on information density and input modality characteristics. Our investigation reveals that overall alignment in contrastive representation spaces improves with model size, but this alignment is asymmetric: time series align more strongly with visual representations than with text, and images can act as effective intermediaries between time series and language. We further see that richer textual descriptions improve alignment only up to a threshold; training on denser captions does not lead to further improvement. Analogous effects are observed for visual representations. Our findings shed light on considerations for building multimodal systems involving non-conventional data modalities beyond vision and language. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/tvl-alignment.

This extends a hypothesis usually studied in vision and language to a third modality. The authors first find that independently pretrained encoders have nearly orthogonal representation geometry when there is no explicit coupling between them.

summary.tldr: Explicit contrastive alignment connects time series, vision, and language unevenly, with images providing a stronger bridge and richer descriptions helping only up to a threshold.

title: Time Series, Vision, and Language: Exploring the Limits of Alignment in Contrastive Representation Spaces

abstract: Grading in large undergraduate STEM courses often yields minimal feedback due to heavy instructional workloads. We present a large-scale empirical study of AI grading on real, handwritten single-variable calculus work from the University of California, Irvine. Using OCR-conditioned large language models with structured, rubric-guided prompting, our system produces scores and formative feedback for thousands of handwritten, in-person proctored free-response quiz submissions from nearly 800 students included in the paper’s empirical analysis. In a setting with no single ground-truth label, we evaluate performance against official teaching-assistant grades, student surveys, and independent human review, finding strong alignment with TA scoring and a large majority of AI-generated feedback rated correct or acceptable across quizzes. Beyond calculus, this setting highlights core challenges in OCR-conditioned mathematical reasoning and partial-credit assessment. We analyze key failure modes, propose practical rubric- and prompt-design principles, and introduce a multi-perspective evaluation protocol for reliable real-course deployment. Building on the dataset and evaluation framework developed here, we outline a path toward a future standardized benchmark for AI grading of handwritten mathematics to support reproducible evaluation, transparent comparison, reliable deployment, and future research.

paragraphs: This study examines AI grading on real handwritten calculus work from the University of California, Irvine. Its motivation is practical: large undergraduate courses create heavy grading workloads, often leaving students with little feedback. The empirical analysis covers thousands of in-person, proctored quiz submissions from nearly 800 students.

The system combines optical character recognition with language models prompted to follow structured grading rubrics. It produces both scores and formative feedback. Because the setting has no single definitive ground-truth grade, the researchers evaluate it from several perspectives: official teaching-assistant scores, student surveys, and independent human review.

The study finds strong agreement with teaching-assistant scoring, while a large majority of generated feedback is judged correct or acceptable across quizzes. It also examines failure modes and develops rubric and prompt-design principles. The evaluation framework addresses the combined challenges of reading handwriting, reasoning about mathematics, and assigning partial credit. A standardized benchmark is presented as a future direction built on this work.
summary.tldr: A large study of handwritten calculus grading finds strong agreement with teaching assistants and broadly acceptable feedback using rubric-guided language models.

title: Evaluating AI Grading on Real-World Handwritten College Mathematics: A Large-Scale Study Toward a Benchmark

abstract: Geometric properties can be leveraged to stabilize and speed reinforcement learning. Existing examples include encoding symmetry structure, geometry-aware data augmentation, and enforcing structural restrictions. In this paper, we take a novel view of RL through the lens of order theory and recast value function estimates into learning a desired poset (partially ordered set). We propose GCR-RL (Geometric Coherence Regularized Reinforcement Learning) that computes a sequence of super-poset refinements – by refining posets in previous steps and learning additional order relationships from temporal difference signals – thus ensuring geometric coherence across the sequence of posets underpinning the learned value functions. Two novel algorithms by Q-learning and by actor–critic are developed to efficiently realize these super-poset refinements. Their theoretical properties and convergence rates are analyzed. We empirically evaluate GCR-RL in a range of tasks and demonstrate significant improvements in sample efficiency and stable performance over strong baselines.

paragraphs: This paper approaches reinforcement learning through the ordering relationships behind value estimates. A value function expresses how desirable different situations or choices are. The authors recast its estimation as learning a partially ordered set, which represents ordering relationships without requiring every pair of elements to be comparable.

Their method, GCR-RL, builds a sequence of increasingly refined order structures. Each step refines the preceding structure and learns additional relationships from temporal-difference signals, which capture discrepancies used to update value estimates. The process maintains geometric coherence across the evolving structures. The authors develop both a Q-learning algorithm and an actor–critic algorithm to implement these refinements efficiently.

The paper analyzes theoretical properties and convergence rates, then evaluates the approach across a range of tasks. Experiments report significant sample-efficiency improvements and stable performance against strong baselines. The contribution is a way to organize value learning around consistent relationships across updates, connecting the structure of the learned estimates with how efficiently and stably reinforcement learning progresses.
summary.tldr: GCR-RL refines partial-order structures underlying value functions to improve reinforcement-learning sample efficiency and stability.

title: Geometric Coherence Learning for Structuring Value Functions in Plain MDPs

abstract: Building generalist robot policies that can handle diverse tasks in open-ended environments is a central challenge in robotics. To leverage knowledge from large-scale pretraining, prior work (VLA) has typically built generalist policies either on top of vision-language models (VLMs) or generative models. However, both semantic understanding from vision-language pretraining and visual dynamics modeling from visual-generation pretraining are crucial for embodied robots. Recent unified models of generation and understanding have demonstrated strong capabilities in both comprehension and generation through large-scale pretraining. We posit that robotic policy learning can likewise benefit from the combined strengths of understanding, planning and continuous future representation learning. Building on this insight, we introduce UniJEPA, which acquires the ability to dynamically model high-dimensional visual features through pretraining on over 1M internet-scale instructional manipulation videos. Subsequently, UniJEPA is fine-tuned on data collected from the robot embodiment, enabling the learning of mappings from predictive representations to action tokens. Extensive experiments show our approach consistently outperforms baseline methods in terms of 9% and 12% across simulation environments and real-world out-of-distribution tasks.

paragraphs: UniJEPA explores how generalist robot policies can combine semantic understanding with predictions about visual change. Prior approaches commonly build on either vision-language models or generative models. The paper argues that robots can benefit from both forms of pretraining knowledge, bringing understanding, planning, and continuous future representations into the same policy-learning approach.

The model first learns to dynamically represent high-dimensional visual features from more than one million internet instructional manipulation videos. It is then fine-tuned using data from the robot embodiment. This second stage connects predictive representations to discrete action tokens, translating information about visual futures into actions suited to the robot.

The authors report consistent improvements over baselines, with gains of 9% in simulation environments and 12% on real-world out-of-distribution tasks. The findings support the proposed combination of continuous predictive learning and discrete action generation in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a route from broad video pretraining to embodiment-specific control that draws on both visual dynamics and semantic understanding.
summary.tldr: UniJEPA learns predictive visual representations from manipulation videos and maps them to robot actions, improving simulated and real-world performance.

title: UniJEPA: Enhancing Robot Policy via Unified Continuous and Discrete Representation Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown significant potential in scientific discovery but struggle to bridge the gap between theoretical reasoning and verifiable physical simulation. Existing solutions operate in a passive "execute-then-response" loop and thus lack runtime perception, obscuring agents to transient anomalies (e.g., numerical instability or diverging oscillations). To address this limitation, we propose EmbodiedAct, a framework that transforms established scientific software into active embodied agents by grounding LLMs in embodied actions with a tight perception-execution loop. We instantiate EmbodiedAct within MATLAB and evaluate it on complex engineering design and scientific modeling tasks. Extensive experiments show that EmbodiedAct significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving SOTA performance by ensuring satisfactory reliability and stability in long-horizon simulations and enhanced accuracy in scientific modeling.

paragraphs: Scientific reasoning becomes more useful when an agent can connect its proposals to the behavior of a running simulation. Existing approaches often execute software and wait for a response, leaving the agent without perception during execution. This can obscure transient problems such as numerical instability or oscillations that begin to diverge while the simulation is running.

EmbodiedAct connects language models to established scientific software through a tight perception-execution loop. The framework treats interaction with the software as embodied action, making runtime perception part of how the agent operates. Its purpose is to close the gap between theoretical reasoning and verifiable simulation by keeping the agent connected to the evolving computational process.

The authors implement the framework in MATLAB and evaluate it on complex engineering design and scientific modeling tasks. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, improved modeling accuracy, and satisfactory reliability and stability over long simulations. These findings support active interaction with scientific software as a useful ingredient in agents that must reason through extended simulation workflows.
summary.tldr: EmbodiedAct connects language-model agents to runtime simulation feedback, improving scientific modeling and long-horizon simulation performance in MATLAB evaluations.

title: Grounding LLMs in Scientific Discovery via Embodied Actions

abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have significantly improved visual quality, yet ultra-high-resolution (UHR) video generation remains a formidable challenge due to the compounded difficulties of motion modeling, semantic planning, and detail synthesis. To address these limitations, we propose LUVE, a Latent-cascaded UHR Video generation framework built upon dual frequency Experts. LUVE employs a three-stage architecture comprising low-resolution motion generation for motion-consistent latent synthesis, video latent upsampling that performs resolution upsampling directly in the latent space to mitigate memory and computational overhead, and high-resolution content refinement that integrates low-frequency and high-frequency experts to jointly enhance semantic coherence and fine-grained detail generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our LUVE achieves superior photorealism and content fidelity in UHR video generation, and comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component.

LUVE employs a three-stage architecture comprising low-resolution motion generation for motion-consistent latent synthesis, video latent upsampling that performs resolution upsampling directly in the latent space to mitigate memory and computational overhead, and high-resolution content refinement that integrates low-frequency and high-frequency experts to jointly enhance semantic coherence and fine-grained detail generation. paragraphs: Ultra-high-resolution video generation must coordinate motion, meaningful content, and fine visual detail. These demands compound because increasing resolution does not remove the need for coherent movement and consistent semantics. LUVE addresses the combined problem with a staged pipeline that works through latent representations and assigns different responsibilities to successive parts of the generation process.

The first stage generates motion-consistent latents at low resolution. The second increases resolution directly in latent space, aiming to reduce memory and computation overhead. The third refines high-resolution content using low-frequency and high-frequency experts. Together, these experts support semantic coherence and detailed visual synthesis, linking the broad content of a video with its finer appearance.

Experiments report superior photorealism and content fidelity in ultra-high-resolution generation. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of each component. The stated findings favor a coordinated cascade in which motion generation, latent upsampling, and frequency-based refinement each contribute to the final result, rather than treating resolution increase as an isolated generation problem.
summary.tldr: LUVE combines low-resolution motion generation, latent upsampling, and dual-frequency refinement to improve ultra-high-resolution video quality.

abstract: We present an overview of FAB-MAP, an algorithm for place recognition and mapping developed for infrastructure-free mobile robot navigation in large environments. The system allows a robot to identify when it is revisiting a previously seen location, on the basis of imagery captured by the robot's camera. We outline a complete probabilistic framework for the task, which is applicable even in visually repetitive environments where many locations may appear identical. Our work introduces a number of technical innovations - notably we demonstrate that place recognition performance can be improved by learning an approximation to the joint distribution over visual elements. We also investigate several principled approaches to making the system robust in visually repetitive environments, and define an efficient bail-out strategy for multi-hypothesis testing to improve system speed. Our model has been shown to substantially outperform standard tf-idf ranking on our task of interest. We demonstrate the system performing reliable online appearance mapping and loop closure detection over a 1,000km trajectory, with mean filter update times of 14 ms.

paragraphs: FAB-MAP lets a mobile robot recognize previously visited places from camera images, supporting navigation and mapping in large environments without installed infrastructure. A central challenge is visual repetition: different locations can look alike. The paper presents an overview of a probabilistic framework designed to handle place recognition even under that ambiguity.

One technical contribution is learning an approximation to the joint distribution of visual elements. This makes relationships among those elements part of the recognition model, and the authors demonstrate improved place recognition performance. They also investigate approaches for robustness in repetitive environments and introduce an efficient early-exit strategy for testing multiple hypotheses.

The model substantially outperforms standard tf-idf ranking on the place recognition task studied. The authors demonstrate reliable online appearance mapping and loop closure detection over a 1,000-kilometer trajectory, with mean filter updates of 14 milliseconds. These results connect the probabilistic modeling choices to both recognition quality and the speed needed to process observations during a robot's journey.
summary.tldr: FAB-MAP uses probabilistic visual modeling for reliable camera-based place recognition, demonstrated over 1,000 kilometers with 14-millisecond mean filter updates.

title: FAB-MAP: Appearance-Based Place Recognition and Mapping using a Learned Visual Vocabulary Model
